PROCEEDINGS
Interview with John Simmons, June 29, 1976. John, where were you born?
Haskell, Oklahoma.
And what date?
And how long did you live in Haskell?

I was on the farm three years, and I left there and went to Muskogee, Oklahoma. And my first memory of a band was Everett Jackson, who was a sousaphone bass player, and the reason that I can remember it so well, by this wrapping around his head, I thought he was being tortured.
How old were you?

Oh, about four or five. However, there were a couple of other bands in the city. But I could never get him out of my mind. So I've inquired through my mother what the other two bands were in town. I'll come up with them before the interview is over with.

However, we stayed there two years and migrated to Kansas City, Missouri. And my mother was a dance fanatic. And during those days, you know, they didn't have babysitters, so I had to go to the dance with her. And she'd sit me on the bandstand and the musicians were drinking gallons of whisky over their shoulder, and the elderly women would grab me off the bandstand and dance me around the hall, and sit me down. And
generally, these dances were called food shows.
Why was that?

Well, food shows -- food contests -- they would bake pies and cakes, and have it on the banquet table down in the everyone would center, and they'd dance around. Now, the two bands -- leading bands at that time that were stationed in Kansas City was George E. Georgie Lee, who had a sister named Julia Lee. She sang, and later she formed a combo of her own and recorded out of here for Capitol. Benny Moten Benny Morton. Benny had a hell of a band. He wasn't a taskmaster, but he had a good band. I liked his band George E. George E. better than Georgie Lee. Georgie Lee centered his band on his singing, and those days they'd sing through the microphones, you know, like Rudy Vallee.

Anyway, during my stay in Kansas City from -- let's see, '25 to '29, bands came through there such as the McKinney Cottonpickers, Zach Jack Whyte, Jack Allen's Cottonpickers, the Blues Serenaders, the Rice Brothers from Milwaukee, Zilver Randolph, who later I met in Chicago, in the '30s after I became a musician myself. However, I worked for him in Chicago.

Who else came through there? Oh. Barron Lee. It was a band out of, say, something like the Southern part of the South. I don't know exactly which state. Then there was Carmite Thompson, who was a trumpet player out of Dallas, Texas. He was a rather young man. And these bands I heard constantly, like, weekends on the domestics' nights off.

Then, we went back to Oklahoma in '29. And these same bands was coming through Oklahoma. And when I got to Oklahoma, I ran into the bands of Alphonso Trent, Clyde Love, no, Clarence Love, what's this other -- Tee Holder. And the local bands, which was two, one and two -- of course, there were others, but the number one band was Ernie Fields. And he had a trumpet player with him then -- this was like '31. And this kid was 21, and his father was a bandmaster and had a band of his own. His name was Fred Skinner. And he had taught his son trumpet. And he played high notes like Cat Anderson does today. And his (laughs) horn was taped up with tape, gum. However, he died an early death. He was in Dakota, Deadwood, North Dakota. And it was very cold, and he was wearing long johns. And he washed them out that night, and he had to leave before they dried out. And he put them back on, and got what I guess they call lobar pneumonia. Died overnight.
Then another --
Who were you acquainted with in the bands? Were you acquainted with any of the members of the bands?
Yes, but his name rang out the most. I don't have a total recall of -- yes, there was a Basil Stone, a trumpet player, who turned out to be a preacher in St. Louis,
In which band?
In the same band that Dart Skinner, Ned Skinner's son, the one that played the high notes, and -- let's see, they had a tenor

player, I think. They called him "Big Stack." I never knew his real name. And a couple of other fellows. I know their name, but I can't call them. I'm having a mental block. I can see them, but I can't call it.

All right. They had another band there called Al Denny, like, he took the jobs that Ernie Fields wasn't able to fulfill. You know, he was otherwise engaged. And then we had a school band that was out of sight. It was the Rhythm Aces. And then there was a band out of -- the Young band, the Grey Brothers. One of them years later married [Leomin] Lewis, who was a pianist and sang. She was a single.
Do you remember the Grey Brothers' first names?

I can't think of them right now. And, at the same time, Walter Page, who was Count Basie's left hand, had a band of his own, in Oklahoma City. And he was playing Benny Moten bass saxophone. So, now, April 1st is when Billy Morton died from a tonsillectomy. They severed an artery, and he hemorrhaged to death. And, meanwhile, I was hoboeing out here. I got to Amarillo and got the word.

Walter Page gave up his band. The band's name was the Blue Devils. And Count Basie organized a band that was broadcasting from the Reno Club. And he had mostly members of Benny Moten Billy Morton's band. So he -- Walter Page joined Count Basie
and started playing string bass.
That was the first time he started playing string bass was when he joined Count Basie?
Yes, as far as my knowledge. And -- what else?
I think you mentioned, when we were talking earlier, that about that time there were only three bands in the country that had string bass...
Oh, yes. Yes, yes. Wellman Brough was with Duke. Pops Foster with Louis Armstrong and Walter Bigham Page with Count Basie.
And did all those bands come through when you were --

Yes. I had a friend around my age, we were both about 11 or 12, I guess, about this time. And his uncle owned a hotel, Small's, and when the bands would come to town, they didn't have a rehearsal hall, you know, like dance hall, they'd rehearse there. And they couldn't read. And the saxophone section would get in one room, and harmonize and set riffs -- that's what they called it in those days. And the trumpet players would get in another room. Trombone players would get in another room. And that afternoon for the dance, they would get there an hour early and hook it up.
So one afternoon, I was out to Barry's Park, where -- I forget who, or -- and Lips Page was playing at that time.

I think it was Benny Morton. And the young lady called me to the door and said, "Little boy, would you give this note to Lips Page?" I say, "Yes'm." And I walked up to the bandstand. I said, "Lady there at the door sent this letter to Mr. Warm Jaws." (laughs)

Everybody in the band fell out in hysterics. Lips got mad. Now, to take you -- when I met Lips in New York, when I got on the same bandstand with him, I said, "What note was that, Mr. Warm Jaws?" And he jumped up and said, "I'll knock you down." He said, "I've only been called that once in my life." I say, "That was me." Small's Hotel
was in --
In Tulsa.
In Tulsa.
Yes. Now, all the bands that came through there, that was their thing. I had the privilege of hearing Louis Armstrong's Hot Five there. And you say, just to speak of any musicians?
Uh-huh.

I had the privilege of playing in the high school band for the benefit of John Philip Sousa. They had a parade of high school bands in Tulsa, Oklahoma. I didn't win any awards, but I played for him. That's a lot that quite a few people can't say.
What year was that?
That was around '33, '34. '33 or '34. Because I had just been playing about two years.
And what were you playing?
Trumpet.
That was the instrument you started on?
Un-huh.
At what age did you start playing?
Well, let's see, I was in junior high school. I guess about 14 or 15. But that wasn't my first instrument.
What was your first instrument?
You'll die. It was a fiddlette.
Fiddlette?
A fiddlette.
would you describe that instrument?

The instrument was about four feet wide -- I mean, not four feet, four inches wide and about four inches in depth. But the bottom was vacant. It doesn't have a back on it. This was for beginners for violin class. So, my mother bought me one and I couldn't stand that squeaking. And I left it in my locker all the time. I missed all my classes. So my mother says, "When are you going to bring your violin home and let me hear you play it?" I say, "Well, I'll bring it home when I think that I can play it to satisfy you." And meantime, I had sold it. Four months before then. Fiddlette! (laughs)

So, how I started playing trumpet. Earl Bostic was a very gifted young man. He would appear on Saturday night, amateur shows, you know, and he'd play the part of Harold Teen. He had the big leg pants and he'd whistle and play ukelele. win first prize And he'd always (unintelligible). So, he was a Catholic, but he was going to public school, because our Catholic school didn't go any further than about sixth grade. But they had instruments.

So the church gave Earl a clarinet so that he could play in the public school band. And Earl picked it up in no time, and he got a scholarship to Xavier University in New Orleans. And when he graduated, he graduated and stayed on as bandmaster for about two years, and he left there and he went New York.

When he got the clarinet, I wanted to be a saxophone player. So I went over and asked them for a saxophone. I was a Catholic, too, at that time. They didn't have any saxophones. All they had left was trumpets. I said, "Well, give me that."
So that's how I played trumpet. All through school, I started on the fourth part and when I finished school, I was a soloist. I passed from the first trumpet to the soloist spot.
What was the name of the high school you want to (in Tulsa)?
In Tulsa, Booker T. Washington High. [George Washington] Then I went to Carver Junior High. That's the same year he
was, you know, acclaimed for the peanut. And they started naming schools after him. And then I went back to Booker T. High, to high school.
And that was a high school band you were in when you marched past Sousa?

Yeah. And my bandmaster was out of sight. He played baritone horn. He was a sergeant in the Army. And he had charge of the band, also. And he had the most beautiful tone on the baritone you have ever heard. And he could play it and you could hear him for almost two miles. He's here, now, but he's a reverend. He gave up music. He had a bad thing to happen to him domestically in Oklahoma. He quit the band and left. And joined the church.
What's his name?

William Jett. Then there was a orchestra leader at school named Charles Grimm. And I asked him to let me play bass for him, because one boy had graduated from his class, named Rufus -- I can't remember Rufus' last name. He played bass and trombone. He went to Kansas City. And Charles Hadnott-- William Hadnott, what am I saying, Charles Hadnott the bass player that's out here now? He went to Kansas City, he didn't even finish school. He dropped out to go to Kansas City to play bass.
Then there was another boy, named Robert Lewis who came out here. He was later known to be called Baby Boy. He
worked with Lorenzo Flournoy's trio for a long while.

The next one to leave was a kid named Commodore Clark. And he was younger than I was, but he had been hanging around the orchestra room and picked up some pointers on his own, you know. He felt as though he could do it. So he left town. He dropped out at an early age.

And going back to this boy's uncle's hotel, I told you, it used to be? He turned out to be a bass player. His name was Thurber Daisy. He worked with Louis Jordan for a long while. Thurber. He was almost full Indian. He lives up here around Fresno now, houseful of kids.
When did you decide you wanted to be a professional musician?

Well, on graduation day, the 18th of June, everyone -- all the males, the male graduates, were supposed to have white suits and white shoes. I'd had my white suit made up, sharkskin, Continental Tailoring, on Fifth Street. Mother gave me money to get my white shoes. Instead of me getting the white shoes, on lunch hour I went across the street on the Island, got down and started shooting some dice. Lost my shoe money. And when time come for the exercise, I'm in there, playing my solo with black shoes on. I'm the only one in the room with black shoes on. You know what she did to me.
So the next day, my jive cousin, he was a booking agent, he says, 'I need a bass player. We're going to Tempe with a show. I'm taking a show up. I'm taking some chorus
girls and a band." I say, "I'll take the job," because I'd had this little experience with the Woodman Brothers. He said, "Where you going to get a bass?" I say, "I don't know."

So one of my mother's boyfriends' thieving friends broke in a doctor's car and stole a cello. " Baby , I got just what you need, just what you need." He come in with this cello. I say, "Oh, man, that ain't no bass. That's a cello." He went and threw it in the ocean. I wish I had it now.
Did you get a bass for the job?

Finally, he traced down a bass, a very small bass, that some fellow had bought and hadn't touched it in about three years. It was in his closet. He had just forgotten about playing music. In fact, he didn't even start.
And so he came back to my mother and gave her a price on the bass and said a certain amount would be taken out of my salary and sent back to pay for the bass.

So the first job was Tempe, Arizona. Outdoors, in the dead of summer. And those gollywhipper mosquitoes. And we were wearing short shirts. I slapped one, you know, slapped the bass, and slap myself, too.

Now, at that time, notes weren't really required to come out of a bass violin, 'cause they were slapping the bass, you know, single slap, double slap, triple slap, spin the bass. [Corner] It was a personality you know. So I said, "Well, I'll get on the bass on the ground floor because there's a whole lot
of trumpet players and trombone players and saxophone players, so I'll try to get in on the ground floor."
So come to find out my cousin was charging me more than I was supposed to be paying. So I quit and came home and organized my own group, that quick.
Playing bass or trumpet?

Base. And I had played three months, and that was an after-hours spot in Sacramento at that particular time that was looking for a band. So I went up to Sacramento. I took four pieces. After hours This is funny. And in Sacramento, at that time, maybe even still, they only had silver dollars and two-dollar bills. And at 12:00 at night, when other places would close, every one would come over where we were. And I'm just dead tired. I'm having hallucinations about pillows and mattresses and things. Why don't these people go home?

And we had a kitty sit in front of the bandstand with one of those old graphonola contr welded to a box. And our salary was guaranteed $25 a week. And if the kitty didn't make it, the owner put the rest with it.

However, the gamblers were there, and they would get in the back and bet how many silver dollars they could throw in the kitty from where they were standing. Baby, At the end of the night, there'd be two or three hundred dollars in the kitty. And before we'd get off, though, I'd be so tired, I'd have to
sit down on the level of the bass drum, and play my bass, one note. One note, and one hand in the kitty.
So whatever I stole, we divided it between the band.
Otherwise, the house would have gotten it?
Yeah. So at the end of the week, I imagine we had made about seven, eight hundred dollars apiece, from me stealing.

Then we had a radio show, KFBK, I think, was the station, and it was sort of a minstrel thing. Like Uncle Tom? And my name was Blimp. And we had this show to do every day. So we were just making money all over. And my feet were swollen, because I was never getting any sleep. And --
What did you do in the daytime?
I was doing the radio show.
Oh.

So I'm just dying. I bought all kind of shoes, all colors. When I got back to Los Angeles, and slept about a week, didn't one pair of those shoes fit because my feet had been so swollen up there. [PAUSE]

Back to this job in Sacramento, there was another night club that stayed open a little later than us. It was the Club Eureka. I forget the bandleader's name. But there were two marvelous musicians, tenor saxophone player named George Neely, out of Oklahoma City, and a trumpet player,
migrated from Kansas City, his name was Flowers. Can't recall his first name. But he had a drinking problem.

After getting back to Los Angeles, and my foot episode, I got another job as a bandleader. And in this job, I had a tenor saxophone player named Hank Full i love, who wrote books, Western books, and no one knew it. And he was getting royalties all the time, during that time. And the piano player was George Crawford, that has a duo, he and a Grand Mason here in Los Angeles. He worked with me. And the drummer's name was Bob Brown.
Now, this was at a Philippino night club, on Third Street, between -- what is it? Spring and Main?
The two streets are a block apart?

Yeah. So we had to be there at 9:00 o'clock. We'd get there at 9:00, and we had to wait until the taxi dancers were over. You know, a dime a dance? And then they would all come. Now, all of them spoke different dialects. Severine Garcia was there every night with his entourage. And, say about midway the night's work, chairs and tables would be flying.
Who was he?

He was a great pugilist. He was the one that Henry Armstrong took the title away from. He was the originator of the bolo punch that Kid Gavilan used to throw all the time. But he was a tough customer. And there would be fighting. So when they'd start fighting, we'd just go back in the empty
room and start shooting dice.
Well, this was still just, what, a year after you'd gotten out of high school, right?

Yeah. So then I left there and went to Central Avenue and started to work for Curtis Moseby at the Apex Club? (WILLARD: The Apex Club?) (SIMMONS: no, what was the name of the club? Nemo.) (WILLARD: The Nemo Lounge.) Yeah. Well, now, Curtis Moseby was a bandleader. Curtis Moseby and his Blues Blowers.
This was about what year?
Oh, years ago.
But, anyway, you joined Curtis Moseby.
I was the contractor of the jobs, and he would collect the money. And no one got paid in the band but Oscar Moore and myself.
This was about what? 1932, '33, or what?
This was '38.
I thought this was still shortly after high school.
Well, no, I'd been to Chicago and come back out here. He had a large band put together and we worked on the pier at Long Beach. And we would have midnight brunch. When? Oh, about 17.
Who all was with the band?
Gaughy Cousby Roberts, alto saxophone player, King Cole's Oscar Moore, guitarist, Singold's first guitar player, a piano

player named Leslie Franklin, drummer, called him Byron Weasel, Walter Mer- ton, and one of the Brooks Brothers, Alfred Brooks, played trumpet. I can't recall all the -- but no one in that band got paid but Oscar and I.
Why?
Curtis just wouldn't pay them.
They just kept playing without pay?

Two weeks. He just kept giving them [Mime] stories, and then I went back to the Moemoe, the four pieces. Then my next job was in San Diego, at the -- what is it? The hotel nightclub downstairs. Ramsey owned the hotel. I'm trying to think of the club that was downstairs. What's the name of it? Well, anyway, I worked in the club, and the leader of the group was a pianist named Nat Walker. And then we had Wee Willie, the alto player that worked with the Honeydrippers, and the drummer's name was Daniels, can't remember his first name. And that was the group.

Then something happened to Nat, and he wigged out. He says, "Why didn't you all let me know that you didn't want me to be the leader of the band?" So they had to send him back to Los Angeles. They sent the Honeydripper down to take his place, and he took the band over. And the drummer left, and Davey Lewis, out of Kansas City, he was the drummer. He played drums, trumpet, two-finger piano like Lionel Hampton, and the vibes. And through the years, there's been a contro-

versy whether he taught Hamp or not. He says, 'Johnnie says, "There's some people over here I want you to meet." I say, "Yeah, okay." I went over and he says, "John Simmons, I want you to meet John Hammond." Well, I'd never heard of John Hammond, and the trade papers at that time wasn't the DownBeat, it was the Tempo. And I get a wire about three days later to appear at the Old Brunswick recording studios, over here on Weston, for a record date. At that time, Benny Goodman was out here to make "Hollywood Hotel."'

So I showed up. Baby Davey Lewis went with me, he was going to play drums on the date. And who am I there with? Teddy Wilson on piano, Red Norvo on vibes, Harry James on trumpet, Baby Davey Lewis and myself. And I don't know what I'm doing. And people are telling me what a great bass player I am.
So, all right, we make this date. Went back to San Diego --
Was it at San Diego you met John Hammond?
Yes. The next week I get another wire, come back for another date.

Now, the first date, it's a collector's item. Just a blues, a blues in two part. Said, "Tell Baby Davey sorry, we can't use him." And Baby Davey being alcoholic, too, he went back to Kansas City and committed suicide.
(Inaudible) Because of that?

Yes. It hurt him. So, I said, "Well, everyone sound great. I'm going back East, into the competition and see what is happening." 'Cause I didn't know what was happening. I wanted to go to New York, but every record that I heard that come out of New York, the soloists sounded like they were playing snakes, so I got cold feet and stopped in Chicago.

And my first job was with Lil Armstrong. And she was on one end -- we were playing the Bacon's Casino. And she was on one end of the bandstand, and the tenor player and the trumpet player and the drummer player was over on the other end of the bandstand. So I'm standing up there by her.
So Roy Eldridge just made this helluva record, "After You're Gone." It was a thing that Louis Armstrong sent him a wire from Europe, saying, "You're the greatest."

So Roy was working at the Three Deuces at that time in Chicago. But the more I listened to him, I'd say, "That dude sure sound like Roy Eldridge, but he's at the Deuces." So intermission comes, they all gathered over there and they were doing their thing, I sat over there by Lil Armstrong, and they called me over and they introduced themselves. So Roy says, "I'm Little Jazz."
Now, I don't know anything about Little Jazz. All I know is Roy Eldridge, you know. Saxophone player was Harold "Dee" Leon Washington. The drummer was West. So my E string

broke. Left me playing with three strings. And this excited Roy. Oh, he just started dancing all over the bandstand. Say, "Man, come on and go down ever to my job with me." I say, "Your job?" He say, "Yeah, down at the Three Deuces." And then I almost fainted.

So I went down there, and as I said, I used to give Art Tatum a fit, 'cause every time I'd pick up a bass, and he was playing, he'd get up, without even looking at me, 'cause I was out of tune, everything was wrong.

So Roy said (unintelligible). I went up to the bandstand, took the base. First note, Art got up, he didn't have to look up, he knew who it was. So I stayed around there, and I worked with a wonderful musician, a bandleader, four pieces combo -- Les Wilcox. He could write and arrange individual parts. He could write music like you would write a letter, in long-hand. No score. This is the first time I had ever seen anything like that. He liked me. And they didn't have a bass player. So I'd go over there and sit, play with them every night. Didn't have a dime. Waitress would feed me one night, bartender would feed me another, band would feed me one night. They would take turns.
So then I worked with bands such as Tony Fambrough, Danny Williams, Johnny Long, black Johnny Long, not the white Johnny Long. He was a trumpet player and a cosmetologist.
This was in Chicago?
Yeah. Tiny Parham, Erskine Tate, Charles Elgar. I'm sure there's more. John Letmann -- that's where Ray Nance was working the floor show when he joined Duke. dope.
That was what club?
Joe Hughes' Club De Luxe. 63rd and South Park. And Johnny Letmann had the band. So Roy came in town.

Now, the local Negroes couldn't work in the Loop without Petrillo's permission. He wasn't about to give his permission, even some of the jobs on the West Side we had to petition for, to get his permission. So Roy says, "I'm opening at the Capital Lounge." That was right next door to the Capital Theatre. I said, "What? Going downtown? Oh, goody, goody, goody, goody."
So we had a good time down there. So when that job was over --
How long did that last?
About four months. So, --
Who else was playing with you?

A drummer by the name of Kansas Fields, Carl Fields is his name, we called him Kansas. He left here Sidney Bechet with Cindy Shea. Dave Young, tenor player that worked with Roy at the Three Deuces, and Rozelle Claxton, beautiful piano player. And Roy had his own tunes and he and

Claxton collaborated on a tune and everyone would ask us what the name of it was, and we'd say, "Nothing yet." And Krupa was appearing at the Sherman Hotel at the time. He had come over there as soon as he got off, 'cause he and Roy were great friends.

So when that job ended, Roy joined Krupa. So Charlie Sherrock had been trying to play like Roy all the time. So when Roy joined the band, Shorty quit. He says, "You got the real thing here now, what am I doing here?" So he left. So Roy renamed all of his tunes, and the tune that was "Nothing Yet," they named it "Ball of Fire." You remember the movie, "Ball of Fire?" That was the theme song. Claxton didn't get a dime.

So this leaves me hanging. Should I come back to California, 'cause I'd worked everywhere in Chicago and I was tired of these repeats. I said, shall I go to Chicago, go to California, or shall I go to New York. So I said, well, since I'm this close, the least I can do is go back to California.
I got to New York with 50 cents. I arrived in Chicago with 35 cents.
What year was this, when you first arrived in New York?
'41. So first thing off the bat, I got a job before I could deposit my transfer, with Stuff Smith. At Kelly's Stables. Then I worked with Frankie Newton.
Had you been acquainted with Smith before, or did they know you by reputation, or what?
No.
They weren't even familiar with your playing?
No. It's just that all New Yorkers figured themselves the greatest, you know, and they had heard me jam. That's how I got the jobs. So --
Where did you jam, in New York?
Yeah, yeah. So after Stuff Smith, I found Eddie Heywood with a trio, at the Village Vanguard. He didn't have a bass player so I'd sit down there every night.
Who was his drummer?
Little boy called Keg Parnell. He used to work with Benny Carter, that's the time that Eddie Heywood was with him. [PAUSE]
July 7, 1976. John, we just played back what we recorded so far, and I think there were a couple of things you wanted to correct, right?

Yes, after listening, I said that I migrated back to Tulsa from Kansas City in '39? It wasn't '39, it was '29. And the stint at Curtis May's (at The Nine) was -- it wasn't '38, it was '37. Before I went to San Diego.
How many clubs did Curtis Mos'by run?
Well, he had that one at that particular
time, then in later years he took over the Club Alabam. And then he had the Last Word. His wife did.
Before the Club Alabam was the Club Alabam, it was the Apex Club, and he ran that.
It was the Apex, yeah?
And I know that he was known as the Mayor of Central Avenue, probably because he ran most of the clubs in that block. Or, those two blocks.
Well, I didn't get out here until '35. When I got here, it was Alabam.
But there were at least three clubs, that he operated on Central Avenue. (unintelligible).
To my knowing.
With he and his wife.
Uh-huh.
I think you were telling me that you went to high school where?

I went to elementary school, Booker T. Washington in Tulsa, junior high school in Tulsa, up to my graduation, two months before graduation, well, I'll say this again for clarity. I went to elementary school in Tulsa, Booker T. Washington, Carver Junior High, and then Booker T. Washington High School, and I quit school because I had been in the hospital due to a football accident, and the doctors advised me that -- told me at that time that whenever you've got a knot
on your head, it doesn't go away, it goes to the weakest part of your body.

Well, me being the smallest man on the team, one of those big 200-pounders stepped on my instep and a knot swell up on it, and it went to my appendix. So I went to the hospital. No visitors, from any of who I thought were my friends. No one come to see me but my mother and my grandmother, they would alternate.

So when I went back to school, I had to make up some subjects. Grammar, math, so while I was in summer school I took up some extra subjects and passed my own class, when the regular season started. Boy, when I got out of the hospital, the teacher would say, "Oh, it's so good to see you back." I say, "Yeah, you jive --." And the rest of the kids, "Hey, hey, hey." I say, "Yeah, un-huh." I looked at all of them out of the corners of my eyes, you know, because I was a participant in all of the artistic things like acting, and literature, you know, we'd do skits on "Macbeth" in literature class. And we had a thing called "Popular Airs," everybody would sing a popular song of that year, and we'd have harmonica bands and had a quartet that aped the Mills Brothers, you know. I thought we was doing something, you know. I come back from the hospital and everybody cold-shouldered me, you know?
So I was in a hurry to get away from there, so I quit two months before graduation, I was -- had my cap and gown
measured, my class ring and pin picked up, and hoboed out here and I could have started to school immediately and graduated mid-term, but they wouldn't give me a diploma.
Why not?

Well, because I hadn't spent enough time in the school, six months, you know. So they sent to Oklahoma to get my credentials. Well, now, Art in Oklahoma was a half unit. Out here it was a full unit. And they only required something like 27 units to graduate from high school. (laughs) And I had 40-something. So I didn't have to do anything but go to my home room class in the morning, and check out in the afternoon, and I'd stay up all night, listening to musicians, and go to school, check in, go home and go to sleep and come back and check out, and I'm gone again.
Did you say you went to band class, though?
Yes, I'd hang out with the bandmaster, Colonel John L. Davis.
And that was at what high school?
Jefferson High.
And do you remember some of the musicians that you hung out listening to? At night?
Oh, yeah. Eddie Byas and Don Byas, Art Tatum, Al Morgan and Eddie Barefield had just left Cab Calloway out here; and some of the local musicians -- let's see,
the Irwin Brothers, they had a band, they played upstairs over the old burlesque theatre on Main, yeah, Downtown, L.A., The Follies, the
Burbank --?
The Burbank. They had a dance hall upstairs. The Irwin Brothers played up there.
What were the Irwin Brothers' first names?
Wow, I know them so well. We'll get it

And the band never took an intermission. One would get off at a time. Oh, and one of them, Chester, he played all of the instruments, and so he would relieve everyone, you know. So I went up there, a friend of mine named Lil Davis played trombone, he took me up there. But the regular bass player was a -- of Spanish descent, his name was Louis Gonzalez, I think. Or I might be mistaking him for the guitarist with King Cole.
Well, anyway, he was Spanish. And he would be glad to see me coming. And Chester would be glad to see me come, you know, because it would give him a chance to play some drums, sometimes, you know.
The band never took a break, but the musicians were relieved by other musicians, so the individual musicians could take a break.
No, they'd just get off one at a time, and Chester would jump in their seat. He was like a utility
man, you know. I can't remember the leader's name, the other brother.

Anyway, I'd go up there and play at night, you know, getting knowledge as I went, and by me being a kid they would all go to after hours spots, you know, buffet flats and things. Peoples' private homes, you know. And meet the girls that they'd met on the jobs, you know. I'd go home with them, but I never did anything, 'cause I was just a kid.
What were you, 17, 18?
Oh, well, I was early 18, looking forward to 19.
Where else did you hear music besides on Main Street?

Let's see, I can't remember this club. It was a gay club, on the northeast corner of Central Avenue, across the street from the Downbeat. And the Mason Brothers had the band there, the Grand Mason and his brother, they had the band. And then after hours spots, Tatum's place, the Apex, back there at the back, on the east side of the street -- no, the Apex is on Vernon, I'm sorry, the one on Central was Harry Bigelow's place. And I don't know what the name of it was.
Oh, I played with a band out here, a large band -- Happy Johnson. He was a trombone player, and -- how did that jump up in my mind? Happy Johnson.
At that period in your life? At that Age? Was that (inaudible)?
Yeah, yeah, yeah.
How big a band was it?
It was a large band, 17, 18 pieces.
Do you remember --
But I was beginning to get notes out of it then.
Who else played in it?

Roy White, Roy "Snake" White, he used to play with Zack White's band, and he played trumpet. But his career came to an early end, because he was the kind that liked to fight police when he got drunk. And invariably, he'd get hit in his mouth, so he lost his embouchure. But he could still arrange. And he had a son, this is a sort of a drag. His son was out to this place where they send you for the drug cure, drug hospital.
You mean nowadays? Synanon?
Yeah, now.
No. Out towards Riverside, out there where -- anyway, his son had been in the Army, and he had turned a narcotic addict, and they had a riot out there one night, and the police shot and killed him.
Anyway, getting back to the musical scene, who did I hear? There was a drummer named Blimp -- can't remember Blimp's last name. Dennis was a baritone saxophone player. Arthur
And he had a brother played trumpet, I can't remember his name, first name, presently. And --
You mentioned hearing Don Byas in Los Angeles. You had known Don Byas in Oklahoma, hadn't you?
Yes. I was supposed to audition for Don as a trumpet player, and before I could get to the audition, he went off and left the band. Dropped out of the university.
That was when you were still in Oklahoma.
Yes.
And you knew him when you were living in which town in Oklahoma?
Tulsa. But he was from Muskogee. And --

You lived in Muskogee when you were very, very young. SIMMONS: He was known as Don Carlos. That was his middle name. Don Carlos and the Langston Wildcats. And later he dropped the Carlos when he become professional, and made it Don Byas.
And so you met him in Tulsa when he played there with his band?
No. I had a couple of occasions to go to Langston University with what they called the Hi-Y, the Boys organization. And I heard the band there.
At Langston University.
Yeah.
Which was --
Around '33.
So did you see much or hear much of Byas while you were in Tulsa? How did you come to be (inaudible) being preparing to audition for him?

Through his girl friend. She went to high school in Tulsa. Her name was Rosalind Russell. She left when she graduated from high school. She went to Washington and married some politician or someone. And she had told Byas about me. So she was going with Don Byas, I imagine, during that time and coming into Tulsa, and she would go out there and --
How far as Langston, Oklahoma from Tulsa?
Oh, about 20-some miles. Now, let's see, I'm getting in this --
What was he doing in Los Angeles, when you heard him here? With whom was he working?

He wasn't working with anyone. He was just -- had blown everyone away, jam sessions. There was two tenor players here. One would see how loud he could play, and the other one would see how much he could play, you know. But both of them were good tenor players. And Andy Anderson was more in the Coleman Hawkins style, and the other one was Bob Darcy, whom I used in one of my bands in New York. He ended up driving cabs when I broke up the band. He wanted to kill me
when I broke up the band. So he started driving cabs in New York. And he died in New York.
Is he the one you said tried to see how loud he could play?

Yeah, yeah. He'd get these baritone reeds and cut them down, you know, to put them on his tenor. But Andy moved up to San Francisco. I don't know if he's still alive or if he's still playing or what. He was an ex-bass player and he gave me some pointers, tenor saxophone player. He was out of Ohio.
Did you play in any of the jam sessions around town, or --

Yeah, yeah, yeah. Let's see, Fletcher Smith was generally the piano player, but Red Calderon would play mostly. I got a lot of tips from him, 'cause he had been playing, I guess, a year or two before me. But we both arrived in Los Angeles around about the same time.
What else?
How long did you stay in Los Angeles before you left?

Well, I came here -- oh, I know what I wanted to tell you about. I said that Benny Morton died April 1. I beg to be corrected. He -- that was his last dance. April 1, April Fool's Day. Because I slipped into the dance that night. And that was the night that I hobo'd away from
home. April 1, April Fool's Day, 1935. And when I got to Amarillo, Texas, that's when I got the news that he was dead. So he must have died around about the third.
Did you -- you didn't stay in Texas, did you?
No, we had some real hardships in Texas. That was like the year of Grapes of Wrath, like when -- the dust storms... (recording interrupted). End of Reel 1
You were about to tell me about your hardships in Amarillo, Texas.

Yes. My traveling partner and I, we had learned to shoot pool at an early age. As I said, we used to hobo over to Oklahoma City and watch this boy named Rooster shoot pool and never went to school, and Charlie Christian played the guitar.
Now, Rooster came out here and was playing Bill "Bojangles" for money, people was thinking, you know. He would go downtown with all kinds of money.
You know Rooster's full name?
No. No one ever knew. His name was Rooster. But he looked like Joe Louis. That size, build, face, features, everything.
Who was your traveling companion?
Boy named Quincy Forks.
Was he a musician?

No. He wanted to be a hustler.
So what happened in Amarillo?

Well, we spent a little bit better than 24 hours trying to get out of Amarillo. Like, they had dust storms during that year, '35, which killed all the crops, you know. It was very bad; bad scene. We got on a train in Amarillo, freight, during that time you didn't have to get underneath the train. You could get on the train when it was standing still, you know, get inside the boxcars or, if it was moving, you'd have to get on the flat -- run and jump and catch it, get on the flatcars, you know.

But we'd get inside the boxcars and sometimes we would get between the cars, you know, which -- they called that the -- I forget the part of the train they'd call that. Anyway, we got about -- oh, I guess about 18 miles out of Amarillo, and they stopped the train for a shakedown. And they started at the first boxcar, and the train would move up an inch, and they'd get the others out of the next boxcar, and the next boxcar, until they got all the hobos off the train, at the end, the caboose. And the train went on out into the distance, and left us all out here in this vast space. Well, I guess it was about 20 of us.
And about five minutes after that train left, here comes a dust storm. Boy, you talk about awful. We're not here to talk about dust storms. We're here to talk about music.
It's part of (inaudible) your whole experience, though. I remember the dust storms, from Oklahoma.

Well, we joined hands and started to walk. We couldn't sit down, we'd get covered up, you know. And I was dressed for traveling. I had on about three pair of trousers, about three shirts, a sweater, and a hunter's leather jacket. It was reversible. Three-quarter length, it was leather on one side and courderoy on the other. And you know these tassle caps, that you can pull down over your ears? I had that. And when that storm come, I wanted to pull that cap off, but the only thing I could do was pull it down over my ears, over my face, you know, in order to keep the skin from getting beat off. But that didn't help any. My skin still got beat off my face. My eyelids had scabs on it, my face -- How'd you breathe?
The best we could. Now, the crew dwindled down to a precious few. (laughs)
How far were you from --

Wait a minute, we weren't too far from a junction. I'll never forget it. Woodlawn Junction. But we went through some changes before we got to the junction. We were crossing the highways and cars just had on their headlights, just blowing their horns. That's the only way we kept from getting hit. We crossed the highway and we come on this farmhouse and the other part of the door was a glass pane, and you

could see in the house, and here's three fellows sitting there with their feet propped up one of these pot-bellied stoves, you know. We knocked on the door, Mexicans, whites, blacks, all looked the same because of this dust.

They turned around and looked at the window, and turned right back around the looked at the stove and started spitting on the stove. We said, 'Well, wow, that's cold,' so we walked about a mile further. We don't know what direction we were going. And we walked in, people turned their hounds loose on us, and we were falling over barbed wire fences. Everybody got lost. (laughs)
So -- all I could do was get away from that barbed wire fence, and just stand. Until finally, it let up. And everybody was just standing like I was, like posts; everyone was afraid to move, you know?

So I finally found my partner, my road buddy, and we walked on to Woodlawn Junction. And we see this fellow in a T-model Ford, a two-seater. And he was a preacher. And he was driving into Amarillo to sell some eggs. And we asked him and say, 'How much -- could we get a ride to Amarillo? How much will you charge us?' He said, 'How much money have you got?' We said, 'Fifty cents.' He said, 'Get in.'
So we got in, got ready to get out. He said, 'You have fifty cents, but you can keep it,' he says, 'if that's all you have.' So we got another train. Now, this kind of train

is hard. It wasn't a freight train. It was a passenger train. And at that time, they burned coal and wood in the engine. You know, you'd get cinders in your eyes if you let up the windows, you know? And we're blind to the passengers. Well, the blinds is the part between the postal car and the engine. You know? The locomotive. And it looked like an accordion, you know, that joined the two. And that was the blinds. So we was going to get in there and hide.
So we got as far as -- we went through Tucumcari and Carrizozo, New Mexico and we got to --
You were headed back West?
Yeah, we were coming West. And we got to this town, Dallhart, Texas. And we went through New Mexico and then come back through Texas, funny route.
Anyway, we were there that night. And come to find out no one of my complexion was allowed in that town. See. Read? You can't read? Run anyhow. You know? So, wow. What are we going to do?

So we went up by the railroad station, tried to get this passenger train out of there. So we're going in front of the station behind some railroad ties, that they put on the tracks, and we're hiding. When the train's getting ready to leave, they give the highball -- woo woo, ready to leave, you know.
Well, this passenger train just started oozing off slowly. They didn't give a highball. So my partner and I

jumped out from behind these railroad ties, and we're running down the side, trying to get up to the blind, and the railroad dick had one of these big knob flashlights, they threw it at our heels, and we say "Oh, damn," we turned to our left, getting away from the train, and he turned the flashlight up and seen our complexion. Boy, you talk about Jesse Owens! They ran us all through town!
He chased you?

He did, and then got a posse. Everybody was chasing us. We finally ditched them back at the railroad station. You know how we did it? We got where they unloaded the cattle, and face down in manure. So we hear footsteps approaching. And I've got on all these clothes. I'm cold and my teeth are chattering, scared to death. You know. (laughs) So the footsteps happened to be same Mexicans. They said, "When is another freight train coming through?" "In about half an hour." He said "Why don't you go down by the water tower. We'll catch it down there." Well, that's about -- equivalent to about four blocks. And from the station, it was downgrade.

So we're standing there about five minutes, and they give us the decency of not lighting any fire lights, you know, around the fire. Finally they lit one, we turned out backs to it. And all of a sudden, a fire broke out in one of these general merchandise stores. About two blocks from where we
were standing. So we had to move on. Down a little further. 'Cause they'd swear we'd done it, you know.

So we look up, and here comes this train. And gathered up speed coming down the -- see, the reason we was about four blocks, now we're about eight blocks, getting away from this fire scene. The train's doing about 60 miles an hour. And I ran to it. This was my first experience hobbing.

I grabbed the ladder and it was just like Lionel Hampton playing his drums. It's beating me all up the side of -- and I never turned loose. Finally, I got more composure and I was the happiest person in the world. When I got my feet down

So my partner, he wouldn't be outdone because he had made the trip out here two or three times. He wasn't letting no novice outdo him. So he grabbed it. And it hung him up He had to hang in there, too, 'cause the train was really moving.

So we got down in the reefer part of the boxcar, that's where they keep ice. It so happened we had caught a manifest, which is where they have fruits, to keep them from spoiling going across the desert. And it goes faster than any express.

Now, we've got to ride down in this ice compartment, with our backs up against the wall and our feet up against this wire screen that divides the ice from the fruit. Otherwise, we'd have been frostbitten, you know, on this ice. So we get to -- Douglas, Arizona, and we get off this train. All right,

we get another one. It turns out to be a manifest, but we got [California] it at a standstill. And we get to somewhere like Indio. The fellow said, "Well, you have to get inside, because if you get caught riding the timbers" -- that's what it is, between the train, it's the timbers, he said, "Get inside, because on the outside, you'll get arrested when you get into Los Angeles."
Someone else was riding the train, too?
No, this is what the railroad dick told us.
Oh, a friendly one.

Well, they didn't want us to stop in Indio, it was a little small place, you know. He wanted us to keep on going, you know. So my friend and I, we rode the timbers. We didn't want to get locked up. 'Cause the train's first stop was at Lincoln Heights, you know? And we wanted to get off the train before Lincoln Heights. WILARD: You'd go to jail there? SIMMONS: AN SO -- yeah, yeah, they called it the slaughter house, then. Because it was about to shake down. Every time a train would pass, a crack would appear in the walls, you know? The iron bars was even loose.

Well, anyway, got ready to get off at Lincoln Park, and this big, big Mexican -- he must have weighed about 300 pounds -- well, now, you know when you get a light from a moving object, you try to find out how fast it's going so that you can get off with some kind of speed to keep from killing yourself, you know.

Well, this big one jumped off the train and stood still and just vibrated -- boing-g-g-g. Stood in this spot. Now, his partner did the same thing, only he was small. He was about my size. Talk about a tumbling tumble weed. He rolled, I guess about six blocks, and when he ended up, he was straddling a switch, you know, a railroad switch. Both shoes off, they was tied up to the top. He was blind for about 15 minutes. He said, 'Well, I guess that's better than going to jail.'

But now, when my partner and I get ready to get off, my partner, he puts his foot down to see how fast the train is going, and he gets off. I put my foot down, drug the sole off my shoe. I come off running, and the only thing that stopped me -- I'll never forget it -- was the El Ray Roofing Company. I ran right smack into it, you know, like you see Bugs Bunny and (unintelligible). That was me. (laughs)
So then we got home free.
What did you do when you first got there? Where did you go? Did you know anybody?

Well, yes, there was a few people there from Oklahoma. In fact, he had a sister -- two sisters out here, and a brother. And my mother was here. She has been here about a year. So it was a big surprise to her. 'Cause I hadn't been out of the hospital too long, you know. And I caught a freight train. She was, 'Johnny, you run off from
home, and Mama keeps calling me on the telephone and sending me telegrams." Boy.
Who had you been living with in Oklahoma?
My grandmother.
What was her name?
Addie. My youngest daughter's name is Addie, named after her. She was a grand old lady. Bill Withers say, 'Grandma's hands'. Boy, she was something else. Which brings me to another story.
Was her last name Simmons?
No. Tucker. Zoot Sims had never played professionally and he joined Big Sid and I down at the Streets of Paris --
That was on Hollywood Boulevard.

Yeah, across the street from Pickwick. And first we had a -- Ben didn't come out here with us. We had Quinichette Paul Clinche, he didn't stay. Allen Eager came in. He didn't stay. And both of them were trying to play like Ben Webster at that time. So, Zoot come in with this funny-looking smile on his face. He's about the color of your sweater, which is red, and shy. Came up, played the keys off the horn. Sounded like Lester Young.
So he lived in the San Fernando Valley. And he had a '35 Ford with a rumble seat in it. And he would drive all the
way over to the East Side from the valley and pick us up, take us to work, take us back home and then drive back to the valley.

So one night, Zoot's family came to hear him play. Zoot got lost. He didn't get on the bandstand all night long. He was bashful, shy. So anyway, one day Zoots driving us home. He says, "Man, I'm tired of driving." He said, "Can somebody drive?" I'm in the rumble seat. I say, "Yeah, I can drive." He says, "Come on and drive." I say, "No, I'm not driving anyone else's car until I drive my own." I had an accident in one of my teacher's cars. Wash the car and drive it over to another school. Drive it dry, you know? Had an accident in it. So I say, I'm not going to drive. He said, "Well, Sid, you're always sitting in the front seat. You ought to be able to drive." He say, "Yeah, brother, I can drive." Say, "Well, come on and drive." Say, "Oh, man, you know I can't drive." I say, "Well, Sid, why do you always sit in the front seat, don't you observe? Don't you do anything?"

Now, Marlowe Morris is sitting between them. Marlow didn't know how to drive. He said, "Well, come on, Sid, you're going to learn how to drive tonight." So he gets Sid over. Now, we're right there by the UP station, the old train station there at 5th and Central. All right. Gets Sid on the wheel, Sid starts smiling, clutching the wheel like it's a gift to him, you know, someone has just given him something for Christmas. You know how he was. Oh, goody, goody.

Zoot So tells him where the ignition is, how to shift, clutch, out on clutch, out on the other one. Sid did this, started off, got up a little steam, and two blocks up we can see this signal changing. Red light pops up. Zoot says, "Put (laughs) on the brakes, Sid." Sid says, "Brakes?" I went under the seat. He had showed him everything. He kept telling him, "The other one, the other one." He didn't tell him the brake. He had reached over Marlow and grabbed the steering wheel, you know, and ended up in the gas station, like a dying fish. I laughed all the way home.
Let's get back to some music.
What year was this? When Zoot was --
So it was in 1944 that Sid almost learned to drive.
Uh-huh.
When you recorded with Benny Goodman for John Hammond, was that your first recording?
Yes, it was.
And you'd been playing bass how long?
Oh, about a year.
How many sides did you record --
The first record date we recorded two sides. It was 'Just A Mood,' blues in two parts, one and two. As I stated before, Teddy Wilson and Red Norvel -- and I'll
make a correction on the instrument, he was playing xylophone, not vibraphones. Xylophone is wood. That's what he was playing at that time. And Harry James and myself.
And on the second session.

The second session was augmented. Had Vito Mussa, Allen Reuss, Archie Rosati -- he's playing with Lawrence Welk now -- had a girl singer named Frances Helen Hunt, I think. What was her name? The one that made the 'Big Apple' and 'You Can't Stop Me From Dreaming.' I don't know what else was left in the can, but we made more than that.
And with your first recording done with those major musicians, was that when you decided to --

Well, yes, well, it made me curious. Because I didn't know what I was doing. I said, well, people can see more in me than I can see in myself, you know? So I'll go back East where things are happening and just throw my hat in with the competition, and see what's being done and what has to be done.

And I stopped in St. Louis, by the way. And I should have turned around and come back home then. I ran into the monster -- Jimmy Blanton. He was playing at Sportsmen's Lodge. with Jeter and Pillars, And if he played a solo, Floyd Smith would play it along with him as a duet. And if Floyd played a solo, he would play it along with Floyd. That's how well they were, you know. WILLARD: Attuned to each other. Simmons: Yeah, and I said, "Wow." And he had played with Fate Marable. Now,

Fate Marable, he must be old as water, because people are still playing with him. Jesse Price played with him when he was a young man. The late Jesse Price. You know? Jimmy Blanton played with Fate Marable.
So, I went on to Chicago, and what did I do it for? I should have went on to New York.
What did you think when you heard Blanton?

I said, 'Wow.' I said, 'I've never heard anything like this.' Well, now, I was playing solos, but not the way he was playing solos. I would jump from the lowest note up to the highest note, you know, unorthodox. But he was playing more orthodox because he had studied under his mother, you know. She was a violinist.
I didn't know that.

Yeah, well, he studied under his mother. And he knew more about the instrument than I did. with Jeter and Pillians And the first record I heard him play , it went like, 'I like coffee, I like tea, I like the girl that married me.' Is that the tune?
Uh-huh.
And I forget what was on the other side. [Crazy Rhythm]
And then the next time I heard him, Ray Nance was working in the floor show -- I think I stated this before -- anyway, Ray had joined the band. Blanton was a watch dog for Ben Webster,

because Ben Webster had had a case of rape on him in Chicago, and was brought out of Chicago. And somehow they patched it up for him to come to the Chicago Theatre with Duke. So Blanton was taking charge of Ben to keep him out of trouble.
What a job.

Now, Blanton didn't drink heavily, you know. He'd sip a cocktail now and then. He was very, very -- well, I would say he was a pretty man. He had Indian in him. He had straight hair, high cheekbones, oh, he was something else, really. Dressed beautifully. Had good taste. Dutch boy collars and things like that. Something that you'd never think of wearing, you know? He'd never meet himself twice, you can believe that. Like women wearing dresses?

And I got to Chicago, and this fellow, Tiny Parham, he was a huge man. And he played organ in the Savoy Ballroom. For the skaters, and pre-prize fights, you know, like organists play for ball games and things like that? He was the house band. He played the organ there all the time. However, he would call in for dances. So he called me and asked me, he said, "I understand you're new in the city." I said, "Yes." He says, "Would you like to have a job this weekend?" I said, "Yes." So I went to the job, expecting to work with him, and it was with Lil Hardin, not him. He was playing the part of booking agent, too, you know. He had a couple of bands working around town under his name at the same time. And the -- this little inci-

dent passed. Then I started working around Chicago with the Tony Fambrough, Danny Williams, they were all around my age, 'round 20, 19, 20. Andrade -- I can't think of his -- Vernon Andrade I think. I have it somewhere. Back of my mind. Worked with Erskine Tate, Carroll Dickerson. I worked for Lee Collins. He's a legend, from Louisiana. We worked for a place similar to 52nd Street, on that Calumet City, right on the borderline of Indiana, in Illinois.
When you say 'similar to 52nd Street,' you mean there were a lot of clubs?
Yeah. We got paid two dollars a night. We had to pay the driver fifty cents, and we got a meal. So actually, we made a dollar and a half a night, and whatever we got on the weekends.
So I worked for Lee Collins.
Who else did you work for?
A boy named Sonny Thompson, that tried to play all Lester Young's solos on the piano. He played all full chords on the piano. And I can't recall the drummer's name.

Then I worked -- not for, but with the legendary Punch Miller, with the All Stars on 43rd Street in Chicago. I forget who had the band, but he would always -- he was a fixture there. He'd play there all the time. But I never knew that Punch had the historic background that he had till this book came out on

his life, whatnot, and Charles Elgar -- he's an old timer, I worked with him, and Clarence Black, used to have the pit band at the Metropole Theatre across the street from the Regal, Jimmy Smith -- Jimmy Bell, I mean, and Rip Bassett. Rip Bassett was a guitarist that had worked with Eddie South.

Now, there's a name for you. Eddie South was equipped for symphony, but he was ahead of his time. He had studied abroad and everything. But he played modern jazz as well. So he played better jazz on the violin than any violinist, including Joe Venuti, Stuff Smith, any of the rest of them. Because it was clean, in tune, and he knew what he was doing. The Dark Angel of the South. That's what they called him.
Earl Hines told me that he was in a hotel in Chicago, where he was playing with a white band, they dropped a screen in front of him so that the people that were there to hear him couldn't see him.
Oh, yeah?
Because they couldn't have mixed bands on the bandstand in Chicago.
Well, did they tell you -- did Earl Hines ever tell you about the band that he had, that they had a big automobile wreck, and all of the reed section played violins?
No. What is -- is playing the violin related to the automobile accident? Wait a minute. Tell me the story.
Wait a minute now, let me see. Yeah, it was Earl's band. I was thinking maybe it was Earl Fletcher. It was Earl's band.
All of the violins, all of the reed men, doubled on violin.
Do you remember who those reed men were?

Well, I remember Omar Simeon, but I don't know whether -- if he was with the band at that time. Darnell Howard, I remember. I don't know if he was with the band. I think he was a replacement for some of these fellows because they got killed in the accident, you know?
You mean, there was an accident and he lost his whole saxophone section?

Well, the majority of them. And at that same time, Chick Webb, he was playing at a saxophone section where all of them played flutes. In the early 30's, Chick Webb and his Chickadees. So flute's nothing new today. They played, too. Legitimately, they played. Yeah, that all -- yeah.
And you heard Chick Webb in Chicago?
No, I heard him on broadcasts, from New York out here. Like, I heard any number of bands on broadcast. They'd had national hookup out here, you know. On Saturdays, or something like that.
Who else did you hear that made an impression?

Oh, I heard the Rhythm Band. I heard the Blue Rhythm Band. I thought it was at first Mills Blue Rhythm Band. But it was just the Rhythm Band. I heard Don Redman. I heard Claude Hopkins, Fletcher Henderson. Who else, who else, who else? I heard the Mills Brothers. Of course, I'd heard them first on the Lucky Strike Show, in the early 30's, when they were first discovered.

Oh, I heard any number of bands. Like, every week they had different bands, you know, that I heard in California, in Los Angeles. And then one week, Louis Armstrong's band played the whole week, broadcast. I heard Duke, naturally. And they had a poll going on then that I was unaware of, until I was almost out of high school. And like, a poll ran something like Duke Ellington, Fletcher Henderson, Don Redman.

Oh, this other band that I was trying to think of -- Speed Webb. He was around the Midwest. Speed Webb and his Blue Devils. He -- Speed Webb was a leader, singer, and he also played drums. And he had a band called Speed Webb's Hollywood Blue Devils.
He wasn't around Hollywood.

No. He was from around Buffalo, Indianapolis. He just barnstormed, you know. But he wound up out here and he named his band that. And guess who he had in the band? He had Vic Dickenson, he had Roy and Joe Eldridge, Gus Wilson

and Teddy Wilson. And Eli Robinson and Reunald Jones, who we called Jonesy. So that was quite a band. Two brothers, sets, you know. The Wilson brothers and the Eldridge brothers. That was something else.

I want to ask you something about what you said about Calumet City. You said it was like 52nd Street. Tell me more about that. How do you mean? You said there were a lot of clubs, were other major musicians working in them, was it only a weekend situation?
No it was a weekend situation; but the ones that were steady were caucasians, you know. When they wanted a black ethnic group. it was weekend, like Saturday night, you know.
But there was music steadily there?
Yeah.
How close is Calumet City to Chicago?
Oh, about--let's see, you had to go through Gary--no, you didn't have to go through Gary, you had to go through Robbins, Illinois, to get there. I'd say about 15 or 20 miles.
So it probably drew some from Chicago, the audience.

No, mostly from Indiana, because it was right on the Indiana state line. The Hoosiers -- and while in Chicago, King Kolax, he stole a repertoire from this musician that I told you -- Les Wilcox? I went over and played with him? They didn't have a bass player and they'd take turns feeding me? You recall?
Uh-huh.

All right, well, Les Wilcox was an epileptic, but very few knew. And he always complained about a toothache, and he would drink gin to ease it. And hold gin in his mouth all night when he wasn't playing the horn. And he wrote music, like, individual parts. He didn't write scores. And he always would ask me to go home with him while they would write, keep him company, you know. And I would go with him, and tell him the truth on myself. We were smoking grass, then.

And he would write so he was exhausted and so I would go home and go to bed. Now, Kolax, who's true name was William Littles, they were supposed to come out here, under a banner of Ruth Ellington. But she decided not to make the trip. So Kolax and the band has already rehearsed and everything, and they had the uniforms and everything and at the last minute, she pulls out.
So he takes Les' music and comes out here to Los Angeles, and played one date at the Elks Auditorium, and they
were stranded.
Well, did Ruth ever front the band? Or was it just a plan to --
No, no, she fronted the band. When and where, I don't know. But she did, I mean, because I've heard her name crop up several times.
This was in what year?
That I played with King Kolax out here?
What year that Ruth had -- Ruth's name was around as a band leader.

Well, this was around early '37 that I played with King Kolax out here. But then I ran into him in Chicago, and they had a hall there, the Warwick Hall. Where all musicians graduated from, like Gene Ammons graduated from there with King Kolax.

But on Thursday nights, Mr. Hall, that owned Warwick Hall would donate the hall to the Musicians' Union. Like, they had segregated unions then. 208 It was a black local, and 10 was the white local. That was Petrillo's union at that time. And they'd have two bands, one on one side of the house and one on the other. And whatever money was made would be split up amongst the musicians. This'll kill you. We'd end up at the end of the night splitting up 35 cents apiece, 50 cents, a quarter. Place be packed. Hall was stealing all the money. Boy, those were some funny times.
some funny times.
Well, were Kolax and Ruth Ellington actually associated?
No, no. Les Wilcox and Ruth Ellington. And she -- Les decided not to make the trip. So Kolax slips in the steals the music and brings the band out.
Did Les Wilcox and Ruth actually work together?
I don't know. But I met him after I got to Chicago, you know. I'm trying to think -- after they got stranded, Lena Torrance's mother took them in up at the hotel and let them live up there free.
Lena Torrance being a Los Angeles model.
Yeah. And part time actress. And I'm trying to think of this bar on the north side of the Elks, he would give Kolax' band a meal a day.
That's the Elks Auditorium at 40th and Central, right?
Yeah.
Used to be a chili rice place down there someplace. Can't think of the name of it.
No, but this was this bar and they served food as well. It'll come to me before it's over with. And shortly after Kolax arrived on the scene, King Cole came in

Shuffle Along to town with the Shuffalong Show. That was Flournoy Miller and Mantan Moreland. They had the show. And they had a chorus line and Nichodems, that has the Ebony Avenue Workshop for Actors.
Nichodems' Stewart Studio.

Yeah. He was in the show. And Olivette Miller, who was Flournoy Miller's daughter, playing the harp as a specialty in the act. And if she could play harp, I can. At that time, you know, as a novice. But she learned a little. But I heard great harpists, you know, out of studios. And comparing her with them, you know, was just about where she stood. I'm sorry to say it, but it was her shortcomings, you know, not mine. Ain't my job. (laughs)
And after playing the Lincoln Theatre for a week, they became stranded.
The whole show?

The whole show. So, one by one, they started going back to Chicago. Finally, there's a bass player left, who's name was Henry Fort. They called him Brother-in-Law Brother Ford. And he left and they say, 'They tell me that you're about the best bass player in town. Would you consider working with me?' I say, 'Yeah, I'll work with you. Beats sitting around Kolax doing nothing.'
So we went to a club called the Ubangi, over on Long Beach Boulevard. Exquisite little club. And the chorus line had dwindled down to about four or five. In fact, they had
augmented some Los Angeles girls in the chorus line. You know?
Which chorus line are you talking about, the Ubangi or --
Yes, at the Ubangi. It was about three shuffle Along girls left from the Ubangi -- I mean, from the Show. And then they got a couple more Los Angeles girls to put in there.
So when I got the bass job, when the bass player went home, and that left it a septet -- seven pieces. And at that time, Nat could only sing one song.
Which was that?

Roses of Picardy. And he sang it beautifully. I thought he had the job, you know, could sing then. But he was too shy to sing, you know? He never even thought of it. As I'd say, he'd bit his fingernails off, trying to get new thoughts, you know. I mean, he would bite them off into the quick, down to the cuticle almost, you know? Where his fingers -- the ends of them would turn up on the ends, where he had no fingernails.
Piano player.
Yeah. He was a hell of a piano player. He could have made it as a pianist, you know.
He had, so far as people who appreciated piano playing, didn't he?
Well, when I went to San Diego, he

wanted me to come back up here, and he got a job at Fox Hills, at 20th-Century Fox, with a trio, and he called me up and said, "I've got a job for a trio." I said, "Man, I don't want to work in no trio. I want to work in a band, you know? I don't want to be an act." He said, "Well, we're getting paid pretty good, got a contract, blah, blah, blah." I say, "Well, I like you, Nat," I said, "but I don't like no trio, man."
So --
Didn't you tell me that he had a big band?
Yeah.
How big?
It was about 17 or 18 pieces.
That was with -- shuffle Along
With the Shuffalong Show.
I see. And that was his band.
Yeah.
Who all played in it?

Oh, boy. Let's see, he had Sax Mallard, out of Denver, Colorado, alto player; a boy named Johnson, we called him Head, 'cause he had a [poll wrinkled] head. He had one of them saddle heads. So we called him Head Johnson. Trumpet player. And who else? Oh, a boy played tenor saxophone. That played with dentures, and they were always loose. We called him Gummy. But his name was Wright. I can't remember

his first name. He would do most of the arranging for the band. And who else was in the band? Oh, a trombone player named Atkins. Played good trombone. I can't think of his first name, either. But he finally wound up working up working with Earl Hines. And John Ewing, at the same time. And another trombone player that committed suicide, shot himself in the head. I think he was drunk, playing Russian Roulette. Roulette, roulette. All right.
Well, with this band, we were supposed to be making 18 dollars a week.
Wait a minute. Which band is this?
King Cole, at the Ubangi. We were supposed to be making 18 dollars a week. But we was kicking back six.
To the club.

Yeah. So that made everybody make 12 dollars. Well, by me being at home, I could afford to work for that amount. But they were starving, you know. And I had to buy all the grass for everybody, 'cause I was at home. I didn't have any problems, you know, so I kept the band high. And the chorus line, too. Whoever.
Well, anyway, youth and folly. I was having a good time.
After that broke up, that's when I went to San Diego. But I didn't go directly to San Diego now. Nat got a job some-

where as a single. I can't think of where it was. And his wife -- he would leave money with me to take his wife, Nadine, Shorty Nadine, he called her Shorty, wherever she wanted to go, if she wanted to go to the movies or a dance, or wherever. You know, he'd leave money. And the three of us were almost inseparable, you know. We all liked the same things, the same -- you know. And when he'd come home, we wouldn't be anywhere, we'd be sitting there, you know. Getting loaded off grass.

And he smoked grass, too, God bless the dead, until he started singing. Then he stopped smoking completely. To protect his voice, you know. We all have our little idiosyncrasies and things, I mean, but this is the truth.
At that time he still used the name Coles, with an s on it? That was his original name.
Nat King Cole.
Originally he was Coles. And when he began to get popular, he dropped the S.
Oh, oh, oh, when he got popular, then he dropped it. King Cole. But when he had the band, it was Nat Coles.
That's what I thought, 'cause I know that Nadine still uses Coles, right?
Uh-huh. She remarried.
Up until the time she did, she still --
Yeah, yeah.
And he and Maria were Cole.
Uh-huh.
So were the members of the band at the Ubangi largely members of the band that he -- Shuffle Along --
That he brought out here, yes.
Were you the only exception?
Yeah.
And then, he went to play a single, and
And I would keep his wife company while he was gone.

So during that time, Flournoy Miller tried to produce another show, called 'Slim Pickins', at the Wilshire Ebell. And we'd rehearse for I don't know how long. And the René Brothers was writing the music -- Otis René and what's the other one --
Leon?
Leon. They was writing the scores, music for the show.

All right, after all this rehearsal time and everything, we opened the first night, come back the next night, the stage hands wouldn't open the curtains. They went on strike because we didn't have the funds to pay them, you know. So we opened and closed in one, after all of that.
How long was the show in preparation?
Oh, I think about six weeks. And the name of the show was 'Slim Pickins'.
Did it ever get performed?
No. No. And --
Who all was involved in the show? 'Shuffle'
All the hangovers from Sufflin 'Along' -- Mantan, and Nichodemus Stewart, Flournoy.
Was Nat involved?
No. The Rene Brothers played piano. I played in the pit. Lee Young played drums. I can't remember who else was in the band.
When you said Nat got a job out at Fox Hills, I was that at a club, or --
No, it was a golf course, I think.
Oh, the Fox Hills golf course.
Uh-huh.

It's still there. And there was one -- oh, I know who it was. This boy, Nat Walker, who had blew his top down in San Diego? He was playing in the pit band, but Rene would rehearse the band in the pit, you know, and the show. So Nat Walker walked up 2nd says, 'John,' he says, 'Nadine likes you.' I said, 'Oh, man, I don't want to hear that.' I said, 'We're friends.' He say, 'No, but you don't see her looking at you the way I see her looking at you.' I say, 'Oh, man, you're jiving.' I run into him again in Chicago. Old family week, we
had a ball, you know. Went everywhere.

Then he came to New York, in '41. Was working in Nick's Village, in the Village, for something like 35 dollars a week, and wasn't getting paid. And I wasn't working. I was living with Al Hall, the bassist, that was working with Teddy Wilson's small group. And I met him in Chicago, and he told me that any time I came to New York that I could stay with him until I found a place, you know. So I took him up on it.

So every night, Nadine and I would go for a walk down by the Hudson River, up by the George Washington Bridge, that'd be our route, smoking grass. And then we'd come and sit overlooking Coogan's Bluff. That's the Polo Grounds. It was on Edgecomb, and you could look right over at the ball game, off of Edgecomb. If you had binoculars, and you could still see them, playing, anyway.

And she and I would sit down on a bench, just before we got to the Roger Morris Hotel. Now, this is -- Roger Morris Apartments, excuse me, Roger Morris. Because Cootie Williams had an apartment there, Canada Lee had an apartment there, Timmy Rodgers had an apartment there -- all the big performers had apartments there. And I lived in the next block, with Al. And Nadine lived around the corner, on St. Nicholas.
So we sat down on the bench that night, and we were smoking, and she says, "Johnny," she says, "when are you going to make love to me?" I said, "Oh, Nadine, don't say that." She
says, "Yes." I said, "Nat's my friend." She said, "Well, who do you think more of, my love or his friendship?" So I said, "Well, this bears some thinking, you know."

So we got up off of the bench, and no sooner than we got off of this bench, a car come around the curb and knocked the bench down on Edgecomb Place. Even with the Polo Grounds. She says, "See? I'm good luck to you." She said, "On my advice, (she had said,) let's get up and go," you know. So the devil made me do it. He reared his ugly head, and I took her up to Al's, and we had an affair, and she fainted. Scared me to death. I thought she had a heart attack. I was throwing water on her, the mattress was all soaked.
So Nat wanted children. And he found out that she was pregnant, and he was announcing it down every -- "Shorty's pregnant. Shorty's pregnant. Shorty's pregnant."
So one day, she came out of the apartment, where they were living, and she didn't have time to wait for the elevator. She started to walk down the steps --
(Recording interrupted)
End of Reel 2. Nadine was coming down the stairs.
(Unintelligible)

Yes, yes. On cue. She couldn't wait for the elevators and so she decided to walk down. And she got her foot caught in the carpet or this metal that they use on the stairs, you know, and she fell down the stairs. As a result, she had a miscarriage. And Nat flipped. He called

her and hollered and screamed at her. She says, "I don't know what you're hollering about. It wasn't yours anyway, it was Johnny's." My best friend. He came to me and he says, "Johnny, I don't hold any malice against you," he says, "because you could only do what she allowed you to do." He says, "and I've known all along that she liked you, because she would talk about you even when you weren't around." He say, "So I know this was her, not you."
He still, after that, wanted me to join his group.
How did he and Nadine get along after that?
Well, they filed for divorce.
So it was you, and not Maria, that broke them up.

No, not really. Because they didn't file for divorce directly behind that. Maria was the cause of it, but this -- they had separated for a while, thinking about it, divorce. And they stayed together for a while, until Maria showed on the scene.
He continued to ask me to join the group. I didn't want to join the group. I wanted to be in the band. At that time, I was playing with a quartet.
What quartet?
I forgot who was in the quartet. It was at the Three Deuces. Pearl Bailey was singing, and all she

could sing was 'St. Louis Blues.' She was getting 35 dollars a week. And they had a gay young man called Willie Dukes sing Honeysuckle Rose, honey, suck my nose, and Peewee Marquette, you know he couldn't sing.
Was that -- what year was that?
That was, let's see, around '42.
How long had PeeWee been on the scene then? Do you know?
No, I don't. And then they had a girl named Ann Robinson, that could scat like Leo Watson. And she had a big mouth like Martha Raye, only bigger. And she had a nice figure.
Tom Whaley told me about her.
Who?
Tom Whaley She worked someplace uptown, right?
Well, she worked at the Village Vanguard for a while. And then she worked at -- what was the name of this place uptown? It was an after hours' spot. I can't think of the name of the place.
Tom described her exactly as you did.

And she ended up getting strangled to death. I don't know how it happened. But she had a secret love. And I can't bare it, because he's my best friend. And he and his wife and living a wonderful life, growing old and

mellow together. I'd hate to bring this up at this late date. That's one of my little goodies that I have to keep to myself. She used to sing 'Chloe' And boy, when she didn't do to "Chloe" -- slush, slush. Now, she would scat. But this is a funny thing. No one in the club made over 35 dollars. Every-place that was working professionally -- 35 dollars.
You mean, all over town, or just the Second Street?

Fifty- Second Street, and the Village, too. Only Nat didn't get his 35, he didn't get paid at all. He had one of these Buick Torpedoes, you know, the torpedoe back, where it's slanted?
