That was, I'd say, around '41, and anything that he bought, Oscar Moore had to buy something better. Because Oscar had money before he joined Nat. What do you call it, a -- an inheritance. He and his brother inherited some money, from the mother. They lived in Arizona, I think. And it must have been an awful big size. He must have owned a lot of property or something, man. 'Cause he had a lot of money. Then he ends up going with this girl, Oscar Moore, that is, when he left King Cole. He had been going with this girl for quite a while. And she was very loyal to him. And he knew her father. But the father had more of a crush on him than the girl did, because he'd go fishing with the father, you know. Anytime he wanted to go fishing, "oh, have your reel ready, we'll be ready," you know. Then they'd go and talk.

So the father in talking to Oscar, told him, he says, "When I die," he says, "I'm going to will everything to you, 'cause I know you'll take care of my daughter." And this father had parking lots all over Los Angeles proper. Oscar Moore hasn't touched a guitar since. No one knows where he is or how he can be found.
Well, the girl, was that Mamie?
I don't know who she was.
Well, did he marry her?
Yeah.
Seems to me his wife's name was Mamie.
I don't know. I sure would like to get in touch with him. Just for old times' sake. And laugh at Curtis Moseby.

I think that he and I got paid mainly because my mother knew Curtis Moseby, and she was a pretty tough customer, you know. And I think Oscar threatened to shoot him if he didn't get his money. So everyone else had to go for the okey-doke.
Curtis Moseby was not reliable so far as pay went?
No.
But yet an awful lot of people worked for him.
Yeah. Everyone else got the business.
Just like, he wouldn't pay people, Benny Goodman gave everybody the ray.
Benny Goodman did what?
Gave everybody the ray. You're not hip to the ray?
No, I'm not hip to the ray.

He'll have his eyeglasses down on the tip of his nose, and he'd be looking at you, you know? You'd be reading the music. You'd have a feeling that he was looking at you, you raise up, he'd be looking at you. Giving you the ray. Everybody in the band, so they give him the name "the Ray." You know?

The band -- this was an experience, oh, boy. 'Cause I never should have got that thing. We had a tune -- I can't recall the name of it. Something about the sun, like, big preamble introduction, you know. And leave a bar out, and Big Sid would say, "Quit your squawking. I hear your talking," you know.

So, time come for us to leave the Sherman Hotel. We were going to fly to Toronto. I didn't tell you this, did I? I had to fly to Toronto. And Big Sid was afraid of airplanes. So was Vido Musso. So Vido called up long distance and told his wife to send a wire, that the immigration authorities wanted him out here. So he got in his car and drove to Toronto. He was there when we got there.

So Big Sid, with all the coaching of everyone in the band, we got him on the plane. So he gets even with the wings, where he can look out the window. We hadn't even taxied out to rev up. He saw this oil bubbling out from around the engine, he got up and went to the tail end of the plane. (laughs) So now, we get to Toronto. They're supposed to have reservations for the band. What's the name of the hotel in Toronto? King George? King Edward? James? Something.

Anyway, they didn't have accommodations for Big Sid, Cootie and myself. So Pee Wee Monte, who was Benny's private valet, you know, pulled Cootie over to the side and said, "Don't worry, we'll get you a room. Stay here." So Sid and I, we go out. Sid goes to the -- gets a cab and goes to the train station. Sees a red cap, calls him over. "Hey, brother," he says. "Where can I find a house of ill repute?" I said, "Sid, I don't want to see any women. All I want is a bed." "Well, brother, where you find a woman, you find a bed."
So this is his thing. This is what killed him. You know? Women killed him. Around the clock.

We get to Toronto, and we find one of these houses. I'm upstairs, just sleeping away. And I wake up on my own, and I holler downstairs, "What time is it?" And they told me. We were half an hour late already then. I went downstairs to the next floor, woke Sid up. I said, "Sid, we were at the exhibition grounds a half hour ago." He said, "What?" And he

jumped straight up and landed on his feet in the middle of the bed. You talk about getting dressed. We get to the exhibition grounds, and we had forgotten our badges, our pass to get in. So then they had to send someone way over to this tent that we were playing in, so they came up and recognized us, you know, and got us in and everything. We get to the back of the tent. Benny Goodman says, "That'll be a 50-dollar fine." I say, "Yeah? After the ball is over. You ain't going to take no 50 dollars from me." I say, "How do you know that I've even been to bed?" You know? I said, "But Cootie got a bed, didn't he?" I said, "If you take 50 dollars out, I'm going to take 50 dollars out of you. Now think abbut that."

So we got on the bandstand. They came up with this same tune, "quit talking, I hear you squawking." They left that opening. Sid says, "T W A, take it away." The band folded. The people on the dance floor didn't know what was happening. The whole band is laughing, and here they are, dancing. Benny said, "That'll cost you another fifty." Sid just looked up in the air and paid him no attention. He didn't even look at Benny the whole night long.

So they had a Blue Law there, you know. Couldn't work on Sundays. So, like, we worked Saturday nights, and we took a bus, chartered a bus, to Oneida, New York, a resort, upstate New York, and had an electrical storm. Oh, it rained. But this played havoc on my bass strings and Sid's drum heads. You know,

they drop and get out of tune very easily, you know, when it rains. And there was no air conditioning. They had one of these large restaurant fans, you know, one of those tall ones, in front of the bandstand. Beautiful shell, good acoustics, but it was burning up in there.

Mel Powell is on one end, and Lou McGarity is on the other end. And Mel Powell says, "Caw caw," signifying. And Lou McGarity would give it right back to him: "Caw caw." I'm picking a note, tuning, taking a tune. Benny says, "Come on." And I screamed back at him, "K M A," you know? So when we got off, he says, "What's wrong with your boy?" Sid says, "Phonograph" got to play the part of Clark Terry.

So we get back to Toronto, play that night, and we played without any words. And when we left there, we went to Frank Daly's, Meadowbrook. And the way the brass section that he had -- something like five trumpets, after you added Cootie with the band. Cootie didn't have a book. He'd just have to get up and play a solo, cold. You know. But he had Billy Butterfield, Jimmy Maxwell, couple of other trumpet players, I don't remember their names. And he had Lou McGarity and Cutty Cutshall playing trombones.

Now, the brass section, instead of patting their feet, they tromped, alternating from foot to foot, you know. Blump, blump, blump, blump, like they was marching. And Big Sid was pounding the cymbal to sound over them, and this is

making me give up all the strength that I've got, as small as I was, to be heard. I heard this whistling in the distance, like someone was hailing a cab. And looked up, and he's pointing at me to tell me to be quiet. WILLARD: Benny? Yeah, to play softer.
Now, you know my feathers dropped. I didn't feel like playing the rest of the night.
Did he get by with fining you the 50 dollars he threatened?
No, he didn't fine me.
How about Sid?

He didn't fine him, either. So now, we're at Frank Daly, you know, Pee Wee's helping Benny to change, helping him to dress, rather. And Sid and I were over in another corner, watching a checker game, with our backs turned.
So Benny asked Sid, he says, "Sid," he says, "What happened with that boy, Gillespie in Cab Calloway? Sid says, mum-mum-mum-mum, and when he said that, he tore out of the dressing room.

Well, everybody wanted to laugh. Including me, I cleared out of the dressing room. Everybody on the bandstand just cracking up. Looking at one another, and the more they'd think about it, they'd go back into it.
So when Benny came on the stand, he looked at everyone real strange. Now he had sent Ziggy Elman some money to rejoin the band, 'cause Ziggy had some liquor stores on the
Eastern seaboard, starting with Atlantic City and going up. So Ziggy say, "Can't come. Need more money." Sent him some more money. Ziggy didn't show up.

One night, he looks down, and Ziggy is standing right in front of him. He see Ziggy standing there and he say, "Pht." Like he's spitting in Ziggy's face. So he comes to me one night, and he says, "There's no point in -- I'm going to try someone else." He says, "There's no point in me dragging you and you dragging me." I said, "Okay." So the next night, I come to work, he had Marty Blitz there. Marty had just left Claude Thornhill's band. Marty's a good bass player.

So I went out in the car to listen to the broadcast. This boy that Cootie and Sid and I had hired to drive us to work every night, the driver say, "I've never worked for Benny. If I had to drive for him, and he says turn here, he'd probably tell me to turn in the middle of the block."

So we listened to this broadcast, we can't hear nothing but bass. Thumping, you know. So I overheard someone say, "How do you like the new bass player." Say, "He's all right, but I'll straighten him out." Marty stayed with the band two weeks. (laughs)

So now, he gets on Sid's case. Like, he'd give the downbeat? Well, he had a couple of vertebrae lacking in his spine. That's what he'd gone to the hospital for. He'd asked Charlie Christian to go the same time he did. So naturally,

his wig was loose. So he'd give the downbeat, he would -- Sid would take the downbeat and naturally, he's supposed to hold the tempo there. Dancers on the floor. He started rushing things, you know, like, "Make it faster, make it faster." You know. Thinking that -- you know, "Make it swing, make it swing."

So when they come off the stand, Sid collared him. Said, "Looky here, Pops, you give me the downbeat. I'm supposed to keep that tempo." He says, "As long as you've been playing, you know it's unprofessional to change the tempo once the dancers are on the floor." He says, "And all that rushing that you're giving me, that doesn't mean a thing to me as far as swinging the band," he says. "I'm going to swing. Now, if the band isn't swinging, it isn't my fault." You know?
What did Benny say?

Benny didn't say anything. They had a record date coming up in the next couple of days. He hired Jo Jones. Now, he fired me without notice, but -- mind you. And I went to John Hammond and told him about it. John gave me two weeks' money. Well, now, since when did Benny do something without saying something to him about it?

So he went out the next night, after he fired me, they were up on the mezzanine, fighting like two women. Hands in front of their face and striking out with the other. That was funny. John Hammond, brother-in-laws.
Anyway, Sid -- they had this record date coming up,

but they didn't tell Sid anything about it. So they hired Jo Jones. And the tune was "The Earl." The union wouldn't let it go through because Sid was still with the band, see. So they made him cut it over again. Cut it without drums. They wouldn't let him do that. So he had to let Sid do it. And Sid didn't want to do it as badly as Benny didn't want him to ,either. You know.

So Sid put in his notice. And it ended with Frank Daly engagement. So now, he tells Cootie, he says, "I'm going into the New Yorker. You stay with me and I'll help you form your own group." Okay. Now, in Harlem, they had a place called Rhythm Club, where musicians go and look for jobs, instead of going downtown to the union. And downstairs, under the Rhythm Club was MURRAN'S Bar.

So Big Sid and I were at MURRAN'S, drinking, you know, hanging out together. I wonder how we was getting along. But about the time that we know they're taking their first break, Cootie comes walking in the door, crying big crocodile tears, he called him every name in the book. "He fired me, after promising me everything."

So then Cootie had to form his own band, with the money he had made with Duke, the money he had made with Benny, and he paid for rehearsals. So I went, just to get paid for the rehearsals. I had no idea to play with Cootie. None.
Why?
Hm?
Why?

Why? 'Cause his wife ran things. A la Gladys Hampton, the late Gladys Hampton. She'd make out the checks and pay the fellows off and everything. Cootie didn't have a word to say. So I knew I wouldn't like that. I went to rehearsal.

So while I'm rehearsing, Sid say, "Come on, brother, let's go back to Louis Armstrong. Let's go with Louis." He had been with Louis before. I say, "Yeah?" I thought I was small. I say, "Well, who's going to buy the uniforms?" He says, "Mohawk'll buy them." I can't think of his name, a little cut down to his bitty dude, played bass. He had had my uniforms

Anyway, I went with Big Sid. And every town that we approached, you know, the itinerary, Sid had played them before, and everybody knew where they were going, when they arrived. Now, Prince Robinson, he used to work with Duke years ago, a tenor player. He was supposed to have been a threat to Coleman Hawkins during that time.

And Prince would set a price on a place. He'd go to a place and say, "I'd like to pay you a dollar just to leave my bags here and wash up." He'd say, "I'm not going to sleep here tonight." He'd do that. He knew how to do it, and he'd eat out of paper bags all the time. And he's got his money and he's saving his money, 'cause he was going to marry this girl
in Montreal. He's going to make this tour to the West Coast and come back. Quit the band and go to Montreal and marry.

So everybody on the train is gambling-- Velma Middleton, Humph. M. HILLIARD; Shelton Simmons Sonny Woods, what's his name, yeah, and someone else. Always played poker. Velma and Sonny Woods always won. Louis Russell was in it, too.

So somehow, Prince Robinson lost his traveler's checkbook. He got up -- we had broken the train down completely level. Everything was a bed except the back of the train. The back of the seats, we had just uncovered them and let them down, you know. So Prince turned snow white overnight, his hair. Honest to God. His hair wasn't grey, it had, you know, tinges of grey, and the next day it was almost snow white. Worried him to death. Someone found it and was playing games on him. And they finally give it back to him. And he just laughed. He say, "Yeah, where'd you find it?" He say, "Man, he says, just as we're getting off the train, I found it in the men's room, behind the toilet." He say, "Yeah, well, I must have lost it in there when I pulled my pants down."

Boy, but that Louis Armstrong tour was something else, baby. We got to Atlanta, Georgia and they had chicken wire down through the middle of this auditorium. It was a dance. Whites on one side, blacks on the other. If the dance gets too good, the blacks got to leave, you know. If the music got too good, and some more whites wanted to get in there, the blacks

had to go. So the dressing room was backstage, you know, it was an auditorium, like, you know. And the dressing room was behind the curtains. Here's this dude had been to New York Twin brother several times, he's real hip, clean. He said, "Man, some of my best friends are colored." The first time I heard that expression, you know. That didn't rub me right. I'm waiting for him to say that magic word so I can jump down his throat. He didn't come on with that. He says, "We had a colored nanny." I say, "Whew." Yes, he said "colored." 'Cause I'd have been on him like white on rice if he'd said that magic word. Yes, anywhere. He says, "We nursed her breast." I said, "Well, man, you're a lucky S.O.B." He say, "What do you mean?" I say, "I was 21 years old before I sucked a Caucasian breast." And Louis said, "Oh," and held his mouth as though someone hit him in it. He said, "You're going to get us killed down here." I said, "Well, he asked for it." You know? He turned the color of your blouse. And he made a quick exit. He didn't stay around for very much longer, either. Just lucky that we were leaving the next morning.
So all kind of things happened on the road. We came out here and stayed eight weeks in the Casa Mañana. It used to be the Cotton Club, in Culver City.
Was Frank Sebastian still running it when it was the Casa Mañana?
Yeah. On the way back, we had the
same itinerary going back.

Oh, had a fight on the bus. This'll kill you. We had just left the Orpheum Theatre here in Los Angeles. And it was two girls in the dressing room, and I knew them before I left Los Angeles. They used to hang out with the redhead kid, called Red. He later hung out with Lee Young. And we ran into them, Big Sid and I walked in, and we say, "Hey, Nancy, hey, Penny." Well, Nancy ended up marrying Lucky Millinder. Tall girl, red hair. And so, Sid and I ended up taking the two of them out to the dressing room. And meanwhile, Louis is waiting for Lucille to join them on the road. "Moms get here," he say, "everything be all right." He used to have fever blisters all on his mouth. Got to Oakland, he waved the band out, he says, "Sorry, folks. Can't carry on. Chaps gone." And everybody in the band laughed at him, except Sid and I.

So we had a trumpet player there named Frank Galbraith, called him Smoothie. He plays a beautiful trumpet. And he held it up until Louis was able to play. Wherever we went, they explained to them, you know, that Louis wasn't able to appear, but we think you're enjoy this young man's playing. Give him a hand. He'd come out with a handkerchief in his hand like Pops.
So anyway, we'd get a bus in Cheyenne, Wyoming. New bus driver. Different bus. We're going all up through Idaho
and Falls Montana, everywhere, you know.

So we got off -- I think it was Idaho Falls. We got off the bus. But before we got off, Big Sid and I rode together. This was our seating. But I was up against the window and I couldn't sleep at all 'cause Big Sid was leaning on me as a pillow, and his legs was out in the aisle. And he's just sitting just opposite Louis Armstrong on the other side. And they would tell jokes from one town to the other. And I would -- every time I would hear them repeat one, it'd be just as funny as it was the second time, you know. And I couldn't remember any of them today, unless a situation arises, you know. Then it'll come to me, you know.

But had a valet, private valet, for Louis, but he wasn't really a valet. He was a snitch for Joe Gasser. You know. What's going on, and he was supposed to call in at certain times, you know, how many weeks or what, you know, to see what's happening with the band. And it was Bob Smiley.

So every time Sid would get up out of his seat, Smiley would come down and sit in Big Sid's seat to talk to Louis, you know, just across from him. So Big Sid was up front, standing in the stairwell, you know, looking out the highway. Come back, here's Bob Smiley sitting in his seat. Say, "Man, how many times have I told you to keep your mm out of my seat?" He say, "I oughta knock you down." So Bob Smiley pulls on his lapel and says, "Well, boy, that's what you got to do."
And he stood up and when he stood up, he went down.
How big was Smiley?

Well, Smiley was almost as tall as Sid, but he didn't have the weight that Sid had. Sid hit him once, he went down. And Sid -- that's the first time I've ever seen him angry. People said a whole lot of things to him, but he just couldn't stand Bob because he knew that Bob was a snitch, you know.

So Louis says, 'Let 'em fight.' Velva - Middleton went into hysterics, 'They're fighting, they're fighting, they're fighting.' He started to say the magic word, Louis did. 'Let 'em fight, let 'em fight.' Bus driver almost run the bus off the road. 'Let 'em fight. Sid Catlett and John Simmons, they fired when they get to Chicago.' I said, 'John Simmons? How did I come into this?' Dumb, you know? 'I still say John Simmons. You and Big Sid Catlett, would-be pimps and press hogs, gamblers. You're fired when you get to Chicago.'

When I get mad, I cry out of one eye. I started crying out of one eye. 'Cause I didn't have anything to do with that. I don't know where he's coming from, you know? So I got off the bus in a hurry when they stopped, waiting for him to step off, 'cause I was going to pop him right in the mouth. And it just so happened that when he stepped off, and I drew back to hit him, Big Sid snatched me out of my shoes. He said, 'Man, you hit that man in his mouth, you'll never play
another note of music in your life. You'll be blackballed for (laughs) life." I say, "I don't give a damn." So we didn't speak anymore.
You and Louis?

Yeah. But Sid had told me, he said, "Now, you have to watch Louis. You'll think everything is going along fine," he says, "and after a while, he gets his habits on," you know. But I couldn't even understand this. Come to find out, he was mad because Sid and I took these two girls out of his dressing room.

Now, by this time, Lucille has joined the band. We get to Minneapolis and he has a birthday, the 4th of July. I had a pound cake box, tin, full of marijuana. And Louis called it 'spiscondi.' Where he got that name from I don't know. So I went by his room and knock on the door to give him a couple of spiscondis. He never worked with it. He'd wait until he got off and get with his typewriter and hunt and peck jokes. When he'd write someone a letter, that would be his letter. He'd send them a joke. You know. And he had a joke book. Now, I don't know when it's going to be published or what, but that's what he would do. Write jokes every night. Get off of work, put some salve on his lips, handkerchief on his head, visor, it's funny looking.
Anyway, after I give him his birthday present, everything was lovely. And all was forgotten and forgiven. But we

had another knick knack in the band -- George Washington, trombone player. He was sort of on the byside. He was 21 before he even knew whether he wanted to be a man or a woman. And he accidentally married a woman. And he had a son, but as years went by, he felt this other thing coming out stronger. So he had a love affair with Israel Crosby, the late Israel Crosby. And they would lay on the back seat of the busses, from town to town. But invariably, once a month, we would have to leave George Washington, just like a woman. We'd have to leave him wherever we was. Now, he would see boys out in the audience. He'd get them backstage somehow, buy them clothes. Next day, he's got a woman with him. He was just funny. Everyone was trying to put him on me, (laughs) I say, "You want him to get hurt?" We had a good time, though. He'd tell me and Sid all of his inner secrets, you know. What he would do and what he wouldn't do, how did other people react to him and everything. We'd sit and just laugh.
Now, --
I was curious about something, about Benny Goodman, when he was going around, exaëting 50 dollar fines. What kind of salaries were you making?

Well, I was making 125 dollars a week, salary-wise, but then I got paid for wearing the uniform. And I got paid for extra record dates. And I got paid -- we did the Holland Furnace broadcast show, 'Tuesday at Ten,' that was a tune that he recorded, 'Tuesday at Ten.' And actors and actresses
would come and do little funny skits. And I'd say my salary at the end of the week would be -- maybe, about 300 dollars.
What do you mean, you got paid for wearing the uniform?

This was union rules. With the white union. I didn't know it, either. Black union, never. You had to buy your own uniform, you know. But it come up. I was paid for weating the uniform, I was paid traveling time, you know?
Did Benny often exact fines he -- snapped at people when he was made, or was it just a way of venting his anger?

No, it was a way of venting his anger, because he didn't have anything to do with the money. His wife handled the money and paid the band, you know. She issued the checks. She'd send them out, from New York. Lady -- what's her name? John Hammond's sister. Duckworth. Was that her name? Yeah.
When you and Sid were still with Louis was the pay similar to the one you --

Oh, no, baby. We had to buy our own uniforms, and they were monkey suits. You know, stage uniforms. Looked good on the stage, but you couldn't wear them in the streets, you know. And you had to buy them yourself.
Whereas with Benny, they were suits you could wear all the time?

No, no, it was just band uniforms. You know, I mean, if someone left and left a uniform there, you'd just have it altered, that's all. But like, with Louis Armstrong, you know how much we was making on one-nighters? World War II? We'd have reserved cars on trains, going through the South. Eleven dollars a night. And they was taking out of my salary to pay for the uniforms that they had to have made up in a hurry for me. Stealing me blind, and I didn't know it. Everybody else is sniggling and I didn't know what had happened.
Well, didn't the other people have to pay for their uniforms?
I imagine so, but they was making more than 11 dollars a night. You know.
Who set the prices, Joe Glaser?
Yeah. Joe Garland was the band director. He's the one that wrote 'Leap Frog,' Les Brown's theme song. He's the one that wrote that. And when he left the band, he opened up a pool room.

But when we got back to New York, Baby, I did it before Barney Ross. Kissed the Pennsylvania Station's ground, time I got there. Never no more. - One trip through the South was enough for me. You know?
You said you had private railroad cars.
Oh, oh, yeah. And they would even stop and take that away from us. You know. Some woman would

come back there and she'd say, "Oh, here's some seats back here," Big Sid says, "Ma'am, this car's reserved." She said, "Don't any magic word -- "have any reservations." He says, "Madam, I beg to differ with you," he says, "and you are lower than whale dung on the bottom of the ocean. And get your buttocks out of here. We're not bothering you, don't you bother us." And Louis is standing there, guarding his lips. You tell Louis, Pops, say, "Louis, Bob say we just saw a fight, dude got hit in the mouth by a two by four."
First thing he'd do is put his hand up to his lips. Everything that happened, he was guarding his lips all the time.

So now, the military, they took many a car away from us. They had priority. And they'd put us off in a little one horse town, milk trains ran through and they would pass us by. And we'd be sitting on these big -- I guess you've seen them years ago, they had a -- looked like a wagon where they'd carry your baggage on. Flat, with wheels, and a tub. We'd try to sleep on them, waiting on a train and an express would come through there and throw cinders everywhere. And, boy, you talk about dirty. On top of our complexion, our paint job.

Now, we get to -- where was this -- I'm trying to think of this town where we had such a hangup. It was in Macon, Georgia. Macon, Georgia. We were using cars at this point. And we ran up on the highway to Erskine Hawkins' band truck. We pulled up to see what the trouble was, and he said they had

left them there to guard the instruments. So we drove on in to Macon. And while we were in Macon, the band truck driver fell asleep at the wheel, you know, behind the wheel. But he was off the highway, on the soft shoulder. So dark fell upon him. He was still asleep in the truck. So a flashlight shines down on him. He says, "Nigger, get that goddamn flashlight out of my face. Don't you see I'm asleep? You can wake a man up better than that." The door opened, they pulled him out, say, "Nigger, we've been watching you all day." And they whipped him something awful. The highway police with those big-knobbed flashlights, long ones, billy clubs, blackjacks, they must have messed up his teeth, broke his nose, damn near put his eyes out. Both eyes is closed, ribs broken, arm broken, you know.

So we get into Macon, and we got to play this auditorium. I don't know where Erskine Hawkins is going to play that night. But we played the auditorium. And in front of the auditorium is sort of a triangle that comes up, you know. Let's see, if the auditorium is on the west side of the street, the triangle would be headed south. Then you'd cross the triangle and get on the other side of the street. The East side of the street.

All right, we had a -- I hate this, why can't you just say people, instead of Caucasian or white or colored or black? We had an audience in the balcony and it was a black dance, so you know who the audience was, right? But if it

had sounded too good, they would have taken over. So at the end of the dance, the band valet, his name was Mutt, came back and said, "John, you and Sid. There's a soldier out here that wants to see you all. Say you are the only two in the band he know." I say, "Yeah," well, I was dressed, I'd changed. Sid was still standing there, soaking wet. He was trying to dry off, cool off and everything.

I said, "Sid, I'm going to go across the street and get some cigarettes and Pepsi, and I'll see who it is." And I get outside the dressing room, and I see a friend of mine from Gene Krupa's band. By name of [Murphy DeFono] He had a jet black hair with a lock hanging up front, you know, nice looking guy. Trumpet player. Now,he hadn't had any Army training, boot training at all. He was in the band. Here comes this Macon, Georgia policeman, with his jeans on, his cowboy boots, and his hog leg hanging down -- hog leg, you know, handgun, hanging down to his knee, Boston Stetson hat. "Where you going, boy?" Talking to Murphy. Said, "I'm going back here to see John and Sid. They're friends of mine." "You got to get out of here and put some charcoal on your face first." And he shook him down and found some whisky on him. Got the whisky bottle in his hand. Well, I followed them on out. And he turned him over to the M.P.'s. Right there on the triangle. The M.P.s beat hell out of him. They beat him so he urinated on himself. And something else, I guess. The city police joined in, with

billy clubs. "You Yankee son of a bitch. Didn't we tell you not to speak to no niggers down here?" "But they're friends of mine." Whop, whop, whop. He was adding to the injury, you know. And they almost killed him.

So he has one of these native girls, with my paint job. "Boy, why don't you go on away from here. You ain't doing nothing but causing trouble." Well, this brings me to my senses. Naturally, I'm next. So I went on across the street and got the Pepsi-Cola and the cigarettes, and went around the triangle, you know. And went back inside and said, "Man, they're beating hell out of that man out there."

They took him out of the band, and put him in the infantry. Without any boot training at all. So he got to Paris, and started drinking. And somehow, he struck up a conversation with some Sengalese soldiers. Well, and they said words to the effect of, "it seems like you got a problem," or "you're afraid to fight, or what?" And he ran the story down to them, you know, he says, "I don't know nothing about fighting. Never had a gun in my hand, you know?" And the conversation went on and on, told them about the M.P.s, and the commanding officer, whatnot. So about a year later, I ran into Murphy on Broadway, there by that amusement place on 52nd and Broadway, where they have all these little gadgets you can peep through and tricks and things.
I ran into him on that corner. "Murphy." "John."

I said, "Man, the last time, you looked a mess, all on our account." He said, "No, it wasn't on your account. It was on account of my bullheadedness," he said, "and forgetting where I was." I say, "Well, how did you make it through the Army?" He say, "I got put back in the band." I say, "Well, what happened?" He say, "Well, the M.P.s and commanding officer came up missing in action." He said, "And when they called my number, I told the new C.O. my problem, you know, that I had never fired a gun or anything. I was in the band and everything, what had happened. So he put me back in the band. So everything came out all right after all." He say, "I don't know what happened to them," he say, "but I had planned something for them anyway."
After the Army, did he go back to playing?

Yes, he went back and rejoined Gene Krupa. And it was very good to see him, you know. It took a lot of -- how shall we say -- blame off my shoulders, because I really felt that it was Sid and my fault, you know. 'Cause if we hadn't of been there, he wouldn't have been there. You know, that's one way of looking at it.
It wasn't your fault.
When you traveled South, what did you do about living accommodations in Southern cities? Did you stay on the railroad car?
We stayed on the railroad car.
Like some other bands.

Yeah. Now, like, when we got to Louisiana, I got to meet some of the old timers, that other people hadn't met, that were legendary, you know? And I never had an idea that I would meet them. Like, Bunk Johnson, he was supposed to have been Louis Armstrong's idol and teacher. Bunk showed him a few things on the trumpet. Kid Ory I met out there, and I met him here in Los Angeles. So we had a sort of a relationship going. I met Ed Garland out here. But he happened to be in Louisiana at the time, because it was near Mardi Gras time. He'd come that Mardi Gras.
Did you hear them all play?

I tell you what I did hear. I heard blues for the second line. This is where they were going to a funeral, to a burial, and they're playing church songs, the band, and coming back, they were swinging. Kicking their heels, and the night before they had had a wake. And everybody there dropped something of what the person liked in the casket, you know, whatever it was -- a fifth of whisky or whatever, you know. Take it and live happily ever after death, you know. If there is a hereafter. I don't know. No one's been back to tell us about it. I don't know. Could be. Still have to find out. I don't know. I feel like -- as though I've been here before. I don't know what form, but I run into things and say -- it's frightening, you know, like a fantasy. Like, I'll find myself
in a house and I'll say, "I've been here before," you know? And actually, I know where every room in the house is. You know?

And I meet a person, and I say, "I know you." I mean, it's like -- what do you call -- not a premonition, but, well -- what is the word? What is the word? Well, well, I won't dwell on the word. But it's like something supposed to have happened, anyway. What is the word that I'm using, you know?
Predestined? Deja vu? Fate? I don't know what you're --
No, it's --
(Recording interrupted.)
interview two
July 8, 1956. John, I want to go back to Oklahoma with you.
All right. You go. I'll stay.
Tell me about your father.

Well, he was my father, and gave me my complexion, and that's all I can say about him. He was a musician. He played tuba in the church. I think they had a tuba and a piano, drums and a violin out of the family, in the church.
What church was it?
The Simmons Community Church. See, my grandfather owned this huge ranch. He was one of the few Indians that didn't go to the reservation, you know. And all of
this land was given to him. He never worked for anyone in his life.
Given to him by whom?
By the government. See, he was there during the time IT -- Indian Territory, that was what it was before Oklahoma.
Up until what year? In 1907, Oklahoma became a state.
Uh-huh. Well, he was there long before then.
What tribe was your grandfather from?

Creek. And oddly, I never heard my uncles or aunts ever speak of their grandfather, you know? And here in the last year, I've been trying to trace my family tree. And one of my cousins come up with my great-grandmother on the Simmons side -- I forget what her name was. I was told, but I've forgotten. She was a princess, an Indian princess. And her father sent her to Kansas City to school. And around about that time, a gentleman of your paint job European had a covered wagon. He was headed West. And he saw this beautiful Indian princess. And he stopped in Kansas City, and somehow, he got to woo her. And he married her. And I never heard my grandfather say anything about any brothers or sisters. You know, this real strange family, the Simmons family. So --
Was the man in the covered wagon Simmons?
Yes. He was white. Caucasian.
But that was where Simmons came from.
Yes. So my bloodline is all messed up.

So how I got my complexion -- my grandmother on the Simmons side was jet black, and she had a language of her own. Like, she's sit on the front porch in her rocking chair, she would quilt and make dresses and things like that. And rock all day long.

And she used to see a mile through her glasses, down on the end of her nose. And, like, she'd say, instead of saying 'my', 'I', she'd say 'unnas.' "Unnas children, unnas grandchildren." She'd say, "Unnas going to do this. Unnas going to do this," you know.
Where does that come from?
That was her own thing.
Do you know if that was some region -- (unintelligible)?
Not that I know of. She said unna.
And we all called her -- my grandfather and grandmother, Big Papa and Big Mamma. Because they were big. They were the heavies.
And I asked my mother, I say, "How old was I when you would put me across you lap, and I would start crying?" And she almost dropped what she had in her hands. She said, "You

couldn't have been more than 18 months old." She say, "I was changing your diapers." I say, "Well, the reason I remember this was because she would always hang my head over your left knee, and my head would be hanging off, and I would get this sensation up on a nostril, you know, like when you swim and you get too much water up your nose and it sting and burn? Well, that's the sensation I get every time she'd changed my diaper.

And when I would see her trying to get me in that position, I started raising hell. So she says, "You can remember that far back?" I say, "Sure." And like, we had to go through one of the pastures from our house on one of the knolls -- like the -- all the property, the main house was like the hub of a wheel, and the children's homes were up on a knoll around the house. So all the roads that led down to the main house, they could see them coming before they got there, you know.

So they dressed me in short pants, romper suits. You ever heard of rompers? Well, that's what I wore. And as big as my feet were, I couldn't stand -- I'd sit on the porch, everyone else would be having fun. I'd sit on the porch and be tugging at these pants legs, trying to get them down over my knobby knees. I had rickets, but I didn't know it. I didn't know I had rickets until I was a grown man. Had a, you know, a X-ray. They said, "Did you know you had rickets?"
"No, that's the first I heard of it." Well, you know, during those days, people didn't eat properly, you know.
And I believe you were telling me that your mother also was Indian, right?
Yes, she's a Cherokee on my grandmother's, on her side. The -- oh, boy, her name is all messed up. Anola Hayes Baldridge.
That's your mother's name?

Yes. Now, my grandfather, at times he would go by the name of Hayes, and at times he would go by the name of Baldridge. Then I was led to believe that they were two different men -- Hayes and Baldridge, two of my grandmother's husbands. And whichever one she was with, that's the name that she used.
And her grandfather, a witch doctor, his name was Koosah. How you spell it, don't ask me. Ain't my job. Koosah. (Laughs)
And that was your mother's grandfather?
Yes.
And this is through the Indian side --
Yeah, yeah, yeah. Cherokee side, yes.
And this was all -- all of your ancestors were Oklahomans.
Yes.
So how long were your mother and father together?
Three years.
So do you remember much about your father and his music?

No, the only time I would hear him play would be on Sundays. But they all tried to run my mother off the farm, because my father was never home. He was a rounder, you know? And when he was away, his brothers would come up to the house and try to steal the horses, to ride into town at night and different things, you know, and go different places. 'Cause they couldn't take any of my grandfather's horses, you know. And in his absence, they'd come up and steal chickens and my mother would stand there in the door and pick them off, like she had a shotgun, and the shells she would use, she would load them with hot pepper, with fat, you know, with fat meat? And put hot pepper on it. And she'd bust them in the butt every time she hit -- every time she'd shoot, she never missed. Called her 'Deadeye Dick'. And she could handle a handgun the same way, you know, and she had the advantage because she would stand on the porch and she could see these figures, you know, crouching, coming up the hill, you know.

Then the next day she would go visiting, say, 'Hello, there, Frank,' and hit him on his buttocks, and finally she would hit the right one and they'd jump. 'What you running up there, stealing my so-and-so-and-so-and-so.' You know.
How far out of Haskell was the farm?

Oh, let me tell you this. These romper suits, she would clean me all up and send me down to the big house to visit, you know. Well, I had to go through a pasture to get there. I'd get down to the foot of our place, it was barbed wires around it and we had a fence -- a gate there, you know. And that led me into the pasture.

Well, one day I had on a red one, and I know bulls didn't like red at that age. So when I opened that gate, I started running and hollering, 'Open the door, open the door.' Before I'd get even within hearing distance, they could hear me. When I got there, I'd have crocodile tears 'cause the bulls was going to get me, you know.

So I asked my mother, I says, -- after they struck natural oil and gas on the property, before we left there, I asked her, I says, -- after they had to get rid of all the cattle, I said, 'How many head of cattle did he have?' He had horses, cows, and bulls in this pasture that I had to go through. And just before you made the turn to the main house, he had a place for sheep and he had a place for goats, and on the right, was the corral, you know, for the horses. And he had a silo there, and -- oh, he was -- you know, had everything in order, you know.
And she says, 'I don't know how many cattle he had in that pasture.' She says, 'That was the small pasture.' I said, 'What?' She say, 'He had three pastures.' I said, 'Well,

I never saw them." They had one across the creek by the church, and one over -- 'way over in the southwest corner, wherever that was. And they had more cattle over there than they had in the one I had seen, you know.
So she wouldn't attempt to tell me how many cattle he had, livestock, you know.
Your father's name was what?

My father? John W. Simmons. And he goes by the name of J.W. He's alive, in Oklahoma City. Jive, henpecked. Incidentally, I called him last night and told him how henpecked he was. He says, "Is that what you call me, boy?" I say, "Yeah." Say, "What you want me to do?" I say, "I want you to be a man." "Well, if I was you and you was me, I wouldn't talk to my father like that." I said, "I'm not talking to you like a father," I said, "I'm talking to you man to man," I said. "Like, I can't recognize you as a father," I said. "You haven't done anything for me in your life." I say, "My uncle has been more of a father to me than you," you know. I mean, I don't know what, why I did it, I mean, the devil made me do it. I just woke up, feeling that way, you know? This was during one of my getups yesterday, while I was trying to sleep. I called him in broad daylight, 3:00 o'clock.
You left Haskell when you were five.
No, when I was three.
When you were three.
Uh-huh.
And that was when you went to Muskogee.
Uh-huh.
And you were telling me, at one point, your mother booked bands.
Yes.
Where was that?
That was in Sepulpa, Oklahoma, that was just out from Tulsa. Sepulpa and Sand Springs, they were all close together in West Tulsa.
That was later, and that was when you were how old?
Oh, I imagine I was about nine, I guess.
When you were living in Tulsa.
Yeah, we'd been to Kansas City and come back to Tulsa. And --
How did your mother happen to get into band booking?

Well, she was a manicurist in the barber shop. And invariably, she met all of the bands that came through because they would come through for manicures and things like that. Anything to look good, the haircuts and the manicures. And I met a lot of them that way besides going into these rehearsals. And I met Louis Armstrong getting a manicure,

when he had the Hot Five.

And behind meeting all these musicians, someone told her, say, "Nola," say, "You and your getup," they say, "Why don't you get all these musicians, you know, this one dance hall, why don't you start booking bands, you know, see if you can get a band down here for you," you know?

So she started inquiring and finally she did. And they had a sort of a frame dance hall. No enclosure at all, just looked like a frame of a house, you know, with a dance floor. And it was right on the bank of the Arkansas River.

Now, what bands there were, that she booked in there, I can't recall any of them. But she said she had Alphonso Trent there once, and she had Effie Jackson there once. But I don't recall who was there, because I never did go down, you know, to the river because I was living with my grandmother.
Well, when you were living in Tulsa and when you mentioned about the band rehearsals and the hotel, do you remember what bands -- you said you were carrying messages from the one section to --

Oh, yeah, yeah, I remember. Bands that I've mentioned here on the tape, prior to this, bands like Effie Jackson, Tommy Douglas, Benny Moten, Georgie Lee, Pee Wee Towles, Holder, Alphonso Trent, Clyde Love and Clouds of Joy, Nat Towles, -- that's one that I had forgotten, out of Nebraska. Lloyd Hunter, out of Denver. Just all the bands that was barnstorming,

they always made Tulsa. And then there were other bands, like I made notes on them, but I didn't bring them with me, that was traveling with the vaudeville shows, you know, like the Whitman Sisters, and Bessie Smith's entourage, and Ma Rainey and her Rabbit Foot Show, you know. Yeah. Like, they had a bunch of female singers during that time that I can relate to.
Bessie Smith came to Tulsa?
Yeah. She had her diamonds in her teeth and they would shine and light up the place, and then when they'd get up against it, she'd have the diamonds taken out and pawn them.
Was this -- the section rehearsals in the separate rooms, was this something you remember about a specific band, or all the bands?
All the bands did that. You know?
What kind of messages did you carry for them? Musical messages, or --

No, I'd go to get sandwiches and things, you know, and go ahead and get cigarettes for them. 'Course at that time there was no such thing you couldn't sell cigarettes to kids, you know, because they just knew that you were going to get them for your parents or a grownup, you know. And that's how I started smoking. (laughs)
Do you remember individuals from that time, when you were a boy?

Well, I remember a distant relative of Booker T. Washington. His name was Booker T. Pittman. He played alto saxophone. He had a sort of a Indian complexion, hair that went along with it. And when I got to New York, he was just retiring. I got to hear him at Cafe Society, just as I got to New York, and I never did hear any more from him.
Who was he playing with?

I think he was with Alphonso Trent, I think. And then Oscar Pettiford had a brother that played tenor saxophone. I can't remember his first name, but he could really play. And you know, Oscar Pettiford was from Oklahoma and he was born on the reservation. Until his family moved to Minneapolis. They were all from Oklahoma.
Did you know Oscar at all?

No. I met him in Minneapolis. When I was with Lena Horne. We were doing a show up there, I forget the name of it, the club. I remember a trumpet player, a little short trumpet player, and the trumpet was so long, it was almost as long as he was tall. His name was Orange or Owen or something of that order. I never could get distinctly, but his last name was White. And the Douglas Brothers. They played reed instruments, woodwinds.

Oh, they had a big, huge guitarist named Jim Dandy. Now, he and Charlie Christian would have a battle of the guitars.
Where was this, in Tulsa?

No, they would do their battling in Oklahoma City. He would come through there with various bands, you know, like one nighters or something, they would come and gig for him, you know. I seen him often, with different bands.
Did Charlie Christian come to Tulsa?
No. Charlie Christian eventually -- primarily was a bass player. And his brother taught him guitar. And his brother is a guitarist.
You mentioned that your mother used to put you on the bandstand with the bands, and that was when you first got acquainted. What bands did you share the bandstand with?

Well, Benny Morton and Georgie Lee. Oh, I forgot to tell you. Georgie Lee went out to lunch, as we say today, you know. He would stand out on the corner and just look. So his sister, Julia Lee, took over the band. And eventually it broke up, and then, the next I heard of her, she came out here and formed a small combo to record for Capitol. And that's the last I heard of her.
And the McKinney Cotton Pickers, I sat on their bandstand. And I don't remember who all in it, the personnel, at that time.
You mentioned food shows. Were those day or night affairs?
Night affairs.
And was that something that went on --

They had -- no, they had a regular dances, but most of them were food shows, you know, locally. Trying to make money, George Lee would maybe be in town, or Benny Moten would be in town, and they didn't want to miss that bread, that money, they would whip up a dance real quick and have a food show.
And people would cook and have contests to see whose pies were the best and whose cake was the best and all, and the band would end up eating it all. 'Cause they were half starved anyway.
Do you know if that was done in very many places, or if that was a custom peculiar to Tulsa?

I don't know. This was in Kansas City. Yeah. And Jap Allen's Cotton Pickers. I sat on the bandstand with them. I sat on the bandstand with Zack White. Oh, and I sat on the bandstand with Sy Oliver's band, but I can't recall who he had in his band. This was long before he had any idea there was a Jimmy Lunceford. He had his own band.
Did you make any friends with any of the musicians that you met on the bandstand?

Oh, they all would play with me, you know, roughhouse, you know. Rough me up, you know. Pick me up and throw me in the air and throw me from one to the other, you know. And I love it, every bit of it. And Carolina Cotton

Pickers, Walter Page and the Blue Devils, I think I mentioned earlier that he had a jazz session, and O RAN Page, Lips Page and his band, and he broke up the band and went to Kansas City and joined Basie.
And Buster Smith, one of his saxophonists retained the band in Oklahoma City. I don't know who he had in the band.
You mentioned that some of these dances and shows were on the domestics' night off.
Yeah, that would be Thursday nights, like, they worked for the whites, you know, out in the aristocratic part of town, you know, the aristocracy, you know.
Now, like in Tulsa, where the rich people lived, they called that the South End. And the maids' night out was Thursday night, you know.
So, therefore, there were a lot of events scheduled on Thursday night?
All the bands knew.
A band would always get a gig on Thursday night.
Yeah. Local band or out of town bands, they said, 'Well, we can always go through Tulsa on Thursday night, even anyone else hasn't booked it up,' you know. Or Saturday night.
Saturday night, that was the maids'
night off, too? Saturday night was --
Saturday night would just be the town.
Were the dances segregated?

No, this was -- see, the town was divided, because the world -- not the world, but the United States' greatest race riot, I mean, race riot, not looting or anything, you know, race riot, was in Tulsa, Oklahoma.

In the early 20's, I was a baby. The Ku Klux Klan -- how it started, there were two black brothers coming from the South End, half crocked on the bus. And they sat down in the front of the bus. They refused to get in the back of the bus where they were supposed to be during those times, you know, ride in the back.

And they were reported to someone, I guess the Great Vizor of the Ku Klux Klan. But at Booker T. High, overlooking Booker T. High was a hill where they made bricks. You know, they had their kilns and their ovens and everything up there. And they called that the Brickyard Hill. And from anywhere in Tulsa, if a cross was burned on this hill, you could see it all over town.

So that night, they burned a cross on the hill. And Ku Klux Klan at that time, they rode in touring cars. Are you hip to touring cars? Well, you know how many people they held. Well, each member of the Klan had a hound and a bullwhip.
Now, all of the icemen were white, all of the newspaper

men were white. And they knew how to gain entrance to the Negroes' homes, for deliveries. Like, the paper man, he would throw the paper on the yard, you know. But the iceman, he knew to go around the back, and he knew how to hit the screens a certain way, where the latch would pop up, he would put the ice in the box and walk out the front door and the door would lock behind itself, you know.

And in front of our house was a boilerworks. Well, a boiler is like the basic part of a oil derrick. It has holes, diameter, say, about four to six inches around in circumference, and we would get in the part where they would burn the fire, you know, just like a locomotive engine. And we would look out these holes, and play Indians and cowboys and say, "Dow, dow" through these holes, you know.

Well, the whites got this message and they let themselves in these Negroes' homes and left them in their beds, dead. They stationed themselves under these boilers and as they ran out of their house, they'd shoot them down. And they all ended up walking out of town to a picnic grounds, called Jenks. And they had them all rounded up out there. And they would tie them up and whip them, some of them that had been bad actors before, you know, that they had it in for.
And one of the policemen there, his name was Smitherman -- well, this happened before he was a policeman, they cut off one of his ears and made him eat it, and say, "Isn't

that good?" And said, "Yes." They cut another one's privates off, made him eat it. He hemorrhaged to death, naturally. Another one, they -- what's the word? Castrated, and made him eat his balls, his testicles, you know?
Who told you the stories of all this?
My mother and my grandmother. And they tell it over and over so much that I feel so that I was there, you know.

And somehow, the blacks got messages outside the city, on the phone. At that time they had those old windup, ring-ring-ring-ring-ring-ring phones, and they called. How they got the word out, I don't know. Maybe a car, someone left town in a hurry, you know, to get away from it.

But the outlying towns got this message, and they came in. Like, the town was surrounded. They broke in all of the pawnshops and got all the firearms that they have, plus the arms that they already owned. And you talk about killing. They killed awhile. They called in the state militia and the National Guard.

So the town was divided by the railroad tracks after that. And the Negroes from then on owned everything that they needed. They didn't go down to the white part of town for anything. Unless they just wanted to go down to sightsee, you know, coogling, you know, windowshopping. We had our own theaters, our own grocery stores, our own drug stores, own hotels, own
funeral parlors, our own schools.
When a band would come to town, a traveling band, and play, say, Thursday nights in the Negro section, would that band maybe play Saturday night in the white section for a white audience?

Sometimes. There was a dance hall there called the Skyline. That was a public dance. Now, when Duke and Cab came to town, Duke would generally play the convention hall, and Cab would be at some arena where they held hockey games, you know. It was an arena, like.
Did everybody go, or was it restricted?
No, this was black dances, you know.
Was there ever anything that both blacks and whites could go to?

No, no, no. I recall going to Duke's concert at the convention hall. I scaled the wall. Scaled the wall. You talk about a cat walker. I scaled the wall, bricks, and let myself in a window. And during that time, the tune "Lazy Bones" had just been composed, and Ethel Waters was singing with the band at that time. And Bubber Miley was with the band, and I forget this other -- Freddy -- what the hell was his name?
(laughs)
Guy .?
Hm?
Guy? Or Jenkins?

Freddy Jenkins. Freddy Jenkins was very personable. He was a personality man. Oh, he'd spin his arm, they'd play a solo. Otto Hardwick was in the band, called him Toby. Now, he mastered the soprano saxophone then. To me, he got a better sound than Sidney Bechet. And Johnny Hodges played some good soprano saxophone.

And they were playing "East St. Louis Toodle-Oo," and what's this tune: (sings) Dun-dun-duh-h-h--. "Chant of the Weed." that was Don Redman 's tune. That was one of the few tunes that I heard him play, that he didn't write. And I can't remember the entire program for the evening.
Was that the first time you saw Duke?

Yes. Oh, fabulous, because he had a light man to travel with him, at that time. And for different moods and different things, they'd have different colors, you know. And up through the years, he maintained this opening this way.

Like, it'd come up, and all you'd see is the silouettes. Or sometimes, a real low baby pink, and then it'd lighten up and you could see the band, you know. As the band would play louder, the lights would come up. Oh, he was a real showman. Beautiful man. Beautiful musician, beautiful composer. No one will ever surpass him. Music is never mastered, but no one will ever surpass what he has offered to the music world. The Duke, William Edward Kennedy. The greatest. That's my opinion,
one man's opinion.
Do you suppose maybe you began to get the glimmerings of ambition to be up there on the stand when you saw shows like that when you were --

No, I just loved music. I loved any of the arts. Right now, I have a hankering to -- for bit parts, you know? As a character actor. Because it's always been a secret desire of mine, to act, you know. That's what I thought that I would be. But somehow, I took a detour to the music. And I'm still looking forward to the acting.
You mentioned Ernie Fields. Was Fields a Tulsa band?
Yeah.
And Walter Page.
He was out of Oklahoma City.
But you saw him in Tulsa. Right?
Not the Blue Devils. I saw him in Tulsa with Benny Moten.
When did you see the Blue Devils? You did see them, didn't you?

No, I never did hear his band. But I was aware of it. Like, sometimes he would make trips to Tulsa by himself, just to come over to Tulsa, you know, when he was idle. Say, 'Who's that?' Say, 'That's Walter Page of the Blue Devils.'

The first time you told me about marching post Sousa, last year, you mentioned him, I made a note that you said in 1931. Then, earlier on the tape, you said it was in '33 or '34. Which date do you think it was?

Well, let's see, I started -- I got out of grammar school when I was about sixth grade. That's when I left grammar school. I went into a junior high. I played trumpet the last year in junior high, which was 7th, 8th and the 9th grade. Then I joined the Varsity band, the high school band, at Booker T. High School in my sophomore year. So it was my sophomore year. So what year would that have been? Yeah.

Let's see, when I left Tulsa when I was 17, 16, 15, I was about 14 or 15.
Yeah.
Okay, I was wanted to get the dates to match it. You mentioned Billy Hadnot earlier. Was he from Tulsa?
Yes.
And you knew him there.
Yes. We played on the same playground.
Did you play any music together?
No, this wasn't playing. This was just walking and talking, and getting off in groups. And it wouldn't
be to play.
You mentioned Commodore Park. What did he play?
A string bass.

The story you told about your high school graduation and the white shoes you didn't have, you didn't place it in Los Angeles. Because we were talking there and you jumped from some high school experiences in Tulsa to graduation, but you -- I wanted to make it absolutely clear.
Oh, the --
You left --
I left Tulsa a month before graduation. I left Tulsa a month before graduation.
And then you graduated from Jefferson High School in Los Angeles.
Uh-huh.
You told me off the tape about joining the band at Jefferson. Could you tell me on the tape?
Oh, yeah. Did I tell you on the tape.
No. Not about the Jefferson band. You mentioned joining the band but that's all you said on the tape.

Oh. Well, as I didn't have to attend any classes, I wanted to be around the music, you know. And in spite of having to have this operation and this scar tissue, when I first started back to school, I picked up my horn too

soon, and busted the incision from the inside, which caused a small hernia. And I had three operations in the same spot. And it remained a hernia. And I was supposed to go back to the hospital and have it straightened out. They let me out to gain some strength and get some sunshine and come back. I went back. They said, 'Is it bothering you?' I said, 'No.' They said, 'Well, leave it alone. Don't trouble it until it troubles you,' you know. Say, 'You might live to be a ripe old age with it, and never bother you,' you know.
And the scar tissue has never broken open, you know, like from the outside. 'So, you're in no danger, you know. You can live with it.' So I never did go back to have it straightened out. You know.
Now, what were we talking about before that?
The way you got in the band.

Oh. I had a need to do something in school, you know. So I hung around the band room the first two weeks, and I -- well, school had started and two weeks in school, well, all the members in the band was hold over from the previous semester, you know. And they generally knew what parts they were going to play and who was going to play what instrument and blah, blah, blah, you know.
So the band was pretty well oriented, you know. So I'd stand in the door, and this was in like -- I was disturbing them, by standing in the door. And he says, 'Don't stand in

the door," you know. I said, "I want to join the band." He says, "Well, this band is too far advanced for you to join the band." I say, "I can play." He say, "But we are two weeks into the semester." He said, "It's too far advanced for you." I say, "I played this music," you know? He didn't believe me. "It's two weeks."

I still hung around about two more weeks. So to get me off of his back, he called his favorite musicians out of the band, that would take care of the band in his absence. It was a Hebrew boy, he was like pretty well known academically. He was seeing and whatnot, all the boys, usually had something to do with all the boys on the ground, you know. And running errands for the teachers and things. He was mainly out of the Dean's office. He was a professional snitch, you know. He would let them know everything that was going on in the school grounds.

So he says, "Cohen," he says, "let this kid use your horn." So the first number they pulled was "Caissans Go Marching Along." Says, "Give him your book." I says, "I don't need it." He looked at me. He gave a downbeat. I played it. "Semper Fidelis." I played it. "Anchors Aweigh." I played it. He says, "Hail to the Chief." I played it. Then he started getting easier: "Hail, Hail, the Gang's All Here," you know.
And then, that got him. So he says, "Come on in."

He says, "Is there an extra horn back there?" It was an old, beat-up cornet, it had a thousand dents in it, the valves was stuck. I had to take them out and clean them, and -- what is this little black paper? It's not sandpaper -- emory. Emory cloth. I had to take that and get all the rust off the valves, and then wash them down with ca oil so they would slide. Didn't use valve oil. Used ca oil to wash them down.

And then I dried it as much as I could with clean cloth, and run hot water through it several times to open up the dirt and spit from other, prior players. But I had my own mouthpiece. I still have three mouthpieces that I used with my trumpet, you know. But I didn't have a cornet mouthpiece.

So I took an alto peck horn, that uses the cornet. He say, "You play the peck horn, too?" I say, "Yeah." So, wow. So I got the cornet, and so instead of being in the back line, I sat right next to Cohen. (chuckles)

So Cohen eliminated himself from the band because of this. I had deflated his ego, and he felt a need to be somewhere else. So during recess, lunch hour I'd sit there and talk with him, you know. And after he found out that I had played for Sousa, he couldn't love me enough, you know, because John Philip Sousa was to bands what Duke Ellington was to jazz, you know.
And sometimes I'd come in and he'd say, "Simmons," he says, "we're short on alto horns." That's the peck horn.
"Would you mind playing one today?" I'd say, "Okay." Da-nn-da-nn-da-da, da-nn-da-nn-da-da. Say, "Can you play bass horn?" I say, "Yeah." Say, "Only one finger difference."
He say, "You play the B flat or the double B?" I'd say, "Either one." He says, "Well, you play the B flat." I says, "Okay."
Had you played all these before in Tulsa?
(chuckles)
I had fumbled around with them. Behind the teacher's back.

So he had some string basses back there, but no one knew how to play them. He said, "Do you know anything about strings?" I say, -- well, I know the bass is back there -- I say, "I was beginning to play bass violin before I left Oklahoma." He say, "Oh, yeah?"
So he put two or three with me. I'm supposed to be teaching them. I'm learning myself at the same time, you know.
Had you played it in Oklahoma?

I was telling you This Charles Grimm, that had the orchestra there? Every time they would have intermission, I'd grab the bass, you know. And sometimes Baby Boy -- he was in the band -- he'd let me sit in. And at that time, they had this tune, "The Man From Harlem," Cab Calloway, and "White Heat," and "Mule Face Blues." And I'd get up and I'd play it just from having listened to him, you know, from ear. And he just knew that I could play a bass.
So the Wood n Brothers would come if they needed a bass player. So I was so good in his eyesight he would let me check a bass out over the weekend to go and make this gig.
That was Britt Woodman and Brother Woodman, right?
Brett, William and [Cony] -sp.
Which one was known as brother?
Huh?
Which was known as brother? Which of the Woodman brothers was called Brother? One of them was called Brother.
William, I think, because [Cony] was a tenor saxophone --
And what does William play?
Piano.
And the father's a musician also.
Yeah. The whole family's musicians.
Musical.
The father's name?

I think it was William. William Woodman. I think. And Jesse Sailis was the drummer, and I was the bassist. And the three brothers, they doubled on instruments, like Brett played trombone and alto, and [Cony] played tenor and a trumpet. And then, William played piano. So it made it sound like a big band, you know. Had a little fun. And I left them, Joe
Comfort took my place with them.
Was the gig with the Woodman Brothers as a bass player the first professional job you had ?
Yeah. Still in the school.
Joe Comfort was already playing professionally, wasn't he?
No.
He wasn't?

Uh-uh. Mingus was after me, but much further advanced than any of us, because he had a desire to write as well, you know, and he was hanging up under Red Calendar for dear life, to teach him how to write. And he learned, you know.
Joe Comfort's ex-wife told me that Mingus used to follow Joe Comfort around, begging for pointers on the bass, and asking --
May be. Because I had left town. I don't know. You mean Maidie?
Yeah.
Could be. I don't know. I'd be a liar if I said yes, and I'd be a liar if I said No. You know.
But Joe Comfort, Red Calendar and Charlie Mingus were all around.
No, well, Calendar was the Daddy of the town, you know. Besides Al Morgan, 'cause Al Morgan had a

big time name, you know, having played with Cab Calloway. But locally, Red Calendar was the top man. You know, and he stayed here with his roots. And he had a trip back to New York with Lester and Lee Young's combo, and I don't think he ever went back there to play any music any more. He may have played a concert, you know, like Newport, or something like that. I'm not sure.
Was he also playing tuba then?
No.
It was later on that he played tuba.
Well, he was primarily a tuba player in Georgia. I think that was his home.
I thought it was Virginia.*
I don't know. Somewhere back there.
So he played a tuba there and then he played bass here.
Yeah, string bass, yes. And then he and I were in a symphony band called the Humanist. Did you ever hear of the Humanist?
No. That was in Los Angeles?

Yes. It was a symphony orchestra. And the way it got its name, someone asked -- they'd filled out forms, you know, saying 'What race?' Someone said, "Human." They said, "Who is this that signed 'human race'?" So they named the group the Humanists, you know?
The whole symphony?
Yes.
Was it of mixed race?
Yes. And --
What year was that?
Oh, this was, say, around '48. Eric Dolphy was in the band. Another little boy played oboe. I've forgotten his name. And Red was playing the tuba. And --
Where did the band perform?
There was a rehearsal hall there on Hoover, about 22nd or 3rd on Hoover, upstairs. We rehearsed up there.

So he said, "We're going to have a concert next week, such-and-such a date." And there was a professional bass player here in town, his name was Bob something. I forget his name. I'd recognize it in the directory. I've seen him several times since I've been back here. He was in the band, playing string bass.

So I appeared to the concert. Everyone's dressed informally. I showed up in a tuxedo. (laughs) Well, that's what I was -- you know, assumed you were supposed to wear a tuxedo, you're going to play a concert, you know.
Where was the concert?
Huh?
Where was the concert?

We were playing the same place, yes. That was funny. Yeah. And Eric, the conductor stayed on him. He never was in tune. Eric couldn't get a job in town, a job here in town. And Eric didn't become Eric until he went to New York. But they had another boy that played more saxophone than Eric. His name was -- what the hell was his name? Oh, he died not too long ago. I'll forget it for the present, and run into another block.
So there was what, a sprinkling of jazz-oriented musicians, and then what, classically oriented musicians? All playing together?

Uh-huh. Now, the year that I graduated, that was the bandmaster's last year there. Then they had a black conductor, Brown, Professor Brown. Now, he had fellows in his band, like Lamar Wright, Jr., Dexter Garden, Lawrence Marabel, all of that age category.
They were just one year behind you?

Yeah. Well, not one year behind me. But he took over the band that year. But they weren't one year behind me. They were, like, just coming in from junior high school. And he put out quite a few jazz musicians.
Do you remember Professor Brown's first name?
No, I don't. In fact, I never even went over to the school to meet him.
You never what?
I never went over to the school to meet him.
What was the name of your jive cousin who was a booking agent?
Thaddeus -- they called him Thad -- Hickerson.
Did he play any music, or did he just book?
Well, in high school, he played the punishing instrument, the sousaphone.
He was an Oklahoma cousin who came out here.
Yeah, from Muskogee.

At the time you took the band to Sacramento for the after-hours gig, was there much music being played there? You mentioned one other after-hours place, the Club Eureka, but were there many other clubs? 'Cause you said something about, when the clubs closed, that everybody came to where you --
Yeah, yeah, but they were all dime-a-dance places, you know. And, like, my hours were from nine

until. That was until the last soul got out of there, you know. Like, we'd go to work at 9:00, we were idle from 9:00 to 12:00. And then when the other places break up, then that's when we'd have to start work. 12:00 until.
The musician Hank Fullalove that you mentioned, you said he wrote Westerns. Did he use his own name?
No, no, he used a pseudonym.
Do you know what the pseudonym was?

No, I don't. I can't recall. He ended up being a Marine, and he really looked the part 'cause he was huge, you know. Wore the uniform, looked good on him. The uniform complimented him. And then, when he got out of the service, he stayed in Seattle, Washington. I haven't seen him since.
The hotel in San Diego, with the nightclub downstairs. Did you think of the name of that?
No.
You were saying earlier, you thought it might be Dunbar.
No, that was the name of the hotel.
But not the club.
No.
But the club was in --
The club was in the hotel, on the
ground floor, in the back.
And the hotel was Dunbar. Then you said the owner of the club's name was Ramsey and he owned another club or another hotel?
Another hotel, around the corner.
And it was called what?
The Yesmar. That's Ramsey spelled backwards.
Was there any music there?
No.
And you said the Honeydripper came down. You're talking about Joe Liggin?
Joe Liggin.
And you mentioned a drummer named Daniels.
I can't recall his first name.

Okay, and you said there was a controversy about whether or not Baby Louis taught Lionel Hampton to play drums and vibes. Now, off the tape you said it was generally accepted that he did. Then on the tape you said it was controversial about whether he did or not. What do you think? What did he say?
Well, I don't know, because Baby had traveled so much, you know, before I ever met him, that I don't know whether he and Lionel Hampton ever met. 'Cause, see,

Hamp came up around Chicago, you know? And Baby [Louis] came out of Kansas City. And I don't know if they were both doing the same thing at the same time, or who got what from who. But every time I heard Baby [Louis,] he was doing it before I ever heard of --
(End of proceedings.)
P R O C E E D I N G S
We were talking about Baby [Lewis]. Where did the story come from that he had taught Lionel Hampton?
Well, various musicians, couldn't really recall their names, but I was first exposed to Baby [Lewis] in the midwest. And then when I got to California, I heard Lionel Hampton doing the same thing.
Where in the midwest did you first hear Baby [Lewis]?
Kansas City.
And did you every talk to Baby [Lewis] about it -- about whether or not --
No, no. No, because when I worked with him, I hadn't heard this story of whatever you may call it at that time.
Later, you heard it.
(Inaudible)
Yes.
And did you ever hear whether Hampton ever said anything about it?
No.
Okay, you mentioned the old Brunswick recording studio on Western Avenue in Los Angeles. Whereabouts on Western Avenue was it?
It was around, just north of Olympic on the east side of the street. They have some gallerys there now.
But we had to go in by the side or the back of these places, these buildings on the front.
And you mentioned when you played with Art Tatum, Roy Eldridge took you to his gig in Chicago. And that Art Tatum knew you and your playing. He didn't even have to look up when he heard you --
(Laughter).
-- when did Art Tatum get to know you? In Los Angeles?
Yes.
You played with him in Los Angeles?
No, I heckled him in Los Angeles. Yes, (laughter).
When did he hear your playing?

After hours at the Club Alabam, Breakfast Club upstairs. Art Tatum, Don Byas, Eddie Barefield, Al Morgan. We'd jam up there every morning. And Al Morgan being slow, I'd always run and grab the bass. He couldn't be found, I'd grab the bass. Band start to playing, I pulled the first note, Tatum get up (laughter), there'll be a slight intermission.
That was during your first stint in Los Angeles?
That was in '36.
I think there is a little discrepancy of dates back on the first tape when you mentioned leaving shortly

after high school to go to Sacramento, coming back to Los Angeles, working for Curtis Mosby and then going to San Diego. And when I asked you the date that you worked at the Mosby Club, the Memo, you said '40 something, I think or '48.
No, no, I recall the incident and I can clarify that.
