No, no, no.
That's what I wanted to clarify. Did you then work for Mosby again, after you had been back East?

No. No. '36 I went to Tempe with my cousin. As I said I just graduated the day before. So that had to be '36, not '37. I came back to Los Angeles and went to Sacramento in '36. I came back to Los Angeles and played the Memo. That was '36. I had my own band at the Filipino Night Club in '36.

What else did I do in '36? Oh, I giged around town with the Woodman brothers in '36 off and on when I didn't have my own group you know. And besides this job at the Mimo, Curtis Mosby formed a larger aggregation to play at the Pier in Long Beach and the clientel was mostly sailors, you know. We played and played under good conditions. The only thing is that he did-
n't pay anyone. He was a bad pay. But by my mother knowing him, he didn't hold back on my money because he knew that she would knock him down with her pocket book, her purse or draw a pistol on him.
(Laughter).
Your mother is about how big?
(Laughter.) She's about 5'2". Strong as an ox.
How big was Mosby?
Well Mosby was about the same height. He was rotund.
Desmond was tall and slim?
Yeah. And then there was a younger brother, I forget his name. He was a teenager at that time.
Desmond was a dancer?
Yes, he was with the Chocolateers, the group that put out "Peckin".
Uh-huh.
With Ben Pollack. They did this at the Cotton Club.
That's the Los Angeles Cotton Club? Frank Sebastiano Here in Culver City.
Yeah.
You mentioned that your first job in Chicago was with Lil Armstrong. How long did you work with him?
Just, that one night. A one-night gig.
And you said that you worked for John Litman. Did you work at the Club Deluxe or did you --
Yeah, yes. Club Deluxe.
In his band?
Joe Hughes' Club Deluxe. It's across the street from White's Amusement Park.
And so you said that's the first place you said you saw Ray Nance. So Ray Nance was in the floor show?
No that wasn't the first place I saw Ray Nance.
Oh, where was the first place?
Ray Nance was working with Earl Hines.
Before he worked at the Club Deluxe, is that right?

Yeah, I heard Ray Nance when Earl Hines came out here to Los Angeles before I ever left here. He and Trummy Young was with the Band. And they were featured instrumentalist and singers with the band at that time.
So the next time after that that you saw Ray Nance was when you were working at the Club Deluxe?

No, he was still with Earl Hines when I went to Chicago and then he left Earl and I think he worked with Horace Henderson's band for a while. And there was another obscure band, a saxophone player, I think his name was Delbert White. He had a band, all of the bands around other than Earl
Hines, they played the Swingland.
Where was that?

It was on Michigan Boulevard, Garfield Boulevard and just off of South Park, west of South Park. Right at almost, between the and South Park. And it took on various names down through the years but it was originally the Swingland.

When you were talking about Roy Eldridge joing Gene Krupa and he took his music with him and he changed the name of all the tunes and a number called "Nothing Yet," became "Balls of Fire" and then you said it was the theme of a film "Balls of Fire".
Yes, Barbara Stanwyck.
How did that come about that Roy Eldridge theme get to Hollywood?
He was with Krupa's band at the time.
Yeah, but how did-Krupa's band didn't play in the film did it?
Yeah, --
Oh, it did?
Yeah.
Oh, I'm sorry, that I didn't realize. So did they appear in the film or just play the music.
I think they just played the music. They may have been seen, I didn't see the picture. Still have-
How long were you in Chicago before you went to New York?
Four years.
Oh, and you said that Curtis Mosby's wife --
Oh, let's see, I'm sorry, I went there in '37 and I left February of '41. So three years and a couple of months.
-- you mentioned that Curtis Mosby's wife ran one of the Clubs on Central Avenue in Los Angeles. Do you remember what her name was?
No, I don't. Oh, all I knew was Mrs. Mosby.
Was she an entertainer at all?
Not that I know of. She may a -- have been. The Club's name was the "Last Word".
It was the "Last Word," the "Downbeat," the mo. Those were the names of all the Clubs?
The "Alabam."
The "Alabam."

And then later they had a little band after my mother had tricked me back out here from Chicago in '38. They had a band, a place up around 42nd and Third called the "Big Apple". It was primarily a billiard parlor and they empty

it out and made a sort of nightery out of it. But it wasn't a night club in the true sense. Like they had a bar, you know, with a rail you can put your foot on, a band and a dance floor. That was all. No show.
How about Brother's was the after hours part upstairs on Central Avenue, was that operating?
Brother's After Hours Club, yes that was operating.
Oh, you were talking about how active you had been at Booker T. Washington High School in Tulsa. You told me being associated with the Harmonica Band. Does that mean you played harmonica?
Yeah.
You hadn't mentioned that when you talked about your instruments.

Oh, yeah. Well the bandmaster (Professor Jeff) formed a harmonica band. And you know harmonicas have numbers on it and we learned to read on harmonica. And we were going to give a little concert in the auditorium. The day of the concert, someone stole my harmonica. (Laughter). Or I mislaid it, I don't know what happened. I was in the wings while they were out on the stage playing. And the ham that was in me, they started playing 'Turkey in the Straw' and I strutted across the stage doing like a turkey. (Laughter). Broke up everybody. Teachers, students, mother was there, she fell out. (Laughter).
I had to be in the show. (Laughter).
Did you ever get another harmonica and play anymore?
Yes, I got another harmonica. I got a chromatic harmonica but I didn't do much with it.
You never played anymore harmonica?
No.
When you were mentioning the guitar player, you were mentioning a musician named Louis Gonzales that you weren't sure you were confusing him --
I'm almost sure he was Nat Cole's guitarist.
Oh, because I was going to ask you about that. I wasn't aware that Nat Cole had a guitarist of Spanish or Mexican --
Yeah, not Nat Cole, Lee Young. Lee and Lester had this guitarist.
When, where, here?
Here, when they came, to New York and played Cafe Society downtown, they played the Capri, it was -- what was the fellow's name that owned the Swing Club and the place over on Vine Street.
Billy Berg?
Billy Berg. Billy Berg had the Capri and Leo Watson's Band played there too.
Where was that?

I can't recall the location geographically in the City. Because I was taken there for the first and the last time and Leo Watson was appearing there. He was playing drums with chair arms. He didn't have any drum sticks.
(Laughter).
And skatten. WILLARD: When you first got to know Lester Young. where was he living? (Recording Interruption).
Right next door to 802 on Central Avenue, Local you know.
That was Local 767, 802 is New York.
So and his sister could play some saxophone, Irma.
Oh.
Yeah.
Were there three children in the family?
Lester, Lee and Irma. Now Irma has a daughter that can play hell out of piano right now. She's up north somewhere.
What is her name?
I don't know.
Up north, in California?
Well, San Francisco, Sacramento, somewhere around in there.
So you first got to know the Young family when you were --

Now, I met Lee as a dancer. And Lee got hooked on drums behind Cozy Cole[.]. See Stuff Smith came out here and played the Famous Door and Cozy was chewing gum, you know. And this hotel room, he didn't have a practice pad. He had one of these restaurant plates wrapped up in a bath towel and he'd use that for a practice pad. And Lee would just hang around him all the time. And by Lee being a dancer, he had the rhythm concept, you know. And he bought him a pair of drums, a drum set and within a month he was swinging everybody off of Central Avenue, you know,

And then he got in the book. And started learning his paradiddles and his ratamacues and everything flam you know, like Cozy was doing. And he got real agressive as a drummer. He took over the city as a drummer practically because when he joined King Cole. He was, his reading was such that he could conduct a band. And if anyone in the band made a mistake on reading their part, he'd jump up off the drums and go and correct them, you know. And they say "wow".

And when King Cole had an engagement to play, he went in advance to rehearse the band. He was a musician. All just brought it out of him. Now the family, they had a family band and Lester was playing piano, I think he started on the piano. But in the band, he played trumpet and drums. And Lee danced and Irma played saxophone. I think Lee played trumpet
and the father played drums and Moms played piano. I think that's how it was. If I'm wrong, I stand to be corrected. But they all, you know, it was a family band.
That was here in Los Angeles?
No, this was around Texas. They are travelled, you know.
Didn't his father originally have a band with the circus when Lester was very small?
A circus or carnival or one. I'm not sure.
But when they got to Los Angeles, that was after that, right?
Yeah.
And they didn't have a family band?
No.
Was Lester -- Lester was playing around Los Angeles?

No, no. Lester went back to Kansas City and he had an occasion to follow Coleman Hawkins in Fletcher Henderson's Band. But he didn't stay very long because he didn't have that full sound that Hawk had. And he wasn't accepted so he left the band and returned back to Kansas City. But as of today, all of the avant gardes, they're trying to get that Lester Young sound.
So the first time you met Lester was
when?
When he was with Basie.
And where was it that you met him?

Here in Los Angeles, when they came out here. And this was a say around '37. When they made "Swinging the Blues" and "Taxi War Dance", "Every Tub", "Sent for you Yesterday and Here you come Today"; everything they did was good. "Rock-a-bye Basie", you know. And then later on, "The World is Mad", "Harvard Blues", did you ever hear Don Byas play the Harvard Blues with Basie? (Whistle). He told a beautiful story on that. But the band, the reed section was like Lester Young and Herschel Evans. Now Herschel Evans took on the appearance of a school teacher, you know professor, a Doctor or something, you know. He was always erect. Rimless glasses. Immaculate. And he had a beautiful sound, you know, I mean like related somewhat to Coleman's sound, Coleman Hawkins. Only it was a might bit smaller. But had he lived, I imagine his sound would have gotten much larger. And he was the one that played "Blue and Sentimental" and Lester Young played clarinet on that side. Speaking of tenor-players, there a, was another tenor player, Dick Wilson, out of Andy Kirk's Band. But he -- you could barely hear him. He had to be miked, you know; but the things that came out of his horn sounded like snakes. It was a very, he was a very, very nice looking young man, he was an ex-football player from college. He was with Andy Kirk and he was from

Seattle, Washington. And his mother died and that was his only living relative and when she died and left everything to him. He went bananas. He just went out to lunch. It was a long time before he rejoined Kirk. Then when he did join Kirk, he turned Alcoholic(?) alcoholic, drug addict, you name it, whatever you had to offer, he wanted some of it.
He would come off the band stand with one pants leg rolled up like he had been riding a bicycle. That's where he was scratching. (Laughter.) But he could play that tenor.
You mention [LaGranda] Mason and [LaGrande Mason's brother, what was his name?
I can't recall.
What did he play?
Bass. Two bass players.
Besides upstairs at the Alabam, where were the favorite jamming places in the thirties in Los Angeles?

Oh, wow. I can't remember the name. It was a restaurant, oh, wow, you really caught me off base. It was a restuarant and we use to go in the back after it was closed. And then there was another place --
Where was it located?
The restaurant was between 42nd and 43rd on Central. And then there was another restaurant -- see they changed the streets over there.
They put in a street, didn't they?

Because when I went -- when I first came to Los Angeles. The street I lived on was 40th, that was the street that the Downbeat Corner was on. And then they changed that to 41st, you know. So if I mislead you in streets, it's not my fault, it's the City Planner. (Laughter).
Yeah I know, between Santa Barbara and Vernon I think they added a street and changed the numbers.
Uh-huh. We just jammed everywhere we could find to jam -- that's you know -- oh, most favorite spot to jam was around Nellie Lutchers house.
Where did Nellie live?
She lived right around the corner on old 40th Street from the Downbeat. And she was some kind of piano player. This was before she sang. And you wanted to lock up -- you locked up there.
Everybody went to Nellie's house?
Yeah. Uh-huh.
Who all can you remember jamming at Nellie's?

I can remember these, two tenor players I was telling you about. Bob [Dawes] and Andy Anderson were there and Washington out of Earl Hines band was there. And a trumpet player by the name of Lloyd Hunter and Don Byas come in and wiped out everybody (laughter) because see they were trying to see how many choruses they could play, you know, in jamming and when Don Byas came down here, he changed things around.

Like you had to go through the keys every tune that you played, you had to play it in every key. Every night, he would end up with just him and the drummer on the bandstand (laughter). And he went to Chicago and did this at the Club 'Duluxa' run everybody off the bandstand, he went to New York and did it,
Who was usually the drummer here in Los Angeles?

Oh, he'd wear out a million drummers. (Laughter). Oh, just don't go into that. Because he'd play as long as he could, you know, and he was powerful to be such a young man. He played with more force then, then did he in New York. He would take breaths and here he'd say (sound), getting my breath and when he spit it out, it looked like the mouthpiece was going to jump out of his mouth. He would just shake, he was such a small man.
Well, did he have power, when you first heard him

Yeah, yeah. But then when he got to New York, he got more finesse and started to playing fluid and legnit, you know, making pretty sounds, but with things that he played, was something else. In fact, to be truthful, I liked Don better than I did Coleman Hawkins. Because Don went as far as to join Coleman Hawkins, to analyze what he was doing and put with what he would do as well and he

was playing a lot then, you know, to be doing the things I tell you he was doing. And he had an occassion at Kelley's Stables where Hawk was appearing. He played two shows nightly. 12 and 2; the clubs ran until four o'clock in New York at that time. And Don was in the band. And well when Hawk would be getting to work, the place would be packed. People would be sitting there with the assumption that they were listening to Coleman Hawkins, when they was listening to Don.

And Hawk would get up and play his number, you know, his specialties and walk off when there was supposed to be a turn over. No one moved out of their seats listening to Don, you know. Oh, he was beautiful.
All right, you mentioned that Andy Anderson and Red Calendar gave you tips on the bass. Who else did you learn from?

The bass player that was with the Lorenzo-Picconny, his name was Vernon Gower. Now they use Elks to play Saturday dances at the L's Auditorium on Central and he'd let me come up and sit in with the band. He, would tolerate me, you know, and the band would be giving him the eye, you know, 'get on back up here.' He'd laugh and go and dance and get him a drink or something.
Who were you influenced by?
Walter Page.
Did hearing Jimmy Blanton have any affect

Later, yes. When I first met him it didn't have any bearing because as I say I was playing solos too but not the way he was playing them, you know. But when I heard him play 'Jack the Bear,' (laughter) that shook up Basdom. He was a one man rhythm section, you know. That's probably what killed him, over worked. See him playing Guard Dog for Ben Webster and Duke was generally in front of the band, not at the piano. And Sonny Greer wasn't no drummer.
Then "Sepia Panorama".
It was in Duke's band that Jimmy Blanton was assigned to take care of Ben?
Yes.
I've heard descriptions of Jimmy Blanton as a nice quiet, very friendly, nice person. Did he have any trouble? Was it easy for him to take care of Ben? Ben was kind of volatile, wasn't he?

Yes, but he respected Blanton and his musicianship. He says all right Bear, okay Bear, they give him the name Jack the Bear. So later years, there was three of them: Billy Strayhorn, Jimmy Blanton and Ben. They went out together.
Billy watch Ben too? Billy never --
No. Billy was hanging out with Blanton. So he was a tag along, you know, he was real, real passive, you know.
Yeah, he would never argue with anybody.
No, no. He would have a cocktail in his hands, just smiling, be just as gentlemanly (laughter).
Did you know Ben well?

Yes. I got to know him very well. But I knew Ben in Kansas City, but I didn't know his worth at that time. See I knew him when he was taking piano lessons through a friend of my mother's and I called her Aunt Thelma but Ben studied piano in Kansas City.
What was Aunt Thelma's last name?
Morris.
And Ben studied piano with her?
No, I think his piano teacher's name was Steven's if I'm not mistaken. The next time I heard of Ben he was with Teddy Wilson's big band. Did you ever hear of that band?
No.

Oh, baby. Talk about clean. It was too clean to be a black band. That's the reason it didn't last. Because he had all of the best musicians, he sent out of state and got musicians, you know, he got Harold Baker who later was with Duke, playing first trumpet. He had a famous trombone player out of Detroit, forget his name. He had J. C. Heard on drums, Al Hall on bass. What else, that's about all I can name off hand because I didn't get to hear the band in person,
I heard them on record.
Was Ben Webster always a heavy drinker? Like he was later on.
Ben wasn't a heavy drinker, baby.
He was later on.
He tried to. Ben could smell a bottle and get drunk. Really.
But he used to -- well, all right, I know he got drunk, I guess I don't know how much he drank.

Of course that's the reason he would get -- see we worked together with Raymond Scott, too. Raymond Scott, let's see Charlie Shoverers, Benny Morton, trombone player out of the old Benny-Mo ten Band, and Ben Webster, Specks Powell and myself.

Now when we would have, when we were allowed as much rehearsal time as the show was, right because a half an hour show, we'd have a half an hour rehearsal. And when we'd have a break, Charlie would head straight for the bar, Ben would be right behind him. Charlie would drink, drink, drink and Ben would try to keep up with him. Ben, I mean, he couldn't find his seat. Fall down, knock over the Bandstand, knock over his music stand, his chair. (Laughter). So Raymond Scott called Ben over, he says Ben, he says, don't go out with Charlie, he says, when Charlie plays, his playing is like a graph, it goes up which is unusual because trumpet players tongues get slow when they get
drunk. Charlie says his would get faster. (Laughter). Ben couldn't play a note, his chart would go down. So Ben told say please stop hanging out with Charlie.
Where was that?
CBS in New York. This is the band that Perry Como was the vocalist with and Raymond Scott's present wife.
Dorothy Collins.
Yes, well she was adopted. Raymond and his wife adopted her. Then he divorced his wife and married Dorothy. Warlow, Harry Warlow, that was his real name. Mark Warlow's brother.
Back to Hollywood and the Streets of Paris you mention in your story about Big Sid doing the driving, Marlowe Morris was in the car. Did Marlo Morris play with you?

He was a pianist. A very good pianist. He played more on the stride type of piano playing. Using his left hand, you know. But if you had to swing, he could do that too. He could play some beautiful ballads.
He did quite a bit of recording didn't he?
Yeah.
You mentioned Carroll Dickerson real fast. What about Carroll Dickerson?
Well, Carroll was -- when I met him he

was a sort of rabble rouser. He drank and we had a club room at the musicians union. 208 in Chicago. He was always all mouth all the time, you know. If he got a gig, he would get him a bunch together. He never played, sit in front of the band and conduct it.
You mentioned Erskin Tate.
Yes, well Erskin was the violinist, but he didn't play when I worked with him. He conducted. He would just get a group together and play a gig and that was it.
That was when you were where?
In Chicago.
And you mentioned the legendary Punch Miller.
Yes.

What happened to him?

And oh, he was so far ahead of his time as far as (chorus) structure. Oh! He was playing then what they're playing now. In 1941. And he had a heart attack and he was living at 107th and Central Park. I use to go by and visit him quite a bit. Yeah, good a -- old days.

So one night we were playing and he came up and he said, he stuttered you know, he said Jh - Jh - Jh - John to meet you. I say okay. So I laid my bass down. Went back to the back bar, Billie Holiday is standing there. I didn't recognize her, in fact I don't recall having seen her picture, but I heard her records out here before I ever left here. The first record I recall having heard her sing was "Sun Bonnet Blue and the Yellow Straw Hat." And he says "John Simmons, Billie Holiday," I say Wow! I say I sure have admired your work down through the years before I ever become a musician, I admired your work. She say oh man, she laughed and said give him a drink. So I had a brandy alexander. We stood there and talked. Eddie came back and say all right let's go back. She say you all go back I'm talking to John. So we stood there and talked.

She say, you know, I never noticed a bass before, she said "I never heard a bass before," she said I-she just took it for granted that that was something that was supposed to be in the band. She said "I've had a whole lot of bass players and I never heard any of them, but she said "I heard you." She said "to-
night when you get off, why don't you come by the Three Deuces to pick me up. I say what time you get off, she say oh I get off around about three but I'll wait until you come. I say okay.

So I went after her. I'm walking in. She's walking out with company. She bowed her head. I say that's all right, some other time, you know. So I knew some of the musicians on the street anyway. So I hung out with them. Went around the corner, got the last drink before they closed up.
And the next night, I'm down in the Village Vanguard, she showed up down there and collected me.
After work?

Yeah. She was there when I got off. She claimed me. I say wow! Ain't this something! Here's someone I've admired for years, has turned out like this. I've got to go for her. Wow! I'm not going to be no Mr. Holiday, I'm still going to maintain myself, you know. My dignity. I'm John Simmons, I mean I'm not as great a bass player as she is a singer, but I still want to be known as John Simmons, the bassist. Not John Simmons, Lady Day's man, you know. So she worked across Onyx the street at the Mike (E) [Osserman] Club for... Osserman, I think, was his last name. And I was over here across the street with Sammy Kaye and Alexander. What is his first name? I can't think of his first name.
Anyway when we got off of work at night. Oh, I'm getting before the thing. When she collected me that night, off

the job, she took me to her mother's apartment, you know. And where she had to sleep, I just couldn't picture it. It was off the living room, it was a clothes closet with glassed doors, you know square glass and she had curtains in there and clothes. A little small bed, hospital size bed. And she wanted me to go to bed with her. Momma was in the living room, sleeping on the couch. I say I can't make it. She's making propositions, telling me what all I had if I had her. I didn't have to go anywhere to look for anything. I say yeah, okay. Bess, I is your man (Laughter).

So, you know, the next day. The next night rather, got off from work, she came across the street and collected me and told a cab driver where to go. She had been out all day getting an apartment. Right around the corner from where Nat Jaffe lived before he died. On 107th Street and between Central Park West and Amsterdam on the fourth floor. Elevator service, but the elevator didn't work. So when we got home the first night, I'm home, she come home later. She say I thought I run into you up at Uptown House. And I tore into her. I say you didn't go anywhere looking for me. You know where we live, you find me here. You know, she didn't do that anymore.

She had been accustomed to whipping her men, you know and they had been holding her back -- "Lady don't do that." She scratching them and tearing their clothes off and all. But I double up my fists and knock her out. (Laughter). She say

"Don't fool with John Simmons, he's crazy." (Laughter). Because I just couldn't stand that you know. No. If we're going to have a fight, let's do it now and get it over with, you know. You whip me or I whip you. And then it's all forgotten, it's all over with, you know.

But come to find out, she was masochist, you know. She was doing things to make me fight her, you know, to go to bed. She'd say things to me like, I was her little boy. I'd say what and we'd be into it again. And I'd be doing exactly what she wanted me to do. I'd say all right.

So one day, God Bless the Dead, Jesse Price came to New York. First person he come to see was Lady Day. That's where I met Jesse Price. So I was leaving out and I say man, come on and go with me. I went outside and got the bus down to 50th and Broadway. No, we didn't get the bus, we got the subway, I'm sorry. And come up on the 8th Avenue side of 50th street. And there was a pet shop across the street and went over and bought a cat of nine tails. Jesse Price was falling over car hoods in hysterics. So the man at the pet shop says, the state only gives us three tails. I say well I have a great dane that is very unruly, I say give me the three. So I say what time will he be ready. He told me. So Jesse, still in stitches. We went to the theatre on 42nd Street to catch a movie and every now and then at the movie, Jesse would think about it and put his hand on his head and just crack up laughing. He'd say man

you're something else. So no sooner we get back home before we could get to work, she had to go into her act. And I showed her this whip when I walked in, just like you show a dog or a cat, you know where he had piddled on the floor, you know, I showed her this whip and I hung it on the door knob. I'm tired of using my hands. And I caught her with this whip. She wanted to jump out the fourth floor. I hit her every where but in her face and the bottom of her feet.

And Monty Kaye, who's executive producer for Flip Wilson, he was running around, running errands for Billy and waking her up for interviews and for different things so he got an apartment next door --

In Oklahoma?

Yeah. For an elder cousin of mine that I admired, he was a young man of the streets, you know. And I'd always like to ride with him when I'd get out of school. I don't remember anything.
I think I said I went to Dallas to the football game. I couldn't play football, so I went with the band.
I don't remember that.

He walked up to me, he says 'hey, Jeff,' just like, saying hey man or hey baby or brother. At that time he says 'hey Jeff. Are you hip?' He says all right, come go with me.

So he's got his violin on his arm and goes on down to the pawn shop, pawns his horn, walks in the back of the pawn shop, comes out and we walk about a hundred feet and he opens up this package of marijuana. I say is that what you went

after? He says yeah. I give him a dollar. I say go get me a pack? He went back and got me a pack. Now all of a sudden it hits me "boing", this is what my cousin was doing, he was pushing marijuana to these pretty girls. This is why he was driving around, you know. So he'd get on the train and go on home that night. I turned everybody on in the band. (Laughter). And the cheerleading squad. The girls too. (Laughter). And the men's room was about four feet wide square, you know. Just big enough for you to go in and do your dues and get out, there wasn't room for two people to go in. We were in there, stacked up high, two standing on the toilet stool and two standing. And if you wasn't smoking, you'd get high anyway. Contact, you know. All the smoke in there.

So the assistant football coach came up to me. He says, I know what you all are doing. You better get rid of that stuff before you get back home, you know. I say okay. So I closed my eyes and then I became aware of rhythm. I heard the railroad ties, you know, the sound the train makes. The wheels on the rail. And I found myself keeping time with it.

So when I got back to Oklahoma, I went back into my old thing, riding with my cousin. So first stop I made, he lit up and I started laughing, he said what you laughing about? I say I know what you doing, man. He say what am I doing? I say you smoking those reefer. Well see, in Oklahoma they had added an R to it, not reefer, but greerfer.
Added a G to it.
Greefers. (Laughter).
Is the same cousin, cousin Thaddeus?
No.
A different cousin.

No, this was Sharpie. (Laughter). So he says all right after he had made his rounds. He says for Friday night, he says can you get out of the house. I says sure, I can get out of the house. He says well I'm ping to take you to a party with me. Well now my excuse to get out of the house on Friday nights was like I was a boy scout and we had a farm-a German was our scoutmaster, Leo Freemouth was his name, Troop 41 from the parish of Santa Monica, Santa Monica Parish, and we would go around in his Ford and pick up the fellows and we'd go out to the farm on weekends and he would assign each one of us a plot of ground to plant something. Teach us trail blazing, teach us how to swim, how to cook, when boy scouts, all of this is merit badges. Lifesaving and what not you know.

I went from tenderfoot to lifescout in one year. Just as fast as I could pass one test, I was right into another one, you know, you can't do that now. You have to spend a certain length of time on one. And I was working on my starout, when I left Oklahoma, so I went off and left that.
And I had planed, I called up the boyscout headquarters

here. I had my membership card. my merit badges and I had my second class badge. But I didn't have my tenderfoot of or my first class, or my life scout badge was on a piece of paper. Like merit badges they give you; they give you the merit badge, and the paper that goes with it. So they say well they don't make insignias now like they did then. I said well I'd like to come up now and pick up mine. I'm an old scout, boy scout, you know.

They say, what year was you in the boyscouts, I say 1932. They say, wow. I weighed something like 114 pounds. So that was my was way of getting out of the house on Friday night for the boys. I told my grandmother, I say Mr. Freemouth is taking us fellows down to the farm, but he won't be down here to pick me up, he wants to meet me on the corner of Greenwood and Orchard. Well that's the main thoroughfare in Tulsa -- Greenwood and Orchard. Greenwood, Tulsa, T-Town, the bottling ground ambulance run every minute. Just as soon as you take someone to the hospital they'd come back and be picking up somebody else. Anyway, I meet him and he takes me to this party.
[Cough]

He gives a signal. I guess a club rap at the door, you know, they open the door and let him in. I got in there and they had one of these huge dining room tables with all of the leafs added to it, you know. And everyone is around it, and glasses of bloody water. I say oh, oh, what have I let myself in for? You know, and I see them sticking these needles in

their arms and things. Well I can't chicken out. So I went on and sat down. He tied me up, which shouldn't happen to a dog. I wouldn't do that to anyone. Even through my addiction, I never ed turn anyone on. Never had any. Well at that time you could buy morphine in the drug store without prescription. Pure morphine, not morphine sulfate like they use here in hospitals, I mean pure morphine.

And it came in the size of like a cube of sugar. And you shave it off, you know. What you wanted. So I got loaded, started scratching and gigling. Of course I never had a feeling like this. But I didn't have any sexual desires, with all these pretty girls around the table.
How many -- so this was your cousin and his friends, how many people were there doing this?
Oh, I guess about 20.
Boys and girls?
Yeah, around the table.
Were they in your age group.
No they were in his age group.
Which was about how old?
Oh about 21, 22. So he and I after I started using, he'd take me with him. We'd break seals on box cars and furnish hotels with supplies, you know, in order to get more morphine. So he got arrested.
Now, in the meanwhile, his mother was dealing. And
that that he couldn't steal from her, he'd have to go out and buy from the drugstore. He and his brother were stealing all of her dope. The brother's name was Sterling. His name was Van.

Anyway, he got busted and got sent to McAlistor State Penitentiary and left me out there in the streets with an eight-month habit. And I'm a juvenile, I can't go into any drug store and get no morphine. (Laughter).

So I had to take it to the bed. Now, my Grandmother is working and my mother is working, I had the house by myself. So I feel like I had to have a bowel movement. I'd get up out of bed and sit on the side of the bed and then I catch a cramp in my back. I'd reach for it, it would then be in my leg. I'd reach for it, I'd get one in my neck. And before I could finish these cramps, I would have had the bowel movement there on the spot. Then I'd have to try and clean it up before my Grandmother get there. Then I'd start coughing and big bubbles of phlegm would be out in front of my face like a bubble gum. And it would pop and then I would go into nausea. And start vomiting. The house was stinking. But it wasn't stinking when my grandmother got home, (laughter) you can believe that.
How long did it take you to kick the habit?
About three months. I had youth in my favor.
But did you go through this constantly? The withdrawal?
Yeah, I stayed in bed, I'm telling you for three months. Because this is pure morphine.
What did your grandmother and mother think?

They didn't know it. They just thought I was sick, you know. So the woman that owned the drug store, Miss Ferguson, she knew that I loved malted milk with nutmeg in it, you know. So anytime that she had a delivery out that way she would always send me a malted milk. And malted milk and milk, you remember milk when it had cream on the top in the bottles. That was the only thing that would stay in my stomach, no solid foods at all for about a month and half before I could eat any solid food.
And then I was sorry I could because it wouldn't stay. Food wouldn't maintain the food value. It would just run straight through me. Well, I overcome that.
So now, when Billie started, I say don't do it baby. I say you don't know what you're letting yourself in for, you know.
How did she start?
Oh, here we go into this thing. A white boy from Dallas called Speck, he was freckled face. He had slipped up to her dressing room and made himself acquainted while

I was at work, you know. Across the street. And introduced her to a hyperdermic, showing how many CC's and everything and her being adventursome, she went for it. And every night that he came by, he was giving it to her free until finally she had to have it, then he was coming back and getting the money.

You know, saying I haven't got anything, Lady. Nope so and so has, how much does it cost, so and so. She'd give him the money and he come on back. But he'd take what he wanted first, you know. So one night when we had an electrical storm and she had fixed before she went to bed. And she would be wringing wet with perspiration. I couldn't stand to get close to her because there -- it would be uncomfortable for her, you know, this body heat.

So I started sleeping on the couch, but I didn't know that this is what was happening. All of a sudden in a clap of thunder and a streak of lightning and brought her up out of this sleep and she landed on her feet in the middle of bed and grabbed her stomach and ran to the bathroom.

She came back in, all nice and quiet and poured her a big slug of scotch, a tumbler of ale behind it. Went to the dresser drawer and she had a ten pound candy box of assorted pills, and she would just reach in there, she didn't pick out a certain one. Just some pills, tossed them up in the air and throw them down her mouth and chased it with ale. And then she might sit down and smoke a joint before she go back to bed.
So at that time, I could go to the lingerie drawer, I could get as high as two-three thousand dollars in her dresser drawer if I wanted it. But I had my own money, I didn't need hers you know.

But one night, I lost some money in a crap game and I went home and looked in her dresser drawer and you talk about trying to find a bra or trying to find the right socks, stockings (laughter) or panties, boy I was throwing things out of that drawer for an hour and when I finally ended up, I found ten dollars.

I say what? Now I know she's got it. I say well I'll being seeing you. So I packed up my bag and I just bought a brand new gabardine top coat, name dropping, from Phil Cromfields Store in New York. And I'm starting out the door and she's hollering, please don't go, please don't go. And like from the bedroom to the living room, we never closed the doors, the glass doors, we always kept them open, those little doors, you know, jammed between the doors, between the rooms, you know the little up lift. She tripped and caught hold of the coat tail of my go boarder coat that I had just bought and tore it right up the back near the seam up to the collar.

I set my bag down, took off all of my clothes except my shorts, just like I was going in the ring with Sugar Ray (laughter), I tried to kill her. Then I got the whip. I got tired of the whip, I got the brush and started pecking her in

the top of the head with it. She tried to jump out the window, I wouldn't let her. I say come on back here, (laughter). So I left. Every night, she was across the street, please come back, please come back. No good. No good. I played, I'd done what I could do.

But I think I stranded her, I think I should have stayed with her a little while longer. But having had it and know what it involved and could tell, I just didn't want to be around it. In the meanwhile, Charlie Parker had just hit the scene too. So this was the Vogue, you know, but she had never thought of doing it until this white boy had introduced her to it, you know.
What year was that?
Early '44.
How long had you and she been together?

Two years. So it ended up, I came out here. She was making long distance phone calls. I'll give you anything you want, I'll stop, please take me back. No good. Hang up in her face. So from then on, I was on all of her record dates in spite of that, you know.

I mean, she'd take time out between records and go in the ladies room, the powder room to try to get herself together. And she'd be in there an hour, an hour and a half. And the session would eventually run into a double session. We didn't mind that, it was money for us but Norman Granz and different

people was pulling their hair. It was running money out of their pockets. So I found out what was happening to her and I was sniffing cocaine at the time, you know. I had graduated from grass to cocaine. Well cocaine don't let you get greasy and what not, it makes you more concerned with your hygiene and your person, you know, how you look. But you get very paranoid. You can't stand a lot of noise.

And people would walk up to me and slap me on the shoulder. Hello John! And when they'd do that, I'd turn around and go upside their head. And I hit a dude, about six-two or six-three and I'd say, oh my God what have I done. Small as I was. So I'd have to take him with the element of surprise. First thing I'd do is stomp on his instep. He'd say 'ow' and start to jumping around on one foot. He'd put it down, I'd get ready and kick his shins. He'd grab them. He grab his shins now and I'd go to his testicles with my foot and he'd grab them and bend over and when he'd bend over, I'd go under his chin with my knee.

And then he'd fall flat ass back. And I'd get up in his face with the heel of foot in his mouth., And play orthodontist, take his teeth out, try to kick his nose off his face. Stick both feet in his eyes (laughter). People would say, 'John Simmons gone crazy. See he's just whipping a everybody.'
So one night. Roy Eldridge and Charlie Shavers were on the bandstand at the Three Deuces jamming, and Charlie was blowing Roy off the bandstand, you know. So Ben comes in and

a white Rolls, went around in a white Rolls, Lady Day and Charlie and I were in the booth drinking. Now Charlie is sitting up against the wall in the booth by his self. And Lady Day and I are sitting over together facing Charlie. And we're facing the door and the meanwhile, Charlie's back is turn to the door.

Say oh my God, here comes Ben, he's staggering in, he can smell the bottle, he ain't had no drink, he just smell one and he's drunk. Say watch your drinks. He comes over to the table and leans over. There's my drink, Billie's drink and rakes them off and Charlie's drink and rakes them off in Charlie's lap. Well you know, naturally Charlie's reaction would be to jump up, you know, to keep them from drowning, off of -- in a hurry.

Ben grabs Charlie and pulled him out of the booth and started to slapping him around the place. I say heh, Ben, don't do that man. Say I know you, John Simmons, you ready to fight. You've been known to whip everybody. Everybody your size. I got something for you. So he come out of his handkerchief pocket in his coat with a straight edge razor. And we're standing at the bar. He say I got something for you. Well the police, plain clothesman, let their presence be known. They was fixing to rap his head with the automatic black jack, you know. But they just -- but the bartender waved him off, say heh, Ben give me the razor or get out. I'm not giving you my razor. He

start arguing. He say look, Ben, you in my premises. I can kill you right here and nothing will happen. So Ben give him the razor. He says, on second thought, get out anyway and come back and get your razor when you get off from work, you know. See you going to upset the place anyway. You've had too many to drink. And I reserve the right to refuse you, you know so go on out.

So I got back on the job. I say hah, Ben, I say you do that shit to Charlie, I say you'll do it to me too. I say and if you do, man, I'll take a killing, but I ain't going to take no whipping. I say as large as you are, you know. There's no way. He mumbled something, you know. Gazed off into space, like he hasn't even heard me, you know. Well, I was ready for him. Never carried a knife, but I pulled my own coat. I say I'm getting so wild with this fighting, I . I won more fights on 52nd street than Sugar Ray did in the ring. Because I'm fighting civilians plus soldiers. See they sent all of the Southern soldiers north, you know, to brainwash them so to see Negro boys walking down the street with white women, you know. Naturally this put them in a fighting mood right away.

And they sent the northern soldiers south telling them broke their morale not to speak to the Negros you know and this This put everybody in a fighting mood. So one night, it's like D-Day. Kelley's Stables was on 52nd street between Seventh and Eighth and across the street was the Hickory House. Joseph Marsala

Mary McPartland, and Mary Osborne, they were over there a lot you know. It was -- Red Nova worked over there and the next block with -- which was Sixth Avenue and they renamed it that The Avenue of the Stars, between Sixth and Fifth, but the clubs was mostly about midway to the block and then they ended and then the 21 Club was further up the street. And that entailed the Three Deuces, The Downbeat next door, Tony's was like a supper club, they had a gate under the staircase, I forget this woman's name, Bill Holiday loved to hear her sing. She'd go in there when she wanted to get away from the everyday thing you know and hear her sing. She would make the tables, you know sit around the tables and there was the Onyx club that Bill worked in, Jimmy Ryan's next door, the Dixieland Joint. The Yacht Club, The Famous Door.

And all of a sudden in -- it was like D-Day. Everyone emerged into the streets fighting. At the same time. Out of all of the clubs. Don Byas his -- hit somebody in the mouth with his horn; Benny Harris had broke his trumpet across somebody's head. And Teddy Reig, you remember Teddy Reig, big and fat as he has been-- somebody had him down beating the hell out of him, (laughter) a little bitty dude.
Don't tell me it was Pee Wee Marquette.
you mean by that?
Denzil Best
No, but Dizzy Buff saved him. Dizzy broke a Coca Cola bottle across his, whoever's head that was on Teddy. But everybody was fighting. So one night. --
The same night that Ben had been --
No, no, not the same night. This is another occasion. This was just the happenings of the streets you know.

So one night, another night, not the same night, Billie and I decided to walk to Fifth Avenue around 51st and come back and we'd each smoke a joint, you know, a piece coming back and when we got back, we stopped about three doors short of Sixth Avenue. And she sit on sort of a stone stoop, you know before you walk up the steps and here come three big huge southern soldiers walking down 51st Street towards Sixth Avenue and they passed by us. "Boy, that girl's pretty! Sure wish we had her down home," say, "in fact, we ought to take her right now." I say "yeah, why don't you try it?" I'm talking to these three bruisers. Because I know she's going to fight with me if I have to fight. (Laughter). So we got up and started to walking, we walked on around and walked into the White Rose and they followed us to the White Rose. And when they looked in the White Rose and saw what was happening, (laughter) this is like a Black Man in the south peeping in a restaurant seeing if they served Black men. They looked in there and saw all this conglomeration of colors and ethnic groups, I invited them and said come on in. (Laughter). They walked out.
And then on another occassion, when Billie and I had a bout with some [sailors] We had been - - went to Vesuvius Res-
taurant. It's an Italian Restaurant on around about 44th Street.
Wasn't it Sicilian ?
Well it was still Italian.
Yeah, I think it was [Frascedelli's] (inaudible). Favorite Note.

MR. SIMMONS: It was close to Sixth Avenue. And all of a sudden it started raining, so we ran across the street to the bar and I stayed there. That's Billie's hangout, the bar. I get outside and I whistle for a cab and a cab would stop and before I could open the door some white man would open the door on the other side and jump in. Naturally the cab driver would take him.

So I called one back to the phone booth and called up Billie's job and had her to get the doorman to get a cab and come down there and pick us up. That's the only way we'd get up there because they was just taking cabs away from us, you know.

So while I'm making the phone call, she had this little wire-haired terrier named Moochie that someone had just given her the night before. And she had Moochie under her fur coat and this white couple was over in the corner with their backs turned to the streets, you know, facing the bar. Lady and I were in the midst of the bar, facing the bar and they were on the end with their backs turned to the bar. If you can visualize this. And the woman and Billie had a conversation going about dogs. And I got there just in time to see "Well
where I come from, we don't speak to Niggers." I say what did you say? "I said, sir, where we come from we don't speak to Niggers.
Who was saying that?

The fellow that was with the woman that was having the discussion with the dogs. He was her escort. So he says and if you would oblige me, you will step outside. I say yeah, right now, and I rushed around there and grabbed him by the coat collar. He wasn't anxious to go then. (Laughter).

So I started pulling on him and I'm pulling on him and Billie's behind him pushing him (Laughter). So we get to the door, he puts his foot behind the door to hang out to keep from going out. And she hit him in back of the head with one of these big thick diamond shaped ash trays. And that made him weakened a little bit and I snatched him out there on the side walk out there in the rain. And I beat a tattoo on that side-walk with his head.

And all of a sudden here come about six of his majesty's seamen. Running to his help. So I stepped back in the door way. And as fast as they stepped up, I would pop one and Billie stepped outside the door to keep from getting wet in the rain. And as fast as he would walk up, I would pop one, the next one that come up was hers. (Laughter). She would hit him in the face with the ashtray. (Laughter). So we had seven bodies laying out there in front of the bar. Finally a cab

showed up. We had done a night's work already.
So we got back. I went to my job. I was sitting in
the dressing room trying to dry off. Try to get myself present-
able for the bandstand. But her gowns was in her dressing room,
so she didn't have any problem changing, you know.

So the next fiasco that she and I had, the big one,
was down at the Vanguard with Leonard Feather had hired Big Sid Catlett
and I to do a record date during the band to accompany
Linda Keene, a Dixieland Blues singer and Avery Parrish was the
piano player. All he knew how to play was 'After Hours' because
he was as nutty as a fruitcake. Someone had hit him in the
head with a barstool out here and had knocked his brains loose,
you know.

He was doing good to be alive. In fact it had depres-
sed his brain and he had to have a plate put in his head and he
had to learn how to play 'After Hours' all over again. He was on
the date. Now, Ben got his price for the date, Sid come to an
agreement on his, mine was supposed to be confirmed, how much
I was going to make for the date because we had to ask for more
than what we had been charging, you know, because Sid was making
a pretty good salary where we were working. Ben was making sec-
ond salary, and I was making the third. So on the record date,
naturally we had to ask for much more money, you know, to pro-
tect ourselves.

So that Leonard comes down. He gives Ben a check, he gives Sid a check and walks out. I say Ben, "Did Leonard leave anything with me?" "No." "Did he leave it?" "No." I say what is that? About three weeks passed, I meet him on the streets. He passes by and refuses to even acknowledge my presence. Don't even speak. And I'd have to stop and watch him walk down the street. And me in my fighting mood, too, you know. I'm trying to psych this out before I grab him, you know.

In the meanwhile, the Esquire, mention on the Esquire thing was coming up, but I wasn't aware of anything like that. Even about to happen. And I was up for the first Esquire award, but I did myself out of that. (Laughter).

One night, on my off night, on Monday night we had a jam session down in the Village VANGUARD And I had just flown in from Chicago. I went to Chicago to get some grass. Had ten pounds of grass in a paper bag sitting inside my porkpie hat on the table. Everybody thought it was my lunch. (Laughter). Well, the most obvious place is that you see it, you know it. If you hide it, someone is going to wonder what you are hiding. No one bothered it.

Now Monty Kaye and Pete Gallaran and the other partner, they used to promote jam sessions on Sundays at Kelley's Stables. They were there. So we -- You've been in the Vanguard, haven't you. You know how you step down the steps going out on the further side of the wall. You come down and walk a step

down the step. I was going to go down the steps and Leonard was coming up the steps. And I grabbed him by his arm. I say Hey man, I say when are you going to be giving me my money? He say what do you mean, I don't owe you any money. And if you want to make an ass of yourself, you do it at someone else's expense and take your hands off of me you jerk.

And when he said that, I went right up against his melon. I broke his dentures, his nose, his eye glasses. Now the waiters to the rescue. Now the cashier was Max Gordon's brother-in-law, Max Gordon, the owner of the club didn't like him. And he was paralyzed on one side. The waiter has my arms pinned behind me and the cashier is going to throw a punch at me. I say well how do you like that. To myself. So by this waiter holding my arms behind me, I just tightened up and put both feet in his chest. (Laughter). He went sailing across the room. We broke up tables, chairs, all of the whiskey. The waiters come out on the losing end as a rule, you know, the waiters win. They didn't win that night because I had my punch with me.

And on the bandstand, was Clyde Hart. He was a pretty good piano player. He always ran around with Art Tatum and smoked a cigar. He was good for chord structure. He played somewhat on the style of Teddy Wilson. He was out here with Stuff Smith's band also. Same time that Cozy Cole was with the band. I think that band, speaking of Stuff's band. He had

Bernard Addison playing guitar. Jonah Jones, Cozy, I can't remember the bass player's name and Clyde Heart. But anyway, at the Vanguard, Clyde was playing the piano, Buster Bailey playing clarinet, Charlie Shavers was playing trumpet. Ben Tharp, Ben, Ed Thigpen's father, playing drums and myself. Now they all stayed on the bandstand. Lester looked up and said whispering grass, (laughter), didn't any of them move off the bandstand. They no fighters, no heart for fighting. Clyde Heart's got his fingers and things to look out after, Buster Bailey has got his embouchure and his fingers to look out after. So they ain't going to fight nothing. (Laughter). So about two weeks later, I get a summons to appear in court. Well the court that I had to go to was right up underneath the House of (Eden?) which is a ladies jail. I'd say around 14th Street in the Village.

So I go to court and they read the charges and everything. Now I can't tell why we were fighting, otherwise I'm going to blow it on Sid and Ben and all three of us will get kicked out of the union. I can't open my mouth.
What, well you told me this story before, you said you were doing it under scale, is that right?
No, no, over scale.
Oh.
Much over scale.
I thought you told me before that Leon-
No. I said Ben got his price, Big Sid got his price,
I mean last year when you told me about it.

No, no, no. No, not under scale, never. No, I always got over scale. I wasn't a scale musician. I never worked for scales in Chicago. Only time that I worked for scales in Chicago, in New York was Stuff Smith, my first job. And then little by little as I felt my worth, you know if they wanted me, I asked my price. If they just wanted a bass player, they'd go get someone else. This is how I found out what my worth was. Sometimes, I under played myself, you know and other times I over-rated myself too, you know. One in one hand and one in the other.

But, I went to court. And he won his suit. He said after we got outside, if anyone ask you what happened, just tell them it's a misunderstanding. He says come on over to the house and have a drink. Now, you know, I'm pouting like mad, I'm ready to blow up like a blimp, you know. I said all right. I go over to his house. He said what are you drinking? I say a glass of water, I'm afraid he going to give me a Mickey Finn, anything to get even, you know. But I didn't tell you the aftermath, after the fight.
I'm on the bandstand the next night, Max Gordon walks

in. I say oh-oh, he's going to bring me the bill. As well as he and I got along, you know, I say he's going to bring me the bill. He sit there until I got off the bandstand. Called me over. I sit down beside him. As soon as I sit down beside him, he threw his arms around my shoulder, (laughter) and shooked my hand and thanked me for tearing up the club and kicking his brother-in-law. That's the part that got it. Otherwise, I'd of had to pay for everything in there. If I hadn't of done something to his brother-in-law, he'd never of forgiven me. One thing that I did to his brother-in-law, he wanted to do all his life.

So he stayed there all night buying me drinks. And he's just laughing all night long. He say I can just see him on one side going across the room. (Laughter). He said, 'did he get up in a hurry, John?' I say 'no, he didn't get up in a hurry.' He wanted to know what did he do after that? I say he went back into the kitchen. (Laughter). Oh, he just laughed all night long. Bought the band drinks. Oh, he was real happy.

But the next night he had the place refurbished with tables and chairs and whiskey. But he was sure glad that I whipped his brother-in-law. And I was glad that he was glad to because I didn't have to pay for anything.
I thought that when you told me this story before, you said that, Lady was there that night?
Yeah, she was.
Oh.
(Recording interruption.)

I stand to be corrected. Yeah, so Monty Kaye and I say our group, we was fighting for dear life, you know, busting chairs over heads and things, turning over tables, throwing the chairs in the whiskey. Boy that was a blow out.

So Leonard and I we didn't speak anymore from then on. Cause all of the, like they had a thing in the Downbeat, the Three Deuces. He and George Simon and Barry Ulanov (Phonetic). They reviewed all records and the star ratings, you know, how many.
Metronome, wasn't it?

Yeah, Metronome, I'm sorry. And the ratings you know. Now any record that I was on, he'd say was a bad record or my name wasn't mentioned on the record. Once it popped up and down in the corner there was a notation. This issue Leonard Feather is on vacation in Miami, Florida. But I blew the Esquire Award by whipping him. Oscar Pettiford had only been in town a week and they gave it to him, you know. Not that he didn't deserve it. I say he's a hell of a bass player. But there were other bass players around by town besides Oscar, you know that had been there, that had roots there, you know. I mean, Milt Hinton was there, Al Hall, who else, Joe Shulman, my shadow, was Thornhill- Claude Thornhill's

base player. He loved me. It was, there was a nice sprinkling rankle of base players around town that could have played it just as well, I mean, but Oscar being a soloist, you know. They took him. I'll go along with it. Because I loved Oscar, you know, second to Blanton, solo wise.

Now I remember a record that he made with Duke that just gassed me, 'Airconditioned Jungle'. Jimmy Hamilton had the clarinet solo and Oscar played rhythm and melody right along with him, it was like a duet almost. He carried the melodic line and was playing the rhythm at the same time. And then this solo that he made on the cello Perdido'. Now that sounded like Charlie Christian on guitar almost.

And this solo that he made with Hawk and Eddie Heyward, 'The Man I Love', you could hear him breathing. Boy he could play. But now he's been not knowing anything about positions or tuning up or anything. He'd just pick up a bass, run his hand over it, find out where the notes was and he would hit it every time.

And the bass neck would just be gooyey from perspiration. I come to work one night, my bass wasn't there. I say 'what is this. Somebody stole my bass.' So I proceeded to get drunk. About 12:00 here comes Oscar walking in with my bass. Man, I had a record date to do and I'm sorry to have this overtime, but I couldn't get into the club to get my bass. I was so glad to get my bass, I wasn't mad or angry at him. I say

okay. And this happened again to me at Cafe Society downtown. I don't know who took the bass but they kept it all night, you know and the next night it was back on the bandstand. And I never carried any insurance on my instruments, you know.

Well anyway, where did we go from here, let's see. We've done the New York scene. Oh, there -- I came back out here to Los Angeles and stayed '47 and '48 and I had an occasion to sit in with -- not sit in but substitute Billy Eckst and his big band, Tommy Potter had pneumonia. So I went out and substituted for two nights. And I couldn't play but two nights. The second night I pulled a callous off my finger trying to be heard through this big band. This big band, band.
Where were they working?
Joe Morrison's Plantation. He had names galore in that band. And then I enrolled in City College to further my music.
In what? '48?
Yeah. Later years, well, something to do, well, you know.
I'm smiling because I was there then.
Yeah? So I took up --
Eric Dolphy I was there then too.
-- Yeah. I took up City College, it was junior college then. I took up piano and solfeggio and harmony and theory. Well I'd had harmony and theory in

high school but I was taking a brush up course on it, you know. But I really wanted to play the piano and I couldn't continue my piano lessons because my grandmother had a stroke and we had to bring her down to my house. My mother's house, rather. And she couldn't stand to hear the piano. So I had to give up the piano. I was renting a piano from Mannings, big red piano that used to be there on the corner of Western and Venice, I had to give up the piano.
And you were there during that year?
Yes, in fact Bob Fox was promoting Jazz Calendar Concerts on campus. Red Calendar played on campus, Eric played on campus, in fact Bob Fox introduced me to Eric.
Well, were you there when Les Brown came and played?
I don't remember, so I may have been. I worked --

Oh, yeah, the music room was --

That was on Monroe. Streetcar turned off of Vermont on to Monroe.
All right, well as soon as it turned, the first --
Oh you mean, the Student Union?
Yeah.
The Student Union?

Yeah. Well that's the -- where they let Les Brown play. But I never got any further than my classrooms. I always wanted to go over to the Broadcasting Room and the Jazz Room and what not but I never made it a -- over there.
The jazz room?
Yeah.
What Jazz Room?
They had a radio --
They had a radio station --
Yeah.
A radio building.

Yeah and then they had a jazz, like a rehearsal group over there. Not organized. You know. And the orchestra was the first thing as the car made a turn on Monroe. That was the orchestra room, right there on the corner and I ran into Don Bagley there and later played with Stan Kenton.
Dick Bock was on campus then, Dick Bock
who started what -- Discovery Records a -- with Albert Marsh. Discovery Records and Pacific Jazz. He wrote the Jazz Column in the Collegian.
Yeah?
And he used to give parties and Dade Marmarisa would and play at the party.

Uh-huh. Well I didn't know anything about that. Well in fact my youngest daughter's mother and her cousin, they always came to school with me. They wanted to play piano. So they would just kill time out on the lawn talking until piano time class was and that was after my harmony and theory class.
And the three of us would get in there and play these dummy keyboards, you know. None of us ended up as a piano player. And spend some time.
Do you remember any of your instructors there?

I think my harmony teacher's name was Scott. I don't remember the piano player's, teacher's name and I don't remember the self-teaching and sight singing teacher's name. It was right across the hall from the harmony and theory. In fact, I was in sort of a maze at that particular time. A dream world, you know.

Huh?

Who were you playing with?

Like the drummers especially, they loved to play with me, you know. After I'd been back - East and been exposed and what not, you know. They all loved me. John Simmons, is back in town, John's back in town, you know. So naturally, I got a plenty gigs. I didn't have to look for any gigs, they could come to me, they came to me.

I'd go on them for fun, you know. Renewing old acquaintances, old lang syne, (laughter). Or this was the year that King Cole started singing. '47. He lived in a house on Avalon just across the street. Like I lived on 47th Street behind the funeral home and he lived on Avalon across the street from the funeral home. And I went over there, and offered him some grass. And it was like the most highly insult he ever received in his life. I say well what is wrong and he say, well I am singing now, John, I had to stop smoking cigarettes and everything else to protect take my voice. I say 'your voice!' I say ain't that something. I say okay. Right on. (Laughter). Okay.
And then he started to doing things with the trio.
You Is or Is You Ain't My Baby." But the one that I liked was If You Can't Smile and Say Yes, Please Don't Cry and Say No." That was Timmy Roger's tune.

Yeah.

Yeah, yeah. Mother asked me last night, she say that building that's circular. Circular out there that's King Cole and Frank Sinatra. What building is that? I say that's the building that Nat Cole and Frank Sinatra built, it's the Capitol Recording Studios. And office building.

Well you do remember so and so and so. And I'd say I got that too and would add -- she would add a list for
me when I got home. Trying to help.

Louis' home town.
Huh?
Louis' home town.
Rock Island. Moline --

Moline.

So we strolled for two nights, and we had one more night before the week was ended. We'd have a day off. The -- not the week wasn't ended, but that was the day our day off would fall on. Ike?
Ike Quebec had joined us later and augmented the group.
Oh.
Which made it sound, oh, too tough. I mean, I'm just only sorry that we didn't record that group.
It was during the first week that Ike Quebec joined you.

Yeah. Boy, that was a beautiful group. One of the best feelings I've had in a long time on a bandstand. One of the few, you know. Where you'd look forward to getting to work. Couldn't get to work fast enough, you know. Because every night someone was inventing something new and they were falling right in line. It was like ESP, reading one another's mind. Everybody knew what they was going to do, you know. It was a beautiful job, but I guess my mouth messed it up. As I said, Charlie was buying the tickets and I suggested to Ike, let's go over to the commissary and get some sandwiches. Well, the waitress there, she was busy, involved with a -- verbal conversations with the engineer, the fireman, the stoker, whoever he is that rides with the engineer. The pullman porters, the conductors, everyone but Ike and I. They're paying us no mind. Well, at this point I'm pretty irritated, you know. Ike's standing there. He's not showing any emotions whatsoever. So I blurted out what I thought, you know. Tell

that waitress so and so and so. And at that particular time, you could hear a pin drop on a piece of cotton, and nothing but my voice rang out. So I walked on out. Ike didn't know how to walk out. He was glued in his shoes. He finally came out. So we got on an empty car, and we picked out a seat for ourselves, and the conductor got on and he says, "You boys will have to change your seats." We said, "Why? It's an empty train. There's no-one on here but us. Why do we have to change our seats?" He said, "Well, this section here is reserved for the conductor," he says, "there's a plaque there." If you looked close enough. I looked back and sure enough, there was a brass plaque. But it was tarnished so it was the same color of the wall, you know, that was behind us. So we wasn't that observing that we saw the plaque when we sat there. Otherwise we wouldn't have sat there, you know. So we got up to move as he had complied, and in our moving, he saw this bottle of whiskey that Al Barnes had given us. He said, "You'll have to get rid of the whiskey before the train moves." I said, "Why?" I said, "We're not GIs, and the seal isn't broken on the bottle." "You'll still have to get rid of the bottle." I said, "Well, man, you --", and he says, "Let's get the niggers off the train." I said, "Oh, my God." I said, "Charlie, he's going after the police." Well, if you knew Charlie, and he laughed, he said, "Oh, no, man. Nothing like that." bubble eyes . Whiskey running out of his eyes, he's

so full of whiskey. He refuses to accept that. No sooner said than done. Here they come from both entrances. "All right, let's get off the train." I stand up, like Richard Pryor. "What's the charges, Officer?" Bam. Blackjack, right in the forehead. I ain't opening my mouth any more. I wasn't going to set the table for them to go any further. So we got out of the seats and started getting off the train, as ordered in the first place. So they handcuffed Ike to me, and they handcuffed Charlie singly and put him in one squad car and put Ike and I in another one. So I'm leading Ike into the back seat. I got in first. I'm pulling Ike behind me. And just as Ike bent over to get in the rear seat, this policeman got up on his toes with a billy club, what we call a night stick, trying to hit a home run, a la Mickey Mantle, Joe DiMaggio, Hank Aaron, say hey kid, Willie Mays, you know, with a tape measure. He hit this man so hard that blood just spouted everywhere. It was like a Texas T.
Where did he hit him?

Right on the left rear part of his cranium, you know. And he got in the car and he's spouting blood all over the lapel of his overcoat. He said, "Look what he did to me, man." And I'm so disgusted, I say, "Yeah, he hit me, too, man. But he didn't strike blood." I'm real drug. So they take us to jail. Now, they've thrown the book at us. We are not aware of this at the time. They put us in jail.

When we get back there in jail, all of the cells was empty. So there was no need for any of them to be locked. So we're just walking in and around, you know, just walking the floors, pacing. Ike is sitting down in one of the cells, nursing his head, trying to stop it from bleeding, with toilet tissue, yet. So we were there I guess about 10 or 15 minutes, and our names were called. We stepped up to this little peephole, a glass window, I guess about a foot wide and about a half a foot tall, just a peephole, you know. So the fellow said, "We brought a -- these fellows wanted to see the one that looks like an Arab." Well, naturally, that was me and my beard and my mouth, you know. So after they had left, about 10 minutes after that, they called our names again. But this time we were ushered out another door. And when we looked up, we were in the courtroom, in a little box, where we're all squeezed real tightly. It wasn't even a fit where we could sit comfortably, you know. It was like sardines in a can, and we was all together. Ike's trying to pat his head. Charlie's skin is oily, and he's trying to get some oil off of his skin, where he'd been up all night. My skin was oily. I was doing likewise. I mean, who were we going to impress even if our skin wasn't oily? You know. The papers had released that we were resisting arrest, disorderly conduct, drunk.
I thought you said you'd been in there 15 minutes.
Huh?
I thought you said you'd been in the cell 15 minutes.
Yeah. But the Judge read off the charges and this was in the newspapers, and the courtroom was full of onlookers. They come in --
Well, how long were you in jail?

Well, it was early in the morning, you know. See, we had played that night and gotten off from work, and then we went through this thing at the station, and then being booked and being put in the cells. We weren't in there any time before the Court opened, you know? Broad daylight. As soon as day hit, the Court opened, because the newspapers hit the streets early and everyone had read it. They were there to see the three people that was going to be in the box, you know. A show. A little excitement for the town, you know. We shook the town up and the town shook us up. So he said, 'How do you plead.' I speak up right away. 'Not guilty.' Charlie doesn't say anything. Ike said, 'Man, come on, let's get out of here, whatever it costs us.' I said, 'Well, Ike if you plead guilty, you don't have any comeback with the NAACP in Chicago or the Urban League, they can't fight the case because you said guilty.' 'Man, no, I might have as much sense as you if I don't try.' He said, 'Let's get out of here.' The Judge said, 'Well, the fine will be --', two hundred and some odd dollars. Well, we took stock of our currency, and we

had enough to get out if we paid the fine. I said, 'Well, what is -- what would bail be, Your Honor?' Then it went up to three bills and something. Well, we didn't have enough, you know, to get out on bail, so we were forced to pay the fine. But I wasn't in too much of a hurry to pay the fine. I guess that was the right thing to do, but I was just stubborn, you know. And I had plans to fight the case through the NAACP, you know. Fair practice, you know. But they didn't see this, their way. So the Judge fined us. Now, I'm looking to walk right out of the courtroom. They grabbed us by the collars and led us back behind the judge's bench and give us mug shots, you know, taking pictures, you know, with a number in front of your chest and fingerprints. I said, 'Hey, man, you're out of line.' I said, 'We paid our fine. We shouldn't be back here.' I said, 'This is a misdemeanor.' I said, 'You're going through this thing like it's a felony,' you know. He said, 'Well, we reserve the right,' you know, blah, blah, blah, to do what we want to do. He said, 'After 30 days we'll return these to you if you want them.' So we got out of jail. Charlie and I go right back to the station to go to Chicago and get a piano player, after we got out of jail. Charlie's got a checkbook and we've got our tickets, from before this happening, you know. So we go on to Chicago, and Charlie said, 'I coughed go down to the Chicago Theater and hit Hank in his mouth, for causing us to have to go through all of this.' So nothing would do but he'd

go down to the Chicago Theater, and waited for Elvin, Ray and Hank to come off the stage. And we got word to the doorman to tell Hank to come out in the alley. He came out, and we walked out on State Street, and we conversed. Charlie said, "Man, why would you leave me like that, without saying a word?" He said, "I've got a good mind to hit you in the mouth." You know, Charlie wasn't a fighter. He says -- Hank says, "Bells." And this really infuriated Charlie. Charlie said, "Come on, man, let's go, before I end up killing this man." So we went up to the Pershing Lounge and proceeded to get drunk until the clubs opened, and then we started club-hopping, and we left the next morning.
Did you actually look for a piano player?

Yes. That's what we were club-hopping. We were looking for a piano player, a musician. We couldn't find one. So we had to go back to Rock Island without one. So we waited until, well, not the first train, but the last train that was running that would put us there on time to go to work. You know, just go straight to work. But instead of me getting off in Rock Island I got off in Moline, Louis' home. I said to Charlie, I said, "They might have a bandwagon there to meet us, you know, when we get off the train." He said, "Oh, no, man," like that. He said, "I'm going on, from the train station to the job." I said, "Okay, I'll see you there." So I went
on to Mr. Bellson's house.
MS. WILLARD: Mr. Bellson being Louis Bellson's father.

Yes. And when I got there he was crying crocodile tears. I mean, actually tears. He said, "The police has been here," and he says, "How do you say this word?" He couldn't even say it. I knew the word he meant, you know. He said, what are you doing with them here in your home? He said, "We have house guests." He said, "Well, you don't have any nigger house guests. Get them out of your house." Now, he said, "If this was my neighbors on either side of me," he said, "I'd kill them with my bare hands," he says, "but I've had my music store here for about 25 years, I've raised my family here and my roots are here, and I can't fight the police. You boys will have to go." He says, "I'm very sorry. Nothing like this has ever happened to me in my life." And he's still crying. He's sobbing. His shoulders is going up and down while he's talking, you know. So I got on the phone. Charlie's had time to get to the club. I told Charlie, I says, "Come and get your things." He laughed, "What do you mean, man?" I said, "Come and get your things." He said, "Well, you've got to tell me more than that." I said, "I don't have to tell you any more of anything. Come and get your clothes." He said, "All right, man. I'll be there in a few minutes." In a few minutes he was there, because you could go through all

three of these cities in 15 minutes. All he had to do was get a cab and he'd be there in five minutes. But I walked. Afterward, from Rock Island to Moline, with my bass and my wet clothes and everything else, getting out of town, trying to get out of town. But I got away from that club.
The name of the club was what?

[Alborn's] Horseshoe. A bandstand behind the bar, you know, at the end of the bar. It wasn't a circular bar. And a nice little bandstand, good acoustics, a nice band. I sure hated to see it go the way it did. Well, in the meanwhile, Buddy de Franco and Louis had received wires to rejoin Tommy Dorsey in Miami, Florida. For rehearsals. But they didn't send for Charlie because they didn't want Charlie in the South, and he was supposed to rejoin the band someplace else. So while we're in Chicago, Hank and Buddy leaves. And we come back, there's no-one there but Ike and Charlie and I. So now we've got to get a local drummer and a local piano player. So I guess we played about three tunes and the bartender comes up to me and he says, 'John, there's three gentlemen back here wants you to have a drink with them when you're finished.' Well, I went back to pay my respects, you know. I didn't expect what I ran into, because I got all my drinks free. There wasn't any point in my going back there, but I called myself being sociable, you know, and as I approached them they said, 'First, which would you rather be called? Nigger or darky?'

My feathers fell. I said, "Well, at this point, I wouldn't advise you to call me anything." Because if this had been in New York, I know what I would have done. I would have thrown a punch across the bar, and that's what they were hoping that I would do, you know antagonize me into doing something wrong, where they could shoot me down. Because I understand one of these policemen had killed a serviceman for urinating in the alley because he wasn't ten feet off the streets. The soldier wasn't too bad, because I told him I'd come in from the other end. But he killed him, you know. So I said, "Well," I said, "I'll have a Slippery Tit."
