And for those of you who aren't acquainted with this particular drink, it's composed of tequila, vodka and gin, three shotglasses, individually. And the bartender said, "We don't have any tequila." I said, "Well, supplement that with some Canadian Club." So I said, "Make that a Slippery Dick Nixon." You know, that was before his time, but you know, Tricky Dick? Richard, nicknamed Dick. So I drank the three drinks, I walked around the bandstand, got my bass, went downstairs, put the cover on it, gathered up my wet shirts that I had produced, you know, by being on the bandstand, perspiring, letting them dry out so I could launder them the next day. I gathered up all of my belongings, walked from there to Mr. Bellson's house. I'm not supposed to be there, but there wasn't anywhere else for me to go but there. So he sat on the front porch with me all night. So the next morning, I guess Charlie spent the night downstairs in the basement, you

know. But I didn't want to have any parts of the club, not any. Do you blame me? So I got in touch with Charlie. I said, 'Well, I just called Big Sid long distance to send me some money. I'm leaving.' He said, 'Well, man, you didn't have to do that.' He says, 'Tomorrow night's pay night.' And he gave us this night off, you know, ahead of pay night. He says, 'So wait for the banks to open and I'll pay your salary, you know, your week's salary.' So we go to the bank. Ike and I stand outside. By this time he has a patch on his head, taped on. And I had a skitty feeling. 'Ike,' I said, 'do you realize that we could be shot down right here in front of this bank, saying that Charlie's in there holding up the bank and we're lookout men, you know?' I said, 'Let's walk down to the other corner and get away from this bank.' So we walked down to the other corner. Charlie come out, he's looking up and down the street. We said, 'Come on down here where we are.' You know. So he came down and he gave me the money. So then I wished them all adieu and went to the airport. So now, as a rule, businessmen are on there getting their final touches to their business out of their attache case, you know, so everything will be in order when they land. But anytime they see a black, this is like a rabbit's foot. They relax. Everyone's not so attentive to anything that they've got to do. They just put down their reclining seats and go to sleep. The plane's not going to drop with a black man on it. You don't hear of that very often. So I got on the plane and just through

curiosity -- it was sparse with passengers, and I counted them, and I was the 13th one. I'm not superstitious, but at this point I'm expecting anything, everything, and nothing at all. You know, anything can happen. But, we made it to Chicago. So I went to the Pershing Hotel, which is on the South Side, and I woke Sid up. We proceeded to drink. And we must have drank all day. And they've got me telling the story over and over again to everyone that came in the room, you know. And I went to work with him that night. They were working at the Blue Note, downstairs.
Did you ever work at the Blue Note?
Yes.
What about Frank Holzfien?

Well, I go^t along with him because I didn't have anything to say to him, you know. He just talked to Louis, and that's all. The side men had no reason to talk to him. So our little Shangri-La was in Louis' dressing room, you know. And I never was too much on table hopping, because people could come out with some of the damndest questions, you know. Where were you born? When did you start playing? Do you come from a musical family? So and so, you know.
Who did you work there with?
Where?
At the Blue Note.
At the Blue Note, I worked there with Erroll Garner.
That was later. That was in '49 or '50.

Yeah. But I knew of the Blue Note before that, you know. So it just happened that Louis was there and I had worked with Louis prior to that. Big Sid and I. So we were all in the dressing room, telling jokes, as usual. I stayed two days with them until I could kind of unwind to go back to New York. Because, boy, you're talking about being tense, I was quite taut.
So what happened when you got back to New York?

Well, I stayed in the house for about two weeks, for fear that someone would say the wrong thing and it would bring out bad vibes with me, and then it would be physical combat, you know. So, when I finally decided to come out of the house, I got on the sidewalk, and it felt like an escalator. It felt like the sidewalk was trying to go out from under me, I was that nervous. So I went downtown that night and got a job immediately, starting the next night, with Thelonious Monk, playing in a mission for Dizzy's big band.
This is 1948, right?
Yes.
Do you remember what part of 1948?
Oh, wow. Well, it had to be the winter of '48, because we were wearing overcoats. What month, I can't tell you that, but it was the winter.
Uh-huyh.
Of '48. Because I told you Ike had his overcoat on down there, and how he Harry was trying to get --
Uh-huh.

Anyway, I got hired with Monk. Monk -- I don't know of any adjectives or verbs to describe this person. He was the father of the be-bop era. Like they had changed all of the charts around like, simple tunes like "Dinah" and "Sweet Sue", they had augmented them and changed them around so that the ones that wanted to come up and jam wouldn't be so quick to jam when they found out there was a different set of changes, you know. And people like -- they would have a Monday night party there for whoever was appearing at the Apollo Theater. They'd have a big banquet table and free food and everything. And one night, they called Henry Red Allen, you know, from Louisiana. He worked with Louis Armstrong for awhile. He worked with the Blue Rhythm Band for awhile. He got up to play. He says, "All right. Play, gates." Everyone said yes or nodded their head. And they started playing "What Is This Thing Called Love?" But they had some different changes. And Red Allen couldn't press a valve whereas he wasn't playing the right note. So he quickly put his horn back in the case and got off the bandstand. Now, this should have been done years before this, you know. Because this would have stopped a lot of people from stealing other people's material and everything else, you know. Like the black writers --
What should have been done?

-- was writing for Benny Goodman, making him a swing band, you know, like Edgar Sampson and Jimmy Mundy, they were writing all these swing arrangements for Benny Goodman. And down on 52nd Street they was letting the Caucasians come and sit in, you know, trying to steal our music. And a lot of them did.
Well, what do you think should have been done? Bop? The augmentation?
Yes. But no-one else should have been allowed to get on the bandstand, in order to cut out these jam sessions, you know, and let people learn the true black form.
Are you saying --
This is the American true art form.
But are you saying that --
From Louisiana.
-- the bop -- so-called bop revolution was --
A new era.
It was strictly conceived to eliminate people from jam sessions?
Yeah.
That was the only reason for --
Especially there at Minton's Playhouse where they were working.
And that was the only -- the sole reason for the new music?
Yes. See, and like Cab Calloway had just had this altercation with Dizzy.
Yes.

I guess you know the story behind that. They had played a lot on the bandstand. They'd throw spitballs. So one hit Cab and he swore that Dizzy threw it. And he was the physical type. He invited Dizzy outdoors after they got off. Dizzy laughed and said okay. So when they got off the bandstand and went out in the alley, Cab threw back and hit Diz and Diz ducked the blow and pulled out his knife and cut him across the buttocks. So he was fired immediately. But he had to pay him two weeks salary to fire him, you know, and passage back home, back to New York. So Diz made it a thing for him to be at Minton's Playhouse every night, to learn this new music. And Charlie Parker hoboed back to New York. If he had been there with Jay McShann, he would have got a taste of it when he was there. So he hoboed back to New York so he could get the rest of it, you know.
Are you saying that Dizzy didn't start it?
No, no, no.
Dizzy wasn't one of the originators?
No, no, no.
It wasn't Dizzy and Bird and --
No, no, no, no, no.
Okay.

Now, Klook Clarke was in this band at Minton's Playhouse. The band consisted of Monk on piano, Kermit Scott, tenor player, that's up in San Francisco now, Joe Guy on trumpet, Kenny Clarke on drums, and a bass player named Nick Penton. Now, Monk and Klook Clarke, they cooperated on these chords, because you see, Kenny Clarke, who was known as Klook Clarke, could play vibes, but he didn't have any vibes, you know. He had some bells. A little, small, compact thing, that he played bells occasionally. But he could pick out some changes and things on these bells, you know. And together they got this thing together. So Diz got it in a hurry. Charlie Christian was coming down and sitting in. A fellow named Jerry Newton was taking all of these jam sessions off on wire tape. They didn't have tape recorders at that time. They had wire tape. And some of them are floating around now, commercially. You know, Minton's Playhouse jam sessions. Charlie Christian, Dizzy Gillespie and Charlie Parker on them. And the first person to record be-bop was Coleman Hawkins. He had Dizzy in the band and he recorded 'Woody'n You'. That was one of the first be-bop tunes recorded. But it didn't go over. It didn't sell. Now, Diz, when he recorded it, he cleaned it up and put his own arrangements in, after he had learned the charts and everything. He arranged his own music.
* Jerry Newman. No, Dick Hecker - wire tape

And he had been arranging all along for Woody Herman for awhile, you know. So he comes out and he records "Hot House" and "Salted Peanuts", with a small combo. He and Charlie Parker and Al Haig, Stan Levy, Milt Jackson -- no, no, Milt wasn't on that session. And Ray Brown. "Hot House", "Salted Peanuts". I forget the other two.
How come they let Stan Levy in?
Huh?
How come they let Stan Levy in?

Well, Stan Levy was a real good brush man, but he didn't make the records. He was with the band, but he didn't record it. Big Sid Catlett recorded it. Now, this is something else that people aren't aware of. When you get a big band drummer, it's hard for him to tone himself down to combo level, you know, and vice versa. A combo man, it's hard for him to step into a big band and play forcefully and be heard. You know, because he's been playing at a certain level, a certain volume. But Big Sid toned himself down. He was always good. Whatever it was, he played it, you know. And played it well. And he played be-bop drums right off the rap, you know. He was on the first sides that Diz recorded. So Diz organized this group, and he had Al Haig and Stan Levy, Milt Jackson, Ray Brown and Bird. And they came out here to Billy Berg's. They followed Eddie Heywood into Billy Berg's. And they took the town by storm. And this was when Bird had his nervous breakdown
out here. He had to Camarillo for a time. And what was the tune that they recorded?
'Relaxing at Camarillo'?

Yeah. "Relaxing at Camarillo". That's where it come from. So when Charlie got back to New York, boy, it was frightening, because he wasn't a large fellow, you know, and when he got out of Camarillo he weighed over 200 pounds, you know. A vast change in his physique, you know, but not in his playing. He was popping keys something awful. And then somewhere in this era he worked with Earl Hines' band. Charlie Parker did.
Didn't he work in Earl Hines' band at the same time Dizzy did?
always full of 5-+
Yes.
Earl Hines told me that where bop came from, it was Dizzy Gillespie and Charlie Parker playing their exercise books backwards in their dressing room to kill time.
Oh, boy.
When I told Dizzy that he got mad.

So Charlie would go to sleep on the bandstand with his shoes off, and they'd have to nudge him for his solo, and he'd walk out to the mike in his stocking feet. And people would just laugh. They thought it was part of the act, you know. He'd go back to his seat and go back to sleep. And he was playing tenor in that band. He wasn't playing alto.
a no, they played flute exercises
They had a wonderful alto player, first alto man, in that group. He was an ex alumni from Roy Eldridge's band, when he had the Three Deuces in Chicago. Scoops Carey.
Yeah. I've heard a lot about him.
[Carey]

But he could take -- he was so windy, he could take such large breaths that the rest of the saxophone section couldn't phrase with him, see, because he would hold out until he would turn red in the face, you know, to get a phrase through, and they couldn't follow him. So he couldn't keep a job because of this. He was just too good, you know. So he was so good that he quit playing music and went back to law school for a year and got his shingle, and he put it out in the Loop. He started passing. He was fair-skinned and his hair was all right, so they thought he was white. And he was coming into the Capital Lounge where Roy and I were working, and he would hold his head down. We'd laugh.

Anyway, after Earl Hines' band, then Billy Eckstine formed a band, and he got all of the stars, you know. And he had -- at one time, he had -- let's see, in the reed section he had Dexter Gordon, Budd Johnson, Little Johnny Jackson -- I can't remember who the other one was. And in the trumpet section he had Dizzy, Fats Navarro, Shorty McConnell, and someone else I can't recall. I don't have total recall on the band. And he had two trombone players. One was Chippie Outcoul and another little trombone player out of Philadelphia. I never

did know his name. John Malachi playing piano. Art Blakey at the drums. And Tommy Potter playing bass. Well, Tommy got a case of pneumonia, so they called me out to substitute for him, and I had been laying off for awhile, you know, fingers were soft and everything, callouses were soft. And boy, it was a labor job the first night. So the next night I went prepared. I soaked my hands in powdered alum and hot water, as hot as I could stand it, you know, until they were water soaked, you know, like you see when you've been swimming too long, your flesh becomes water soaked, little dimples, little dents in it. Well, I didn't dry them on a towel. I just let these crystals dry into my fingers, you know. Fanned them and dried like that. And I went to work that night, no soreness whatsoever. Just like glass. No blisters or anything. The third night, I snatched a complete callous off, down to the white. So I had to give it up. I had nothing to play with.
Where was that? Was that here in Los Angeles?
This was here in Los Angeles, at Joe Marsh's Plantation Club on Central Avenue. That's where all the big bands was playing. Basie played there.
Whereabouts on Central was the Plantation?
It was out near Watts Towers.
107th Street?
It was almost that far. Not quite.
I would say it's near where Dootsie Williams has his place. Dootone or somewhere around there. Doots Music Center.
Yeah. It's around that neighborhood. And all the big bands came through town, they went there, you know.
That was in what year that you worked with B for a few days?
'48. That's when I worked at City College and things, you know.
Before you went back east.
Back east, yeah. Because I had three of my daughters, the only three that I had at that time, I had them out here with me at the time.
Back to New York. You were just going to the Royal Roost with Monk. Right?
Uh-huh.
Then we digressed into bop. Weren't you about to say something about Monk? About working with Monk.

Yes. Well, working with Monk, you couldn't follow him. He played between the keys, he played against the meter, and he would just play all over the piano, you know. It wasn't anything you could follow. If you didn't know the tune, you couldn't play with him. Now, if you're playing by ear, you had to listen to a melodic line. So I

trained my ears to listening to Bags, you know, Milt Jackson. I'd just throw Monk out of my ear. I just closed my ears to him completely. Of course Chuck Parham had told me years ago, in the early '30s, "Man, close your ears." I said, "Man, how do you close your ears?" He said, "Just don't hear it." I couldn't understand that at that time. But I grew up to be a big boy and found out how to close my ears.
Uh-huh. So you closed your ears to Monk, then.

Yes, I had to, because if I listened to him I wouldn't know where I was, you know. I had to resort to everything. I bought Chano Pozo out of cocaine and marijuana, and I'd go to the liquor store and buy me a fifth of VO and a fifth of Seagram's VO, and a fifth of vodka, trying to neutralize the cocaine. And I couldn't get drunk, I couldn't get loaded or anything else, but I was resorting to this to try to get way spaced out to keep up with Monk, and I couldn't catch him. So --
Chano was the connection, huh?

Yeah. So I had occasion to record some bop music with Thelonius Monk, which two of them I remember. One was "Mysterioso", and the other one was "Epistrophy". And we had a vocal on it. He yood Pancho did a vocal on one of them. I forget what it was. But it was out of his key and Monk made him sing it anyway. And Pancho's throat was sore for a week.

Couldn't get him to sing a note. He hurt himself. But at any rate, down through the years Monk has come into being more of a piano player, to the point whereas you can recognize what he's playing, you know, the melodic line. I heard him play "Just a Gigolo" as a solo. He could do it, but in little spots he would put Monk in there. Tink-tink-tink, you know. He would go off kilter for a minute, but he would come back to the melody, you know. But then, when I was working with him, there was never any melody. So Monk was a composer, you know. "Around About Midnight", "Ruby My Dear", and some others to his credit, you know. I can't recall offhand, but I recall playing quite a few of them.
"52nd Street Theme"?
Yeah. Yeah.
He and Dizzy are very tight friends. Right?
Yeah.
It must have been a joy being on the same bill.

Uh-huh. So, during that time, then, after Diz came back from Los Angeles, from where we are now, he came back to New York and organized this large band, and Gil Fuller was writing for him. And they had this arrangement, "Things to Come". Now, they shouldn't have done that, really, because it was so fast and furious, that was too much to lay on

the public all at once, in such a big dose, you know. They should have eased up on the people with it. When that record came out, it scared everybody to death. People started switching from alto to baritone, everything else. It was helter skelter, really. Ben Webster tried to play it and he couldn't get into it. He'd get tied up in it and he'd get so angry he wanted to throw his horn up against the wall. But Coleman Hawkins, he went right into it. He had a piano, and he'd sit down at the piano and figure out what they was doing. And he played it without changing his style whatsoever. Quite a few of them did it. Don Byers just grabbed it right away, boom. He didn't even have to go down to Minton's to get it. He heard them doing it and he started doing it, too, you know. Of course, this stopped a lot of musicians from playing, also, because they couldn't capture it.
You mean that one record, 'Things to Come', or the style?
I mean the be-bop era. They couldn't play the be-bop music, the changes, the charts, because they didn't know what it was.
And it was this big band that was working opposite you when you were with Monk?
Yeah.
In the Royal Roost.
Uh-huh.
And this was the time that "Things to Come" had just come out?

No. They had recorded that when they were at the Famous Door. See, that's when they was in the big band, at the Famous Door. And then they moved from the Famous Door down to the Roost. And boy, the Famous Door, they kept it hopping. They had Kenny Clark in the band for awhile. Then they had Joe Harris in the band for awhile. Joe Harris was a beautiful drummer, very underrated. Quite a few people aren't even aware that there is a Joe Harris. He came out here and stayed a little while, and now he's in Europe. He played with -- what is it -- Clark -- big band for awhile, because Kenny wasn't able to play for awhile. And I understand he had a stroke not too long ago, so that broke up the band. But at any rate, this "Things to Come" was so fast and wild, and if you're familiar with Dizzy's band, he would have the saxophones doing glissandos, and then they started shouting and screaming and tempos flying, you know. Boy. And Milt Jackson had a little Christmas set of vibes, and that was a funny instrument that he had. When he got to New York, he had a foot pedal, but he couldn't sustain, you know. And it was like real inferior metal. Little tiny keys, you know. He had to play with small mallets. Then when he started making some money he bought him a full grown set. Whereas he could play and you know, let a note sustain over until the others, or he could get vibratos out
of it. He couldn't get a vibrato out of his first set. Sounded like he was tap dancing.
Did he record with that first set?

Yeah. Uh-huh. But 52nd Street was the heart, the meat part of music, you know, in New York. If you didn't play on 52nd Street during that time you hadn't lived, you wasn't a musician. If you stayed up in Harlem, you just shouldn't have, you know, because you got lost in the shuffle and didn't anyone know anything about you if you didn't come to 52nd Street. And there were musicians in families that was born and raised in Harlem that had never been out of Harlem. I couldn't understand that. With all the freedom that they had in New York, to do things in New York that you couldn't do anywhere else. 24 hours a day something was happening. I was rest broken for two weeks at a time, for fear I was going to miss something. I'd go home and get in bed, my eyes would pop open, I'd get up and put my clothes on and I'd find some music playing somewhere. A jam session or something, you know. And if it wasn't that, I'd go to an all-night theater, you know, or an after hours spot or something. There's always something doing in New York. And I found out that the native New Yorkers were inferior musicians. Let them tell you verbally, they were the better end. But everyone there that was playing was from someplace else. Maybe from the south or from Detroit or Pittsburgh or Cleveland, you know.
New York was the place to be heard.
Yeah. New York was the -- how do you say? The big leagues.
Where did you go from your job with Monk?

I left there and came out here and brought one of my daughters out here, and two of them were already out here, and my mother had sent me a wire and said come home at once, and sent a ticket along with it, you know. And what I come to find out, she didn't send the wire at all. But a young lady that I had met through Billie Holiday. And she had gotten a divorce from her husband, who was the President of the Motion Picture Cameramen, and she flew back to New York, you know, to see if it was really real, and came back here and got a divorce without consulting me or anything, you know, and then sent for me to come out here, and then when I got here I found out what's what, and I almost flipped, you know. Because the woman had sent for me and I don't even know about it. So I really got caught up in a criss-cross. Not the cross, but the double cross criss-cross.
So, it was when you came back out here, that was -- was that still '48 or was that '49 by then?
Well, '47 and '48.
Yeah, but it was after you were here, going to school, that you were back there playing at the Roost.
Yeah.
Then after --
I had played Rock Island before the Roost.
Yeah, but after the Roost --
Then I came back out here.
Yeah. Then where did you play?
I came back out here with Garner.
Uh-huh. That's when you joined Erroll.
Yeah.
You joined Erroll in New York or out here?
I joined him in New York. See, he said if anything come of the records that I had a job.
Which records were these?
The ones we made out here for Ralph Bass, his first records that made him a hit.
And those were made --
Here in Los Angeles,
In what year?
'48, late '48. And Erroll -- about December, '48.
Do you remember what you recorded with him?
Oh, some of the tunes. "Cottage For
Sale", "Penthouse Serenade", "I'm In the Mood for Love", you name it.
What label were these on?
They weren't on a label. See, Ralph Bass just give us a record date and he took the masters and sold them to Savoy.
So they came out on Savoy.
They came out on Savoy. But we didn't record for Savoy.
Uh-huh. Who played drums on these records?

There was no drums. Yes there was. I'm sorry. The first day Alvin Stoller played drums. He played two days, I think. And the next day or day and a half, Jess'e Price played, till we finished the date. And I never thought that Jess'e Price could play that soft, but he was playing with brushes, so he couldn't play too loud, you know. And Erroll was playing an old upright piano that sounded like a barroom piano, you know, but he got something out of it, that barroom sound disappeared. He was milking the piano, you know, petting it. And I was asking him, I said, "Erroll, what was that?" And somehow he was under the impression that the bottom note was the name of the chord. He didn't know anything about inversions, you know, like you can take the bottom note and put it on the top, and the next note, you know, might be the chord

bass tone, but it's still the same chord. And he'd call me, and he'd say, "This is a B-flat," and I'd hit the B-flat, and oh, I was out of tune. I'd hit the wrong note. B-Flat. And what happened, we were playing in E-Flat and he played a B-Flat chord and he said it was B-Flat and we were in E-Flat, you know. So I moved my position over to his left hand, to watch his left hand. I knew the keyboard well enough to try to anticipate his movements, you know, just what section of the piano he was going to have that left hand in, you know. And I was a bundle of nerves behind this, reading this man's mind, you know. And people say, "Oh, you all sound so good. You sound like a happy marriage." I say, "Well." He took me through the wringer. And like if some celebrities would happen in the club, you'd say, oh, he's going low, now, he's really going to play for them. He would play his worst.
Why do you suppose that was?

I don't know. I don't know if it was stage fright or what. And then he would start to compose. He'd turn around to me and say, "You're on your own." I'd say, "I'm on my own? I've been on my own all the time." This is nothing new. Even the tunes that I knew I had to learn them all over again, because he had a home made set of charts that he played, you know, turnbacks and things. They weren't the standard changes. See, because he played by ear and he played what he heard, you know. So I had to learn bass all over again, his

style. So we eventually got it together and we had three pieces there, and for awhile it sounded like a band, because Shadow [Wilson] and I was accentuating with him at different intervals. I knew where he was going from one time to the next. Whenver he would start an introduction, he wouldn't play an intro. He would just start hitting the bass notes, not any particular ones, just a fistful of bass notes. Blop, blop, blop, you know. Real dissonant thing, you know, not intended to be musical, just a sound. And I knew what tune he was going to play right away.
(Laughter)
When did Shadow join him?

Shadow joined him in '50. This first drummer that he had when he came back from Paris didn't pan out. His name was Harold Wang. He was half Chinese and Negro. And we called him Chink. But he wanted to play with sticks, and by playing with Erroll Garner, he thought he was a star, you know, and he was going to be heard, and he was drowning Erroll out with sticks, you know. So at this time, Erroll asked me, he said, 'Man, can't you do something with him?' I said, 'No, I can't do anything with him. This is your group.' You know.
Erroll went to Paris in, what, late '49?
No, early '49, because he had been in the Three Deuces.
He played the Three Deuces in July,
because I was there.
With Oscar Pettiford and J. C. Heard?
I think so. I remember the Three Deuces had not had jazz, and they were restarting a -- they had not had jazz for awhile, and they were starting a jazz policy again with Erroll's opening.
Oh, really?
That's what they were announcing, and that was like about July, June or July, but I think it was July of '49.
Well, whenever.
And I think Oscar was with him.
Well, I didn't know anything about the Three Deuces starting a jazz policy. I had worked in the Three Deuces before I had worked with Erroll Garner.

Yeah. It had had a jazz policy during the heyday of 52nd Street, but by 1949 there wasn't any music, or there was very little music on 52nd Street and the Deuces had had some other kind of policy and then they were going back.

Well, around that time, they were trying to get rid of 52nd Street as Tin Pan Alley, you know. And they were going to tear all of those structures down and rebuild, supposedly, in order to get the musicians out of there. And as soon as the clubs closed from playing jazz they made all of
those clubs girlie shows.
I think in the Devices
Well, that's what had been along most of 52nd Street at that point.
Uh-huh. So they ran everybody off of 52nd Street like that, and so just luckily, they opened Birdland.
Bop City was open in '49.
Well, Royal Roost was the first one over there.
Yeah. And then Bop City.
Tape - 8
Pat?
Yes?
We were mentioning bass players the other night and I named off a few soloists? You know?
Uh-huh.
And other bass players that played unorthodox but still played in tune. And I left off a couple of bass players that I would like to acknowledge.
Who?

Doug Watkins and Joe Benjamin. Two good, solid bass players, you know. They knew their instrument and knew it well. But they weren't soloists. They were in my category, or I was in their category. We were all trying to be musicians, where everyone else was trying to be soloists, you know. And they played good bass. Joe killed me, though. The first
time I met him he was copying for Luther -- what's his name? Henderson?
Luther Henderson. We were working for Lena Horne at the time, together, and Joe was in the studio copying, you know, getting arrangements finished and everything and giving them the sheets.
Who was working with Lena Horne together? You and --
Luther Henderson.
Oh.

See, I joined Lena, first, Arnold Ross was the pianist. Then he left and Luther Henderson took his place. So I wanted to meet Joe. I went over and introduced myself to him. But I didn't know he was a bass player. You know, I thought maybe he was an arranger or just a copyist, you know. So he commented, he said, 'You play some good bass, man.' He said, 'I play bass, too.' And he was sort of stuttering, like, you know? I thought maybe he didn't stutter, but he was kind of excited or something. We come to find out he really did stutter, you know, sometimes. Not often. It wasn't a regular thing with him, but if you got him uptight in a conversation, you know, where he was really trying to prove a point, he'd stutter in a minute.
So he worked with Lena probably -- was it later on? I know he was working with Lena when I met him in
1950, out here.
Well, see, I was with her in '47.
I see. Because at that time Lena had Gerald Wiggins on piano, Joe on bass and Chico Hamilton on drums.
Uh-huh.
Where did you know Doug Watkins?
In New York. Well, see, Doug came there after Paul Chambers. After Paul Chambers came there, Doug followed. They both come from the same place, you know, Detroit.
Who was he working with?

Well, he didn't have a steady job. He was tiptoeing through the tulips, trying to get connected, you know. Until finally he got a job with Art Blakey's Jazz Messengers, and from there he went on. He was working with just about everybody, you know.
Like Joe did. Joe worked with Sarah Vaughn, Billy Taylor --
Yeah.
-- and Artie Shaw. And then of course he was with Duke for -- on and off for a long time, and then all the time.
Uh-huh. Yeah. Well, like this song with the same name, 'Looking Back'. Just about all of my compadres have departed, you know.
Well, not everybody.
I mean of that era.
Yeah.

Like we said music has a tendency to change every ten to twenty years. Like there was ragtime, changed to dixieland, then it changed to swing, then to be-bop, then the avant-cool school, and then the avant garde. And I don't know what they name it now, what they call it.
Back to '49, you worked with Erroll part of the time. What else did you do in 1949? You weren't with Erroll all of the time were you?

Well, as soon as he came back from Paris, I was from Erroll from '49, the latter part of '49 -- I think it was the latter part of '49. In fact, I'm almost sure it was the latter part of '49. Then '49, '50, '51, '52. And then I got arrested, and he was told not to come near me. It would do something to his drawing attraction, you know.
Who told him that?
Martha Glager.
His manager.
Yes. No relation to Joe Glager.
Uh-huh. She was his manager.
Yeah. She wanted me out of the way because I was telling Erroll the ways of the agencies, you know, and what they would do and whatnot. So with me out of the way,
She's still his manager.
Yeah.
You were arrested in 1952 for what?
Possession of heroin.
Were you using then?

I was sniffing then, yes. And I was drinking whiskey and smoking marijuana and everything else, and I didn't have time to find out if I had a habit of anything, you know, because I was using some of everything. But as soon as I dwindled down to just this one thing, the white horse that they say you mount and ride straight to hell, I got on that white horse, and he took me to hell. But I came back.
When did you first start using?
Well, after they took my cabaret card away from me.
Which was when?

Right after the arrest. I saw all of my salaries disappearing, you know. Where else could I make the money that I had been making money other than in New York? Nowhere. So I said, well, what is there left, you know? All I can play is off nights and three nights at the most in a nightclub and theaters. And fellows would come to me and say, "Hey, John, we want you to go into Birdland with us." I'd say, "I'm sorry, I can't take the job." So I'd have to recommend someone.

And after the recommendation do you think they were thankful? No. They didn't -- no-one even said thanks, have a drink, or here's five dollars, go and clean yourself up, or anything, you know. So I even stopped giving referrals, you know. Find them yourself, man. It's not my job, you know.
Did you do any time in '52?

No. No. I got out on bail, luckily. I had a friend, Gerry Mulligan. I had been sleeping in his studio in Carnegie Hall. He had an apartment, but the studio was decked out whereas he could spend the night there if he wanted to. So I was sleeping up there at nights. And at that time, he had an engagement in Philadelphia, and he was coming straight through New York and was heading straight to St. Louis. He had just bought a '58 Jag. '58? No, I'm way ahead of myself. He had just bought a '52 Jag. Like it was a four door. Do you remember that particular model?
No, but --

It was a small car. It looked like an economy car, you know. But anyway, he drove straight through to St. Louis. In the meanwhile he and his wife were going through divorce procedures, and he had an apartment on 59th Street, just across the street from the -- what was the name of that club? [Premier] I think was the name of it. It was run by -- I can't think of his name. Anyway, he had this apartment on 59th Street. So she had to fly down to St. Louis to get some

papers signed and he found out I was in jail, and they didn't write any narcotic bails at that time, you know. So he sent back $2,500.00 cash by her to bail me out of jail. She said, 'Well, I don't understand this. He wouldn't have done that for Chet Baker.' You know. 'And he's doing this for you, you know.' And at that year I had just turned 40. I said, 'Well, life begins at 40.' You know. So here I am. So she had me over to the apartment that night, and they had just had their first child, a son. They named him Reed.
Reeds, wasn't it?
Reed. Saxophone reed.
Yeah. I thought it was Reeds they called him.

Well, maybe they called him Reeds later, but it's Reed, as far as I know of it. And he had a deformity in one of his legs and they had it in a cast, to straighten it out. And she gave me the extra bedroom and I stayed there for a little while, but I felt very uncomfortable, you know. I felt a draft, by Gerry and I being good friends, you know. I'm living there and she having the dislike for Gerry, you know. So I got out of there in a hurry. But all the while, she was cheating on Gerry. She was going with Bob Brookmeyer. And writing Bob a check out anytime he felt like it, you know. And Gerry and Bob remained friends, you know. No skin off of either one of them's back, you know. When she'd make out the payroll

Bob got a little more than the others in the group. I never -- I don't recall having ever seen her again since then. I don't know if she remarried or what. Well, I don't know of any black or white or shall we say Negro or Caucasian, whatever words you want to use that's descriptive, I don't know anyone that would have done that for me. But at that time Gerry was using lightly, you know, and I would go up to Harlem and acquire heroin for him so he wouldn't have to commit himself out in the streets, trying to find it, and getting arrested and everything. So I was sort of protection for him, you know, in doing this as a favor. And he appreciated it so much that that's the reason he got me out of jail.
So you were out on bail.

And while I was out on bail I joined Herman Chittison and went to Florida. The Court said I could go anywhere I wanted to as long as I was out on bail, just as long as I was in Court on my due date. So I went to Miami during the '52-'53 Season, you know, winter, Hialeah, '52 going into '53, that's the season, you know, in the winter, and I played Mother Kelly's and Clarence Williams, the legendary Clarence Williams, pianist, he's in all these books, his daughter, Irene Williams, was singing with the group. And she was personable. And Herman Chittison was trying to keep her away from everyone, for himself, you know. He's an old man, you know, and he wanted this young girl, and he hired her because
she was young and pretty. So one night we were -- we had left the Mother Collins Club and moved down to the next block.
You said Mother Collins or Mother Kelly?

Mother Kelly's. That's right. I'm sorry. Out of Chicago. And we moved into the Riviera. Well, the band that we followed in there was Chris [Columbus]* and His Blue Flames, and that's where I met Clifford Brown. He was working with Chris Columbus. And Clifford wasn't a great person at that time. He was back in the back, trying to get his fingers together and passages together and everything. He was blowing on his horn between intermission all the time he was on intermission and go right back like we'd never had intermission, you know. Horn constantly in his mouth. And when he got himself together, he got himself together. Once he broke out. And his mouth, visually, it didn't appear as though he should play a trumpet. His lips looked like they were more suitable to play a trombone than a trumpet, you know. They were sort of on the thick side, you know. But he got those notes out of that trumpet. He just manhandled it, you know. Play fast as lightening. No technique, but he played from his soul. And they say geniuses die young, so I know I'm not a genius, thank God. And it's rang pretty true, because all those youngsters that I recall, like Jimmy Blanton, died young. Bud Powell died fairly young. And who else?
Bird wasn't very old.
* Chris Powell
Who?
Byrd.
No, he wasn't old.
You stayed in Florida how long?
During the season.
And then you would go back to New York?

Then I went back to New York on one of my court dates, and my attorney asked for a continuance, and the Judge, he was an Englishman. I forget his name. He said, "No, this case has been on the docket long enough. We'll dispose of it today." I said, "Oh-oh." All of my belongings are in Florida, you know. And it just happened that my youngest daughter -- now, I was going with her mother, she made a trip from here to New York, in case I had to go to jail, to bring all of my things out here to my mother. In the meanwhile, she got her a job at FAO Schwartz Toy Company there on Fifth Avenue, the biggest toy company in the world. Just to be doing something while she was there, you know. And I went to Florida and she joined me in Florida. And we were in this integrated hotel, the Lord Calvert. They later named it the St. John or something like that.
The Sir John.
The Sir John, yeah. Well, we were there for the opening of it, and it was integrated, you know. They had their own security guard.
A pretty place, I think.

Yes. A pretty place. The police wasn't called in there at all. It was out of bounds for the police, you know. So we had a swimming pool there, nice accomodations, like you could enter from the street into your apartment, or you could enter from the inside, by the swimming pool, into your apartment, you know. Apartment. What am I saying? It's one room and cooking facilities and a bathroom, a single.
But it was an attractive, well kept place.
Yes.
Billy Strayhorn showed me pictures of it.

Yes, it was very nice. Everyone was around the pool all day long, you know, and had a good time. So at the sentencing, the Judge says -- he looks at my -- what we call my rap sheet, you know, meaning my arrests. He had almost a book there. A pamphlet, we'll say, of my arrests. He says, "I notice here that you have good character references, good work record." He said, "I see that all the judges let you off lightly." He says, "Well, I'm not going to be the exception. Evidently someone sees some good in you." He said, "So I'm going to give you three years." And when he said three years my knees buckeled, you know, and he paused -- "Probation." And when

he said probation, well then I stood up straight. And then they found a pistol in my apartment, and that was the Sullivan Law. That was another case, right along with this one. And they disposed of that with a $1,000.00 fine, to be made in payments. So then he said, "When this Court is called," you know, "when this session is over, the District Attorney would like to see you." So I went to the District Attorney, and he showed me that he was an honorary member of the Musicians' Union, you know, and everything, and showed me his plaque on the wall presented to him by 802, and said, "Well, that's good." You know, I said, "Well, about this probation thing," I said, "I would like to have it transferred to Los Angeles." I said, "Since I have been going through this case and everything, my mother and my kids and everyone are worried about me," you know. "New York hasn't anything to offer me anymore. I can't make the salaries that I've been making because they've taken my nightclub license. So, " I said, "I'd like to go back to my roots." He says, "All right. You can go." He says, "When are you leaving?" I said, "Well, I'm waiting for the money to come and I'll be leaving." And I had the money in my pocket then. You know, then sent me $400.00 in Miami to pay my hotel bill and fly to New York. They didn't have any direct flights at that time from Miami to New York. SIMMONS: (Laughter)
Who sent you this money? Oh, all right.
So I went to New York and I stayed in
New York about three or four days, and then I came on out here.
By then was that '53?
Yeah. '53.
So did you play out here then?

No, because all of the groups were organized and all the fellows that I had played with prior to my leaving California wasn't playing music anymore. They were in the Post Office, or they was running on the road, on the trains, or they had retired or something. They had departed, or something had happened to them, and they weren't playing music anymore. So the youngsters out here, they didn't know anything about me, me spending all of my time in New York, you know. So I was just another musician as far as they were concerned. And at that time, the union had just merged and they had a party over at the old Florentine Gardens for the merger.
Uh-huh. On Hollywood Boulevard.

Yes. And I ran into a couple of my old cronies. Red Calendar was over there with Jerry Fielding. He played, you know. Different bands got up and played, you know. And I said, 'Well, this looks all right.' So I joined the union, but I didn't get any jobs, because I didn't know anyone, you know, other than the fellows who were appearing down at the Lighthouse, and that was already organized. They had their men down there, you know, that was, how do you say it? Enconced? Is that the word?
Enseanced.
Well, it was Howard Rumsey's gig anyway, wasn't it? As far as bass playing went.

Yeah. But he stayed there so long, though, that everyone was under the impression that the club belonged to him, because he built it up, and he had behind his name being used, Howard Rumsey's Lighthouse by the Sea.
And Howard Rumsey's Lighthouse All Stars. Nobody ever mentioned that John Levine owned the club.

No. So I'd go out there and sit in. Howard would be glad to see me come, and let me sit in in his place, you know, and he'd get out and mingle with the audience, the public, you know. And at that time they had Bob Cooper and Stanley --
Frank Rosolino and Conte Condoli, were they playing out there?
No, they weren't there then. Was it Williamson?
Claude?
Yeah.
Or Stu?
The trumpet player.
Stu. (Williamson)
Stu. He was there. And the pianist, I think, was Russ Freeman, if I'm not mistaken.
Shelly played out there sometimes, didn't he?

Later. But I mean when I first got back there he wasn't out there. So I think Shelly took Stan's place, because Stan went into the photography business. You know, he stopped playing music. He found out he could make more money as a photographer.
He's a good photographer.
Uh-huh. So I got so that I just stopped looking for jobs, you know. And finally, Rex Stewart -- boy, you're talking about off the wall. He had a job out at LeCoco's Supper Club.
Where was that?
In Redondo Beach. Right on the -- what was the main street? Sepulveda?
Pacific Coast Highway?

Pacific Coast Highway. And Rex had a combo down there, him playing trumpet, piano player and drums. And at this time, Rex didn't have any embouchure. He couldn't play a one chorus melody without muffing a note, you know, splitting a note or something. And then he'd let the piano player finish it out. And he was just there fronting and jiving. And Christmas week comes up and he tells me, he says, 'Bring your bass out and sit in with us and maybe make yourself a job and we'll give you what the kitty makes, and if that isn't enough we'll -- I'll take a couple of dollars out of my pocket.' You know. See, and let him hear how it sounds with the bass player.

So for the first week, Christmas week up to New Years, I'm getting kitty money. So New Years night, I told Mr. LeCoco, I said, "Well, I won't be seeing you any more." I said, "I've been here a week, and I think that's time enough for you to decide whether you're going to hire me or not." He said, "What do you mean?" He said, "I hired you the first night." And he had been giving Rex my salary all this time. He said, "Wait a minute." He called Rex. He says, "Rex," he said, "I've been giving you this man's money and you haven't been paying him?" Rex got real busy and he said, "Wait just a minute. I'll be right back." He went borrowing money all over the place, from his admirers and the band and everyone else, to get out of that hole. So he paid me in front of Mr. LeCoco. And we worked another week, and I went over to Rex's apartment. He was the caretaker of these units. I forget the girl's name that owned them. She was a dear friend of his.
Claire?

Yeah. Yeah. So he had charge of the units and his own apartment free. So I went over there one night and I took my girl friend's sons over with me at that particular time. And Rex comes up missing his diamond ring. And for a long time he accused me of taking his diamond ring, but he never said anything to me about it, whereas the oldest son is the one that got the diamond ring. And he's still a criminal. He's in the penitentiary now. Grew up, you know, in
nothing but institutions. And I guess he's institutionalized now. Today I was talking to his mother and grandmother today, and he's started a music program up there.
This is the son of your girl friend at that time.

Yeah. The older son. And she had four kids, two daughters and two sons. And I had met her mother and father in Denver when I was with Louis Armstrong, and she was just about seven years old at that time. I had her on my knee. I said, 'You pretty little thing, I'm going to wait on you.' And she didn't forget it, but I had forgotten all about it. So one night she asked me -- well, I was going with her roomer, and she was quite large, and I knew she was a woman. I find out later she's 17 years old. And I shivered all over. San Quentin quail. So --
After you worked with Rex here where did you play next?
Long and in between I played the Soho down in San Diego with Phineas Newborn, for five days.
The Soho. Was that what you said?
Yeah. And then I came back here and I had a few one nighters with Jimmy Rowles.
During this period --
Then -- yeah, during this period, because, see, in '53, Jimmy Rowles and Irv Cottler and I had a trio together,

over on La Cienega, just before you get to Hollywood Boulevard there's a club over there, and Jack Palance used to sit in a booth every night, (Unintelligible), and we kept the place packed all the time. We were playing all of Count Basie's tunes, you know, "Jiving at Five", and --
What was the name of that? I don't remember that.

I can't remember the name of the club. I think it was the Celebrity Club. But when I came back out here, and I was getting these one nighters and things, the Clef Club was open at that time. And I went in there and I worked I guess about a week, with Eddie Shu , and Art Blakey had just closed, and Eddie Shu followed him in, playing the saxophone and harmonica, and Lenny Bruce was on the bill, so I met him. And later Kenny Drew, the pianist, took me out to his house, and I met his wife, and they had a newborn baby, and they appeared to be very happy, you know. Then time went by, and I found out what was happening.
Yeah. Kitty's almost 21 now.
Yeah?
Yeah. She and my daughter went to school together.
She should be older than that. '53?
Well, my daughter was born in '55 and she and Kitty are the same age. They went to school together.
'55. Oh, I was still out here, because I stayed out here from '53 to '56, till my probation was up.
I think you were telling me it was in '54 that you went to Las Vegas, for the engagement at the --
Oh, yeah, at the Moulin Rouge, this integrated hotel.
Which was probably -- was the first of its kind in Las Vegas.
Yes. The one and the only. The first and the last.
Las Vegas was a very distinctly segregated place.
And it was situated in the dust bowl, you know.
Which is over on the west side.
Yeah.
The section of Las Vegas with the unpaved streets, no street lights.
Yeah.
All like that where, when Negro entertainers would come to town they would have to find accomodations in private homes over on the west side.
Yes. That's right.
And there'd be no transportation over to where they were working.
You've been informed very well. You know your lessons.

Well, I was up there with Duke's band, and I know Duke used to stay -- he was allowed to stay in the hotel where he was working so long as he didn't register. His road manager, who was white, could register, and Duke could sleep there if he promised not to leave the room until time to go out and play the piano. And he couldn't use his own name when he ordered food from room service, and he had to pretend he didn't live there. But the band all had to stay in private homes. So that was the situation, when suddenly someone had the courage to open the Moulin Rouge. The courage or the connections.

Well, then, after they closed the Moulin Rouge down they opened another hotel, the Clark Hotel. And they had a setup for music, but they didn't have a casino or anything like that. Just had a bar, you know, and a bandstand. And the back room was a larger room with a larger bandstand, and they used that for rehearsal band purposes mostly. You know, the jazz musicians that was working on the strip in the main room didn't get a chance to play jazz, so they'd come over there and sit in with the rehearsal band, in order to blow steam off, you know. And then some of them was just learning to arrange, and they was bringing in arrangements, 'Play this,' you know, so we were pretty well occupied after they built the
I was down there in '62 with Louis Bellson. That's where Harold Land and I stopped. We had adjoining rooms, you know.
Was that when it opened? The Clark opened in '62?
No, it was open before that, but I had occasion to live there in '62.
Do you know when it opened?
No, I don't.
Well, now, of course, Las Vegas is open and anybody can stay anywhere, but in 1954 it certainly wasn't the case. Describe the Moulin Rouge, because I never saw it.
Well, the Moulin Rouge had a main room, and when I was there --
By that you mean a main showroom?

Yes. Dinah Washington was the headliner. And they had a comedian there named Willy Lewis. He was funny, but he was funnier offstage than he was onstage. He had a little skit, he'd come out of the audience, you know, and he twirled the baton, that was part of his act. He didn't dance. Just twirling the baton and talking, you know, and he was telling this joke about this fellow that was going to train this flea to talk. So he put this flea in a penny matchbox -- a penny. You can't get that anymore. He had this flea in there and cotton

for his bed and everything, and every morning he would open the box and say, 'Good morning, little flea.' Trying to get him to talk. So finally, one morning, the flea said, 'Good morning.' He said, 'Oh, I've got it. I've got the greatest act in the world.' So he took him to an agent and said, 'I've got an act.' The agent said, 'What kind of an act do you have?' He said, 'I've got a flea.' He said, 'Oh, man, we've got millions of flea acts.' He said, 'No, not like this one. This one talks.' He said, 'If you don't believe me,' and he opened the box and the flea jumped out on the desk and the agent jumped up and swatted the flea and killed the flea. 'A flea.' He killed his act immediately. I didn't see where that was funny, but after awhile the situation sunk in. He spent all this time building up this act, and just in a second's time his act opened and closed in a second.
Almost like the Moulin Rouge.
Uh-huh.
The Moulin Rouge had a casino, right?
Yes.
Was it an elegant hotel?
Yes.
In the manner of Las Vegas hotels.
Yes. It was built on the same plans.
Was it known who it was that opened it, who the owners were?

I never knew who the owners were, but they said it belonged to Joe Lewis, but it didn't. They were using his name to attract, you know, customers. And Marcus Haynes from the Globetrotters, he was one of the matre d's, too. He had left the Globetrotters, stopped playing basketball. And after that he went back to Oklahoma, to his home in Sand Springs.
And Benny Carter had the band there, right?
Yes.
For the opening, or what?
He had the first band there in the main showroom.
A big band?

Yes. A big band. And I missed that one because I was over at my grandmother's house. She had just had a stroke, and I was over there. No-one could find me. And that was the year that Wardell Gray came up dead mysteriously.
By the side of the road. He was working with Benny,
Yeah. No-one ever knew the complete story, because it's very well kept. Teddy Hale knew it, but he went to his death with it on his conscience, too. He never told the complete truth.
Teddy Hale, the dancer.
Yeah.
He was working there at the time that
Ward had died.

Yeah. Yeah. And they arrested him for conspiracy. He was in on it, you know. The shooting gallery where they were all shooting up. So he had just got out of jail and they put him right back in for 90 days.
In Las Vegas.

Yeah. And so when I got there for the second Benny Carter band, he was out of jail. So the hotel served a very short notice on Benny Carter and told him that they were going to pay him two weeks' money in order for Les Brown to come in, the main dining room. So Benny didn't give them any lip or anything. He packed up, bag and baggage, and told the band that that was their last night. And they gave him half of the money and told him to come back the next week and they'd give him the other half, you know, for the two weeks' pay. Well, now, Sweets said, 'Well, man, let's stay here. They want me to take a combo into the Casino, and when Benny comes back we'll get that money and we'll still be working here.' You know.
Sweets, Harry Edison, right?

Yeah. I said, 'All right.' So I'm around in the annex part. I've got me a room around there, you know. I'm not living in the main hotel. Someone came around and said, 'Man, you still in bed.' I said, 'What else am I supposed to be doing?' He said, 'Man, they've got trucks backed

up, they're taking all the money out of the casino, they're closing the hotel." I jumped up and said, "What?" And I'm looking forward to payday the next day, and they're taking all this money out of the hotel. The hotel's closed. Now what do we do? They had combos from all over the United States, some from Canada, playing in the casino, you know, alternating.
Do you remember who?

Well, they had King Kolax there. They had the Platters. That was the Platters' first job. And some group out of Canada. I can't remember the name of it. And they had an organist whose name was Jackie. Jackie Davis I think was his name. He was playing then like Jimmy Smith, you know.
What happened to him?
I don't know. Probably died. Because he was a very good organist. I don't see any other reason to stop him from playing or being known other than death.
How long all together was the Moulin Rouge open? Do you know?
Oh, it wasn't open hardly a year.
I knew it was brief.
A year at the maximum, and I don't think it was a year.
It doesn't seem like it was that long.
No, because it just had time for two bands in there, you know, so it was opened and closed.
I know they had announced a fantastic lineup of stars they were going to have there.

Yeah. Well, the results now, after they closed up the place, all of these performers didn't have any money to eat on, so the hotel served free meals to the performers and the musicians, and we all had to be in the dining room on time. If you missed a meal you couldn't come back and say, 'I'm hungry.' It wasn't like that. You had to be there and sit down and eat, everyone at the same time. So we're trying to get some money to get out of town, you know, a part of our money that was due us. And we didn't know which way to go, so we went to the union, and Harry Sweets Edison drove his Cadillac to the union and Kolax Coleax is sitting in the co-pilot's seat and I'm in the back seat. The union -- it was very large of them -- they collect more tax than anyplace in the United States, in Las Vegas, you know, off of entertainment. And they gave everyone $18.00, which was no more than a plane ride to Los Angeles at that time. That was as far as you could come. All they wanted you to do was get out of Las Vegas and then you could take care of your business from Los Angeles and try to get back to where you come from. But I came back on that $18.00, came back and got my automobile, took my bass home, got my clothes and brought enough clothes for three days and came
So you never got your money.

No. First they said, 'Well, we'll give it to a hospital and let them make a hospital out of it.' There's plenty of space there, you know, if they rearrange it properly they could have had a whole lot of rooms there, hospital wise. And they didn't do that. Then they said they was going to have it as a lecture hall, the main dining room, was going to use it for lecturing, you know. What type of lecturing, don't ask me. And for conventions. Speaking of having it as a convention headquarters for whoever came there and didn't want to live on the strip, they could come there and live cheaper, you know. So, as a result, they just closed the whole thing down. Now, in later years, the hotel part and the annex is open, but the casino and the main dining room isn't. So no-one's liable for our debt.
What did you do after Las Vegas?
Well, I came back here and Sweets and I went to work with Buddy Rich and Marty Page, at the Melody Room on Sunset Boulevard.
On the Strip.

Yeah. And we stayed there quite a while. And then when they left, I stayed on with Benny Carter and Eddie Beall, at the same place. And I went to work one night and they had a padlock on the door. My bass is in there and I had to get the bus home. Benny lived in Hollywood and Eddie Beall lived in Hollywood, so I had to get the bus home. And I got off the bus there at Adams and Western. I was crossing the street and as I got halfway across, here comes a truck down the hill, heading east, his brakes failed, and he hit me and knocked me down. And I just slid off the fender, you know. It didn't hurt me. But I laid there and let them pick me up and take me over to the curb and sit me down, leaning me up against the signal. And I sit there, and I limped over to the truck, got his name and his license number and everything, and he got my address. So the next day they sent an insurance adjuster out to see me. Wanted to know if I was hurt. Well, naturally, I was in my pajamas because musicians sleep late. He thought I was sick, sure enough, in bed. I told him, I said, 'Well, I jammed my fingers, which is my livelihood, when I fell. See, this hand is stiff, this one's swollen. Got a few bruises and got my suit

torn off me." It wasn't torn off me, but oil was ground in it so it wasn't any use. It was a light colored suit, you know, sort of an egg shell color. And they kept sending him around weekly, until I'd hired a lawyer. Now the lawyer said he would get something like 30-percent and I would get 70 percent if it's settled in court. Court battles you can fight forever, you know. And the trucking firm, too, if they had money to fight it with. So finally the adjuster came by and said, "Well, how would you like to settle out of court?" I said, "For how much?" He says, "$800.00". I said, "Oh, no." He said, "Well, how about $1,000.00?" I said, "Well, I'll go along with that, considering my medication and whatnot." I was glad that my instrument wasn't involved, you know. I said, "Otherwise, if I'd been able to get in the club I'd have had my instrument and it would have been broken up." So I bought me a car with the money. Didn't have to ride the bus no more.
Did you ever get your bass back?

Yeah. They had the man that cleans up the club, he had the club open and was cleaning up. For what reason, I don't know. But he was on his job. He had a key. Someone had given him a key to the padlock, so evidently he was cleaning out instead of cleaning up, you know. So after that, I went to Jazz City.
That's Maynard's place on Hollywood Boulevard? Near Western.

Yeah. Yeah. And worked there for awhile with Sweets. Buddy Rich wasn't in the band. And Sonny Criss Christ. And they had this girl drummer. I can't remember her name. She didn't work steady, but she worked maybe two or three nights out of the week. And the piano player, I can't recall who was playing piano. But my last gig there, like they were holding something like a forum of music. It wasn't jam sessions or anything like that. They would get up a hand-picked group, you know, and one person would be presenting it, you know. And this one person happened to be Sam Most, and he had this girl drummer with him, too.
Was she good?
Yes. And I spoke to her out here on the telephone somewhere and -- did I speak to her on the telephone, or met her? I talked to her in person out at the Times. That's what it was.
The Times Restaurant.

Yeah. I said, 'I remember you. I played with you.' She said she was a drummer. I said, 'Did you ever play Jazz City?' She said, 'Yes.' I said, well I played my last job there in late '55, going into '56. I left town about a month early, before my probation was up. My probation officer told me that I didn't have to report back anymore, so I headed on back east, and then someone else told me that they had lifted this cabaret card thing, and I went back all happy, and

I called -- from the airport I called Teddy Rerg and told him that I was at La Guardia Airport and on my way to Philadelphia until my probation was up and then I'd be on into New York. He said, "Man, don't go to Philadelphia." He said, "They'll arrest you if you spit on the ground, and they have the blue law there, too, that you can't work on Sundays." He said, "You better come on into town. I'll send Ned out there." Well, Ned was Erroll Garner's valet, but he was working for Teddy now, at this time. So Ned shows up, I meet him at the Braddock. He was driving Teddy's car, but Teddy never showed up. I got a $14.00 rebate off of my ticket, as I didn't go to Philadelphia. But Teddy was supposed to come down and pick me up and give me some money to get me an apartment. He was going to loan me the money, you know. I waited and I waited, and Ned waited too. He said, "Well, man, I've got to go." He said, "You just get on the phone and continue calling him till you catch him at home." When I caught him at home, he was in bed asleep, and he answered the phone and started snoring in my ear, and I'm whistling and hollering and screaming and everything else, trying to wake him up. And he's snoring. I said, "Oh, this is really something." So I had to sit up in the Braddock Hotel lobby all night long. The next day I said, "Man, why would you do that to me." I said, "You didn't show up when you said you was going to show up, and then I get you on the phone, and you answer the phone and snore in my ear." He said, "Is that what happened?"

He said, "I noticed when I got up the phone was off the hook." He didn't remember even talking to me, even answering the phone. So I got together with him. He got me a few record dates on his label, Roost label. And he was recording -- like we were the house musicians. Cozy Cole and Sanford Gold Goal, a piano player. And --
Whom did you record with?
We were the group.
Yeah, but --
We were recording with singers primarily.
Do you remember what singers?
Well, Beverly White was one singer.

And who else? They don't stick out too far. In fact she recorded several times down there, and one night she brings this male down there with her, it's her cousin, and he sings too. And she introduces him as John Hartman. She said, "Would you like to hear him?" Said, "Yeah." So Teddy got in the engineers' booth, and he walked over to the piano and gave Sanford his key and the tune he was going to sing. Now, at that time he was singing bass, low, like Rick out of the Ravens. He was singing that low, but melodically.
Well, he wasn't new. He sang with Dizzy's big band in '48 and '49.
But I mean as far as records, you know?
He never recorded, then, though, did he?
No. And I had never heard of him.
You never heard him with Dizzy's big band?
Uh-uh. Nope. Anyway, he went from bass to baritone, and he had a wide range. He could even sing some tenor. If need be. But he has never hit his peak. He's more of a supper club singer, you know.
Yeah, he really does it all. I think it has something to do with his reliability and personality, rather than his singing ability.
Really?
Yeah. He has a reputation for no show sometimes.
Yeah?
He is argumentative easily with the wrong people sometimes, like club owners.
Oh.
His performance is pretty consistent.
You mean he's a prima donna.
On occasion. Not all the time. But he's --
Temperamental artist.
And then he is said to have had a habit for awhile, which --
What?
At one point, around the middle of his
career, which lost him a few jobs.
Oh, boy.
But his ability's been there all the time.
Yeah. Well, you're telling me things that I didn't know. I should be interviewing you.
(Laughter)
Wow. Well, I guess I was at the other place when all of this was happening. Maybe I was out here. Or in some other city, you know.
So after you did some record dates with Teddy Reig, what else did you do? This was when you got back to New York. We're now to what, '56, '7?
Well --
What year are we when you're recording for Teddy Reig?
Well, I had recorded with him before, but not as regularly, you know. I had recorded with him when he had Bud Powell on his label.
What year did you record with Bud?
No, I said he had Bud on his label.
Oh. Oh, I see.
Bud was using Max Roach and Curley Russell.

And he had several other acts, you know. Music combos and things. On his label. And I do recall recording with Little Crying Jimmy Scott on his label. You know, Little Jimmy Scott? You've heard of him?
I've heard of him, yeah.
You haven't heard him sing?
I don't think so.

Oh, baby. Nancy Wilson tries to sing like him sometime, and then other times she tries to sing like Dinah. But he was sort of an oddball looking character. He was lopsided. One shoulder was higher than the other. His feet were too long for his size, his height, and he looked like he was suffering from malnutrition. And his eyes weren't focused properly, you know? Like one was off to the side, somewhere. Nothing beautiful about him but his soul. And his phrasing was out of sight. And he sang so high, you'd think that he was a woman. He sang with Lionel Hampton's band for a long while before he came to New York. He had soul, mucho soul. I think KBCA has one of his records. I've asked and asked, and nobody's ever heard of Jimmy Scott out here, other than that one record. I go to record shops and I can't find anything.
What happened to him?
Well, he stopped singing and got married and his wife gave him a son. So he just stayed at home and
enjoyed home life.
Stopped singing, huh?

With his wife and his son, yeah. So they finally begged him to come out of retirement and he started singing again. Like I've got one of his newer things, an album -- I've forgotten the name of it, but some of the tunes on it. "Somebody to Watch Over Me". "The Show Must Go On". "Somebody Needs Somebody, So Do I". "Everybody Needs Somebody and So Do I". And what are the other tunes?
You were talking about the gig with Rex Stewart and another one with Jimmy Rawles, and we didn't really talk about what year those were. Can we nail it down to time?
Well, I returned here in Los Angeles on Pearl Harbor Day. It was December the 7th. And --
Of what year?
Of '60. And I worked a job over at the California Club for a short space of time.
Was that in Santa Barbara?
Yeah. Santa Barbara. That was Christmas of '60. For a saxophone player, and I never got paid for it.
What saxophone player?
I can't remember his name. I hounded him. I went over to his house. I threatened to break up all the

furniture in his house. He says, 'This isn't my house. This is my sister's house,' and he disappeared. I don't know where he went to. Anyway, that was Christmas week, and then New Years, of '60. '61, I don't recall too much of a bang. I guess I was out of it most of the time. Outside of a gig here and a gig there. One nighters, you know.
Well, so Rex was '61.
Rex was '61.
I see. And Jimmy Rowles?
Well, I was gigging with him intermittently, you know.
In the '60s?
Yeah. Because whenever he had a regular group, Red Mitchell was with him, because they were sort of related in marriage or something, you know, so he used him mostly.
In the late '50s you weren't playing. Is that right?
In the late '50s, no. Because they snatched my cabaret card.
And then in the early '60s you were in California most of the time.
I was out here in the '50s, from '53 up until the last part of '55, December of '55. Yeah, '55. And then I was going to New York, you know, because my probation
was almost up and the Probation Officer told me I didn't have to come back anymore. And I wasn't aware that I had to go before a judge to have it finalized.
Yeah. We went over that.
And I got arrested in New York in '57.
That was when you did time.

Yeah. And then they brought up this probation violation. I said, 'What is that?' And the man told me I didn't have to come back. So these -- the probation officer over there says, 'Well, it's just a technicality. We knew where you were, you know, and everything, but you were supposed to see the Judge before you left.' I said, 'Well, no-one told me anything about it.' He says, 'Well, all you'll have to do is two weeks. And you've been in here that long, so forget it.' You know. So the '60s didn't hold too much for me here. Like I continued to use heroin, real heavy then. That's when I started mainlining.
In the '60s?

No. Let's see. It was in the '60s, yes. But like the idle mind makes Jack a dull boy, you know, and it's the devil's workshop. I couldn't get any jobs or anything. I was just hanging out with the fellows, you know.
You couldn't get any jobs because you were using?
Well, evidently, because a lot of

band leaders had the attitude that it was catching, you know. Like a disease or something, you know. And then you're unreliable. They're looking for you at work and you're out trying to acquire narcotics and you come in late or you don't show up at all because you're too sick.
Or if you get busted the name that gets in the headlines is the bandleader's, not yours.
No, I haven't found that to ring so true.
It happened in a lot of cases.
In all my cases they spelled my name loud and clear. Los Angeles Jet and The Sentinel and what have you. All of Johnson's publications.
They gave you good coverage.
Yeah. In fact, in the Ebony Magazine, I forget what issue and what year it was, but they had all the drug addicts in the centerfold of the magazine, The Ebony.
Oh, you made centerfold.
(Laughter)
In the entertainment business or just --
Yeah.
Oh, how nice.
Well, I mentioned the Rex Stewart thing.
That was '61.
How long were you strung out? From when to when?

Well, I got strung out in '53, when I came back here on the probation. I stayed strung out from then until I left here and went back to New York, I continued to be strung out, from '56 up until '60, barring the arrests that I had there and barring the job in Florida. I wasn't using. Then I came back out here in '60, still using, because I bought up some heroin to make the trip here, and I used the last just as we were approaching Burbank Airport. And I got here I didn't know anyone, you know. I actually didn't know any musicians, working musicians. All of them were new youngsters, cropped up in my absence from California. I twiddled my thumbs, goofed, and I said, 'Well, now, if I can sit this long and goof, why can't I use my mind constructively instead of goofing?' So I started getting ideas and then I'd get a good idea and then I'd get a better one and after that I'd get another one, and as a result, I didn't do anything but get ideas. Wouldn't react on any of them, followup, you know.
So when did you finally end it?

'66, I was tired. Like you spend most of your time waiting for the connection to show up. That's the biggest hassle in the world. You can have money and the man's never on the scene. You've got to wait and wait and wait and wait and wait, or else you get burned, you know. A burn is some flea powder, something you can't even feel, you know, and you've spent your last money for it, and where are you going to get some

more money, and you haven't felt anything. You're still sick. It's a horrible life. And a drug addict is undoubtedly the biggest fool that God created on earth, I think. From this standpoint, he doesn't know anything about medicine. All you've got to do is tell him it's heroin and it'll cook up and you can draw it up in a syringe, he'll put it in his arm. You know? And that's how all these hotshots and overdoses and things come about, you know?
But if you knew all this, and you said you argued all this to Billie, way back in the '40s, then how come you let it happen to you? Or is that an oversimplified question?

No, well I said after I seen that I wasn't going any further, like I wanted to commit suicide. Like people say it's a coward that commits suicide. I think it's a brave man that commits suicide, take his own life. Because I'm not that cowardly and I'm not that brave, you know, so I was commiting suicide the slow way, you know. I'd say, well, if I commit suicide, they will lift the record, the cabaret license off and someone will call for me and I won't be here, you know, to answer the bell, answer the phone.
It was temporary suicide.
Yeah. Well, it was a slow, methodical thing, you know. So I just got tired.
So your suicide didn't work out, so you
decided to call it off.
Yeah. But I've been spending the rest of the time trying to live. You know.
When did you develop emphysema?

'69. Trying to make a square dollar. Say work won't hurt you. It killed me. Because after all of these habits that I've had and all of the other things that I've done that was negative to my metabolism, you know, my being, none of them did the damage to me than that job and cigarettes. I let cigarettes knock the pins out from under me.
Is that what the emphysema is attributed to? Cigarette smoking?

A long period of time of smoking, combined with nerves. Nerves goes along with it. You can't have emphysema without being nervous, no, no. And then there's people that get emphysema without smoking, just by being exposed to a lot of smoke, you know, over a period of time. Now, like I started smoking when I was 12 years old. I was sniffing and smoking. Then I had an appendectomy, a ruptured appendectomy, it wasn't ruptured. I'm sorry. It was--my appendix had formed a -- a corruption had formed over my appendix, and they had to operate on me to get this poison out before peritonitis or gangrene or something set in. And I had an alcoholic doctor, family doctor, and he planted his knee in the middle of my spine and pulled my shoulders, and my shoulders was kind of curved

inwardly, you know. I couldn't straighten up, from this appendix thing hurting me so. And when he straightened me up, I fainted right there on the floor. And it started, this thing, to leak, and the Catholics sent me to St. John's Hospital over there in Tulsa, Oklahoma, where they didn't receive any blacks. There was only three blacks there the whole time I was there. One was a basketball player from a little town called Bartlesville. He was a good basketball player, but he got both feet broke. The way the fellows fell on him, the feet was broken in the arches. And another little kid that lived down in Tulsa got his leg broke. He was like a little scavenger. He didn't have any parents. Home was where he made it. He was just raising himself, you know, stealing and everything else. And he got his leg broke somehow. I don't know how he got it broken.
