Probably jumping off a train or something. And they sent him out there. But other than that, there wasn't no more blacks in this hospital. So the Sister out there, name was Sister Bonneville, she suggested that I chew chewing gum for my nerves. I said, 'No, I don't like chewing gum.' She said, 'Well, why don't you smoke?' I said, 'Well, all right, I'll smoke.' I'm getting the license to smoke, now. I can go home and smoke in front of my parents, you know, or ask them for money for cigarettes. The Sister says, all right, smoke, for my nerves. So now, I've been smoking from, let's see, 12 years old up to 59. Wow. Let's see. It'd be -- I started smoking

in 1930, slipping out smoking. Then '34, New Years Day, they had me on the operating table, in '34. I stayed in the hospital, I guess, about six months. They made this incision, and they inserted a bicycle tube in there, for it to drain out. Well, at that time they didn't have penicillin or any myecin drugs or sulfadrug. They didn't have anything like that. So I'm lucky to be here now, you know, for what they had to work with at that time. And instead of this corruption coming out of this incision, it passed by the incision and formed a pocket on the other side. And it healed down to the size of a nickel, which meant all of the corruption wasn't out. So they made another incision, and this time, instead of it coming out, it went back to its original position. So they cut on me the third time. This time, it healed, and I went back to school. I think I mentioned it on a previous tape. Went back to school and picked up my trumpet too soon and ruptured the incision inwardly, inside, you know, tore the stitches loose. But the years fly so you wonder where the time went, you know. Like from that day on, the doctor telling me that I could die from this or I could live to be a ripe old age, I lived every day from then on like it was the last one. You know? So I was a pretty bad boy from then on, you know? I did everything that come along. I was adventuresome and everything else, you know?
I think there was something else you wanted to add to the story --

Yes, to try to clarify the story with Leonard Feather and our altercation. This took place during the record ban, which was between '42 and '44, as you say. And it was either late '43 or early '44 that it happened. Because I had came to California in the Spring of '44 with Big Sid Catlett's group. You know, when this had happened, or shortly before.
And so what you were saying, the reason you couldn't testify in Court --

Oh, the reasons I couldn't testify in Court was because this was a black market record date, you know. We wasn't supposed to be recording. And Big-Ben asked for his price and it was confirmed. Sid asked for his price, it was confirmed. I asked for my price and it was confirmed. So when he filed charges on me, and I had to go to court, I couldn't tell the story. I was handcuffed, because if I had told that I had recorded with Big Sid and Ben on the record date, they would have been thrown out of the union as well as myself.
Did Parrish get paid, do you know?
I doubt it. I doubt it.
You said that you also remembered the name of the number that Big Sid used to --
Oh, yeah. (Singing), 'When the sun comes out,' but they built up this big introduction, you know, and they'd leave a space open and he'd say, 'Quit your squawking,
I hear you talking.
The name of that number was "When the Sun Comes Out"?
Yeah. And then when we got to the exhibition grounds in Toronto, he said, "TWA, take it away."
Tell me how you happened to play bass for a day with Duke Ellington.

Well, through this friend of Duke's, he lived up in my neighborhood. He said, "Duke will need a bass player. How would you like to work with him?" I said, "How would I like to work with him? This is everyone's dream, working with Duke." And he said, "Well, I think I can get you the job." I said, "Okay." So one day as I was passing, he says, "Be at the Capitol Theater in the basement for rehearsal." So I was working with Ed Heyward at the time.
This was what year?

'43. I got off from work that night with Eddie Heyward and went directly to the Capitol Theater, to the basement, and rehearsed all night, up to the first show. We did five shows that day. And at the end of that day, I was some kind of tired, and I went home. I went to sleep, had the alarm clock set. I haven't heard the alarm clock yet. I woke up about 5:00 o'clock that afternoon. I'd missed all of the shows. So Tricky Sam, Joe Nanton, he got a friend of his to replace me. And that's how I happened to work that one day.
The first -- the last day I opened and closed in one. So after that, was when I joined Raymond Scott at CBS.
You told me that you and Eddie Bearfield were the first two black musicians to be on staff at NBC?

Yeah, at NBC. Well, that was more or less a token thing because of the war, you know. It wasn't really because of our qualifications. I know I wasn't qualified for it, because I had never had a bow in my hand.
Well, how did it happen to be you that got the job?
A token.
Yeah, but how -- how --

Well, I was playing little off brand shows, you know, like they had a talk show, a comedy show, called The Three Rs, and Al Rinker -- is that his name? Used to be with Bing Crosby and Harry Barris when they were with Paul Whiteman? Well, he was Mildred Bailey's brother. He was the engineer on this show, and Joe [Rhines] was the conductor. He came out here and worked at NBC when it was on the corner of Sunset and Vine. And Irving Miller was there at NBC in New York. He came out here and worked at NBC.
But did you go over to NBC and apply, or did they come -- did someone you knew tell you there was a job or what?

No, I went and I talked to the contractor of the job. His name was Frank Vanione. And Spitalny was over him. But Vanione screened everyone and did the hiring, you know. And I told him that I had worked with Benny Goodman. They had confused -- they was confused with me working with some other bandleader with the name Goodman, you know. I said, no, Benny Goodman, the King of Swing, you know. Well, however, I played this comedy show in the morning. Then we had an Army and Navy game, whereas they'd have a fellow from the Army and a fellow from the Navy and a pretty girl to come up, you know, and they'd go through answering question things, and the one that answered it right got to kiss the girl.
How about Eddie Barefield? Did he start at the same time you did?
Yes. We both started at the same time.
Did you play the same shows?
Yes.
And you --
(End of proceedings as recorded.)
